Expose a fast dev evaluator (small batch subset) during the agent phase so trajectories can iterate on nRMSE, not only toy sine tests. Ship a reference generator consistent with the HDF5 labels or document the exact integrator used to create tensors. Prefer grading on method families with tolerance bands (e.g., pass legacy threshold plus optional higher tiers) instead of a single razor-thin continuous cutoff that yields 0/18 pass with little discriminative spread among strong solvers. For agent training, add tools/habits for grid-convergence checks on the actual (N, T, batch) schedule and for detecting when self-congratulatory unit tests diverge from held-out trajectory error. For efficiency-sensitive environments, warn that naive explicit FD/RK4 on N=1024 can exceed verifier timeouts, separate from accuracy.

reports.tldr: Verdict: medium. The task intends to test large-scale C-to-safe-Rust transpilation of an AVL order-statistic tree, but the official verifier is misaligned with both the prompt and the hidden reference solution: it always runs a 10M-op timing test under a 120s cap after cargo clean. Several strong agents passed the functional remove_bug tests locally yet still scored 0 via VerifierTimeoutError, so the trajectories teach more about benchmark harness design than about a clean, generalizable model gap.
reports.main_insight: This task–trajectory set exposes a split between the capability CRUST-bench appears to target—faithful, safe transpilation of a ~600-line pointer-heavy C AVL tree with order-statistic metadata—and what the run actually measures. Across 18 trials, every agent received reward 0: seven ended in VerifierTimeoutError after exactly 120.0s, ten hit the 1800s AgentTimeoutError, and one (mimo-v2.5-pro) finished verification in ~13s with reward 0 and almost no work (14 steps, 0 output tokens). The strongest positive capability signal is narrow: at least two frontier runs (claude-opus-4-7 trial 294f9901, gpt-5.5 trial 5bcb440d) implemented bostree.rs, compiled, and passed remove_bug and remove_bug_2 in-session, yet still failed official grading. Reproduction in the sandbox confirms why: test.sh runs cargo clean, deletes Cargo.lock, builds release, then cargo test --release including timing.rs (10_000_000 inserts). The hidden solve.sh explicitly removes that test from Cargo.toml because it is a benchmark, not a correctness gate; with timing restored, even the oracle implementation is SIGKILL’d around 90s on 2GB RAM. Agents who read timing.rs sometimes invested heavily in making it pass (opus reached ~9M elements by step ~35) while the harness never reliably scores that path.
reports.why_it_matters: Benchmarks that conflate correctness, performance stress tests, and verifier wall-clock produce scores that are hard to interpret for model comparison or training. Here, a capable transpilation attempt can look identical to a non-attempt on the leaderboard (reward 0 + exception). For future agent design, the trajectories also show that models do not automatically align local test commands with the exact harness contract: several agents validated with cargo test --release --test remove_bug but never matched test.sh’s full suite and clean rebuild. Fixing verifier–prompt–oracle alignment would immediately make pass rates more informative; separating functional tests from optional perf gates would clarify whether failures are semantic, Rust ownership, or infrastructure.
reports.evidence_from_trajectories: Outcome taxonomy from result.json: 7× VerifierTimeoutError (e.g. opus trial 294f9901: verifier ran 06:25:55–06:29:56, exception_message 'Verifier execution timed out after 120.0 seconds'); 10× AgentTimeoutError (e.g. deepseek trial 02a3d958: agent_execution ~30 minutes then AgentTimeoutError); 1× verifier completed with reward 0 (mimo trial 6970a264, no exception_info). Opus (294f9901): after implementing bostree.rs, step ~31 runs cargo test --release --test remove_bug with 'test test ... ok' and step ~32 runs remove_bug_2 with 'test result: ok. 1 passed'; step ~35 runs timeout 300 cargo test --release --test timing and logs progress to ~9M elements ('sanity check passed\n9000001 elements...'). GPT-5.5 codex (5bcb440d): fixes a balance/name shadow compile error (E0618 at bostree.rs:454), then step with cargo test --release --test remove_bug && remove_bug_2 exits 0 with both tests ok; still VerifierTimeoutError at grading. Deepseek (02a3d958): 58 steps, large bostree.rs edit with todo list through rotations/insert/remove, times out before a clean verifier pass. Minimax (2319c60e): 101 steps, cargo test exit 1 on full suite, later cargo test --test remove_bug exit 1—suggests partial but buggy transpilation. Sandbox checks: bash /insight/task/tests/test.sh on oracle code with timing in Cargo.toml fails timing with SIGKILL after ~95s; solve.sh comment lines 13–14 state timing 'can exceed oracle timeouts' and omits it from Cargo.toml.
reports.surface_failure_vs_root_cause: Surface failure: universal binary reward 0, often labeled status exception (VerifierTimeoutError or AgentTimeoutError). Root cause is bifurcated. For 7 verifier-timeout trials, the likely root cause is harness design—test.sh (lines 41–64) forces a cold release rebuild and runs the timing integration test inside a 120s verifier budget on a 1 CPU / 2GB container, which can exceed that budget even for correct Rc<RefCell> implementations (confirmed SIGKILL on oracle + timing). For 10 agent-timeout trials, the root cause is incomplete or incorrect transpilation of a large AVL/order-statistic tree within 30 minutes—agents were still editing bostree.rs, fighting borrow/rotate logic, or debugging failing cargo test runs. For trials where agents passed remove_bug locally (opus, gpt-5.5), the root cause of the official 0 is verifier–agent evaluation mismatch, not inability to satisfy the functional tests they targeted.
reports.intended_vs_unexpected_insight: Intended insight: frontier agents struggle with end-to-end C-to-safe-Rust transpilation requiring AVL balancing, subtree counts, select/rank, weak references, and bug-regression tests—consistent with 10/18 agent timeouts and long trajectories on environment/bostree.c (~600 lines). Unexpected but valuable insight: the benchmark’s scoring pipeline is not aligned with its own reference solution or with agents’ reasonable local validation; listing timing.rs in the instruction while the oracle drops it from Cargo.toml creates a hidden grading contract. A secondary signal: agents exhibit uneven evaluation awareness—opus and gpt-5.5 scoped tests and made progress, while others burned the full 30 minutes without reaching passing functional tests.
reports.generalizability: The verifier-alignment lesson generalizes broadly: any coding benchmark that bundles micro-benchmarks, cold builds, or resource-heavy tests into a short verify phase will measure infrastructure and test-suite literacy as much as coding skill. Improving agents’ ability to read the exact grading script and match it in final validation would help across Harbor-style tasks. The transpilation lesson generalizes moderately to other CRUST-bench / C2Rust tasks involving pointer graphs and invariants, but this instance’s difficulty is inflated by scope (~full tree implementation) and time budget; it is not as clean a probe as a smaller, verifier-honest slice would be.
reports.confounds: Major confounds: (1) verifier timeout_sec=120 vs timing test 10M operations on 2GB RAM; (2) test.sh cargo clean + rm Cargo.lock on every verify, adding network/compile latency unrelated to agent code quality; (3) hidden reference solution changes Cargo.toml to exclude timing while agents see timing in both instruction and initial manifest; (4) duplicate bin+integration-test targets warnings may add noise; (5) 0/18 pass rate prevents calibrating whether VerifierTimeout trials had correct code vs slow wrong code; (6) one trial (mimo) is a near-no-op and should not be weighted like full attempts; (7) harness/environment exceptions obscure semantic test failures in meta.json status field.
reports.implications_for_future_design: Align prompt, starter Cargo.toml, oracle, and test.sh: either exclude timing from default cargo test --release (as solve.sh does) or document it as an optional local benchmark with a separate verifier profile and higher timeout. Prefer incremental CRUST tasks (rotations only, then remove, then select/rank) with fast deterministic tests. Verifier should avoid cargo clean and lock deletion unless testing reproducibility is explicit; reuse build artifacts to measure code not CI overhead. Report subscores (compile, remove_bug, remove_bug_2, timing) instead of a single binary reward. For agents, train or tool-guard a final step that diffs local commands against the published verifier script. Raise verifier_timeout_sec or drop timing from gating if performance is not the construct under study; keep agent_timeout_sec proportional to expected LOC (~500+ lines safe Rust is unlikely in 30 minutes for most models today).

reports.tldr: Medium insightfulness. This hard ML-competition task exposes a real but narrow gap: agents conflate producing a valid submission.csv with winning a QWK-gated competition. Across 18 trials, 0/18 pass the binary bar (QWK ≥ 0.829), yet many declare success after format checks. The clearest signal is evaluation-metric misalignment—agents train and self-validate on RMSE or round-and-clip regression while the verifier scales quadratic weighted kappa between 0.748 and 0.829—combined with poor time budgeting (8/18 AgentTimeoutError at 600s).
reports.main_insight: The task–trajectory set reveals that agents struggle to run a metric-aligned, resource-bounded ML competition workflow. The verifier gates on scaled quadratic weighted kappa (QWK) with lower_bound 0.748 and upper_bound 0.829 in eval_config.json, meaning naive TF-IDF+Ridge pipelines that merely round predictions often score 0.0 even with a perfectly formatted submission. Trajectories show a performance gradient tied to how seriously agents optimized QWK: quick Ridge baselines cluster at 0.0–0.39 reward, partial ordinal awareness lands around 0.47–0.59, and the best run (gpt-5.5/codex, reward 0.832) explicitly cross-validated with cohen_kappa_score(weights='quadratic') and tuned decision thresholds—yet still missed the pass threshold. In parallel, 8/18 trials ended in AgentTimeoutError after spending most of the 600s agent budget on repeated model iteration rather than shipping an early baseline.
reports.why_it_matters: ML-competition-style agent benchmarks are increasingly used to test data-science autonomy, but this task shows that procedural completion (valid CSV, correct row count) is a weak proxy for capability. If agents systematically optimize the wrong metric or ignore hidden score floors, leaderboard-style evals will mis-rank models and training will reinforce the wrong behaviors. The trajectories also show that time/compute budgeting is not separable from modeling quality here: the strongest modeler timed out while still iterating, which means harness design must measure both quality and workflow discipline. Improving metric inference, local validation against the competition objective, and submit-early iteration would transfer to other Kaggle-like, forecasting, and ranking tasks—not just essay scoring.
reports.evidence_from_trajectories: Verifier bar: eval_config.json specifies compare_competition_ml with quadratic_weighted_kappa, lower_bound 0.748, upper_bound 0.829; scaled reward 1.0 requires raw QWK ≥ 0.829. Outcomes: 0/18 binary_reward=0; rewards range 0.0–0.832 (gpt-5.5/codex trial 5680a89b). Metric misalignment: Minimax-M2.7/terminus-2 (a3a22bcb) reads README, states QWK is the metric in step 2 reasoning, but trains Ridge with cross_val_score RMSE=0.7499, saves submission, and marks task_complete—reward 0.0. DeepSeek-V4-Pro/terminus-2 (58f38652) similarly writes TF-IDF+Ridge, verifies wc -l and header format, explicitly reasons “The task does not specify any accuracy threshold”—reward 0.0. Gemini-3.1-Pro/terminus-2 (6a921068) uses RidgeClassifier, waits on training, declares complete after format check—reward 0.0. Metric-aware success partial: gpt-5.5/codex (5680a89b) at step 12+ runs StratifiedKFold scripts with qwk(); step 32 output shows OOF ridge12 opt QWK ≈ 0.799 and combo opt ≈ 0.803; step 42 writes /app/output/submission.csv with tuned THRESHOLDS; verifier reward 0.832 (~raw QWK 0.815) but AgentTimeoutError at 600s. Claude-Opus-4-7/claude-code (567348ea) builds TF-IDF+handcrafted features+Ridge with cohen_kappa_score imported but finishes in ~5 min with reward 0.586—better than baselines, well below pass. Time failures: qwen3.6-max/qwen-coder (0fa0d45a) creates heavy solve.py with TF-IDF+XGBoost and launches it with timeout 600000 ms at step 8, then AgentTimeoutError with reward 0.0. gpt-5.5/terminus-2 (a5795dfe) only 3 steps before timeout, wrote_sub=false, reward 0.0—same model family, opposite harness outcome vs codex.
reports.surface_failure_vs_root_cause: Surface failure: every trial fails the binary pass (reward < 1.0), and 12/18 score 0.0 on the continuous metric. Many agents nonetheless believe they succeeded because submission.csv exists with 2597 rows and the correct header. Root cause is not primarily environment breakage or syntax errors; it is (1) optimizing proxy objectives—RMSE, default sklearn scores, or mere format compliance—instead of the verifier’s QWK with a high floor (0.748) and ceiling (0.829), and (2) weak time-budget management that spends the full 600s exploring models without guaranteeing a competitive artifact. Where agents did target QWK (gpt-5.5/codex), the remaining gap is insufficient feature/model quality to reach 0.829, not misunderstanding the file format.
reports.intended_vs_unexpected_insight: The task is intentionally a hard data-science competition (task.toml difficulty=hard; tags ml-competition) and the README in the sandbox mentions QWK, so the designed capability is competitive ML under CPU/RAM limits. Agents fail on that core capability: none reach the upper bound. The unexpected but valuable secondary insight is how often agents treat the README’s metric as informational while validating on the wrong score (Minimax uses RMSE CV; DeepSeek assumes no threshold), and how often timeout is the recorded failure mode even when the best submission was already written (gpt-5.5/codex timed out after step 43 wrote submission.csv). That separates modeling weakness from harness/time-awareness weakness.
reports.generalizability: Partially generalizable. The lesson that agents must infer or probe the evaluation metric and validate locally against it applies broadly to competition-style, ranking, and constrained-optimization tasks—not only AES. Threshold tuning for ordinal metrics is somewhat domain-specific, but the higher-level pattern—don’t train on RMSE when judged by QWK—extends to any mismatch between training loss and leaderboard metric. Time-budget thrashing generalizes across long-running agent tasks. However, the specific QWK threshold band and TF-IDF+Ridge recipe are narrow; fixing them helps the ML-competition task family more than, say, SWE or web-navigation agents.
reports.confounds: The user-facing instruction.md never states QWK, the 0.748 floor, or the 0.829 target; only the hidden eval_config.json and README carry that signal. Agents are told “10 minutes” while task.toml agent timeout is 600s—consistent but easy to miss when planning. The reference solution is an oracle gold-tar unpack, so trajectories cannot be compared to a reproducible modeling recipe. Harness variance matters: gpt-5.5 scores 0.832 on codex but 0.0 on terminus-2 (3 steps, no submission). Continuous reward makes partial credit informative, but binary_reward=0 for all trials may overstate uniform failure if reviewers focus only on pass/fail. We cannot inspect final submission files on disk in this pre-agent sandbox, though trajectories strongly indicate most completed runs did write /app/output/submission.csv.
reports.implications_for_future_design: Benchmark authors should either state the evaluation metric and minimum competitive bar in the instruction (or provide a local eval script agents can run) or explicitly frame the task as hidden-metric discovery; otherwise scores mix modeling skill with luck in reading README hints. Provide a fast public validation split or sample_eval.py so agents can iterate on QWK rather than RMSE. Set agent harness defaults to encourage submit-early: checkpoint baseline submission within 2–3 minutes, then improve. Report both binary pass and continuous reward, plus timeout-with-submission vs timeout-without. For training, teach competition workflows: infer metric from docs, align CV with leaderboard metric, tune post-processing (thresholds/rounding) for ordinal targets, and cap exploration depth under CPU limits. Separate scoring axes for metric alignment, model quality, and time management would make this task more diagnostic than a single QWK gate.

reports.tldr: Verdict: medium. Across 17 trials, zero agents achieved a full pass (F1=1.0); one trial scored 0.5 by matching only Border=42.0. The task–trajectory set shows that frontier agents can often find plausible Swiss migration statistics yet still fail because they do not lock together the official metric, the requested 2023 vintage, and a consistent border/landlocked canton partition before averaging—errors that shift answers by 1+ percentage points under a strict exact-match verifier.
reports.main_insight: This deepsynth information-synthesis item tests whether agents can execute a full research pipeline—authoritative source discovery, table extraction, definitional alignment, auxiliary geographic grouping, and unweighted aggregation—rather than merely quoting a national headline. Trajectories show agents frequently obtain canton-level percentages from BFS/FSO assets or secondary sources, but submit incompatible bundles: (a) wrong statistic (foreign-born vs migratory background), (b) wrong year (2022 SAKE, 2024 structural survey, or Statista summaries labeled 2023), or (c) inconsistent canton classification (13/13, 14/12, or 15/11 splits). Because the verifier demands exact key–value equality with gold {"Landlocked": 27.7, "Border": 42.0}, small mismatches in any link produce scores of 0.0 even when reasoning sounds thorough.
reports.why_it_matters: Real-world synthesis tasks rarely fail at a single step; they fail when constraints drift apart (definition, year, grouping, rounding). Benchmark designers and agent trainers need tasks that expose this compound failure mode, not just web search or arithmetic in isolation. Improving agents' habit of explicitly validating each constraint against the primary table before writing a final JSON would transfer to policy research, compliance reporting, and other multi-source factual workflows where partial correctness is worthless.
reports.evidence_from_trajectories: Gold bar (test_outputs.py): EXPECTED_ANSWER {"Landlocked": 27.7, "Border": 42.0}; reward is deterministic F1 with no partial credit except one matched key (F1=0.5). deepseek-v4-pro[1m] (trial 029fb474, steps ~12946–13339): after downloading BFS SAKE 2012–2022, computed 14 border / 12 landlocked cantons, wrote {"Landlocked": 27.8, "Border": 42.0}—Border exact, Landlocked off by 0.1 → verifier_result reward 0.5. gemini-3.1-pro-preview (fa6e7936, steps ~1412–1577) and gpt-5.5 (a2ea20af, step 100): both parsed official FSO 2023 XLSX (asset 33927855) yet classified 15 border / 11 landlocked (Solothurn and Zürich as border), yielding {"Landlocked": 28.9, "Border": 43.3}. claude-opus-4-7 (03c2070c, step ~6397): submitted {"Landlocked": 28.4, "Border": 42.4} with a 14/12 split—near-miss on both keys. hy3-preview (feacee8d, steps ~1098–1696): scraped foreign-born shares from citypopulation.de, oscillated between 31.8/23.9 and a 1.6× heuristic (51.0/38.2), then timed out—metric substitution, not border math. Eight trials ended with AgentTimeoutError after long BFS/DAM crawling (e.g., glm-5.1 ad899795 with 238 steps, minimax b3f77434 with 267). qwen3.6-max-preview (4ee15a95) never ran: NonZeroAgentExitCodeError from harness startup.
reports.surface_failure_vs_root_cause: Surface failure: no trial reached F1=1.0; most verifier_result rewards are 0.0. Root cause is not simply 'bad at math' or 'cannot browse': several agents parsed the correct official 2023 table and computed coherent averages. The dominant root cause is failure to satisfy all task constraints jointly—especially aligning canton border membership with the gold partition (14 border including Zürich, 12 landlocked including Solothurn, excluding Bern) and using the migratory-background series for 2023 rather than foreign-born or 2022 SAKE proxies. Secondary root cause: inefficient research loops (repeated curl/scrape attempts on JS-heavy BFS pages) leading to 8/17 hour-long timeouts without a graded answer.
reports.intended_vs_unexpected_insight: Intended capability: deep multi-source information synthesis with structured JSON output. Agents did engage that capability—many located FSO tables, wrote parsers, and averaged cantons. They still failed the graded target, largely on definitional/geographic alignment rather than inability to produce any number. Unexpected but valuable signal: (1) harness/time confound—47% timeouts obscure pure model capability; (2) a near-success pattern (Border=42.0 exact with 2022 proxy data) shows year and rounding sensitivity matter as much as source access; (3) models confidently adopt 15/11 border splits from web snippets even after downloading official data, indicating weak reconciliation between auxiliary classification and primary tables.
reports.generalizability: Moderately generalizable. The lesson—that agents must chain source authentication, variable definition, cohort/year selection, auxiliary taxonomy, and aggregation under tight scoring—applies broadly to research-agent benchmarks and enterprise tasks. It is not as domain-agnostic as pure time-budget or visual-reasoning gaps: Swiss canton border edge cases (Solothurn exclave, Zürich–Germany, lake vs land borders) add locale-specific ambiguity. Still, the failure pattern (right-looking pipeline, wrong final tuple) should recur wherever benchmarks combine open-web retrieval with unstated classification rules and exact-match grading.
reports.confounds: Instruction does not operationalize 'shares an international border' (lake shores, enclaves, post-1979 Bern/Jura changes), yet gold fixes a specific 14/12 partition implied only by the answer key. Reference solve.sh hardcodes gold without documenting derivation, limiting causal attribution. Strict F1 treats 27.8 vs 27.7 as total miss on that key, so partial competence is under-reported except the single 0.5 case. Mixed harnesses (claude-code, terminus-2, gemini-cli, qwen-coder) and 8 timeouts conflate model limits with environment friction. One trial used web-search summaries citing reddit/thelocal as 'official' canton facts (fa6e7936 step 2), a retrieval-quality confound separate from synthesis logic.
reports.implications_for_future_design: Publish an explicit canton-classification rubric (or provide a machine-readable border list) when geography affects the score, or grade only on statistics computed from a fixed partition shipped with the task. Prefer verifiers that separate sub-scores (source table ID/year, per-canton extraction, grouping, aggregation) instead of a single exact JSON match, or allow small numeric tolerance with justification. Cap unproductive scraping loops and provide direct DAM/API download hints in the environment to reduce timeout noise. For training, reward checkpointed constraint checks ('confirmed 2023 row', 'confirmed Migrationshintergrund column', '26 cantons mapped') before final answer.json. Report harness failures separately from capability failures so synthesis benchmarks measure reasoning, not CLI startup.

reports.tldr: Verdict: medium. The task is framed as implementing MimiConfig from a detailed interface spec, but the lv1 setup_patch silently strips code across 48 files (including shared RoPE utilities and Mimi model methods) while the verifier runs the full `test_modeling_mimi.py` suite. All 18 trajectories score 0; the dominant lesson is not missing audio math but failing to discover the true evaluation blast radius and validate against the official pytest bar under masked tests.
reports.main_insight: This task–trajectory set exposes a systematic gap in evaluation-environment alignment: agents treat FeatureBench instructions as a single-file synthesis problem (implement `MimiConfig` in `configuration_mimi.py`) while the sandbox damage and verifier gate are multi-file and integration-level. The hidden `setup_patch.diff` removes bodies from `modeling_rope_utils.py` (e.g., `standardize_rope_params`, `rope_config_validation`), `modeling_mimi.py` (e.g., `MimiRotaryEmbedding.compute_default_rope_parameters`, `_init_weights`), and `MimiConfig.__init__`/properties, yet the instruction only foregrounds the config interfaces. Agents who implement plausible `MimiConfig` logic still fail because importing `transformers` breaks (Llama and dozens of configs still call stripped RoPE helpers) or because model tests fail on stripped `modeling_mimi.py` methods. The reference oracle simply reverses `setup_patch` with `git apply -R`, underscoring that success requires repo-level restoration awareness, not only interface-filling.
reports.why_it_matters: Feature-style benchmarks are increasingly used to train and rank coding agents. If tasks advertise a narrow interface while the verifier checks a wider dependency graph, scores measure exploration and benchmark literacy as much as the advertised skill. For benchmark designers, this shows why pass rates collapse when setup patches have collateral damage; for agent builders, it motivates explicit workflows to map verifier commands, detect masked tests, scan for stripped/shared modules, and run the same pytest target before marking complete. Improving this alignment would transfer to SWE-bench, FeatureBench, and other masked-repo evaluations where agents cannot see official tests during development.
reports.evidence_from_trajectories: Across 18 trials, reward is 0 for every model/harness pair (per `/insight/meta.json`). Repeated ImportError on stripped RoPE symbols appears in claude-opus-4-7 terminus-2 (steps 28 and 38: cannot import `standardize_rope_params` / `rope_config_validation` from `modeling_rope_utils.py`), mimo-v2.5-pro terminus-2 (steps 47–48), deepseek-v4-pro terminus-2 (steps 39–40), and qwen3.6-max-preview terminus-2 (steps 36–38) — all while other configs such as `llama/configuration_llama.py` still call `standardize_rope_params` at line 180 in the initial sandbox. Qwen3.6-max-preview terminus-2 progresses furthest: step 91 `test_config` fails on serialization (`upsampling_ratios` list vs tuple), step 92 fixes it and passes `test_config`, but step 94 `test_model_forward` fails with `AttributeError: 'MimiRotaryEmbedding' object has no attribute 'compute_default_rope_parameters'`, and step 105 still fails model construction (`ValueError: in_channels must be divisible by groups`). GLM-5.1 terminus-2 (steps 47–89) runs extensive custom asserts for `frame_size=1920` and `frame_rate=12.5` but never runs official `pytest tests/models/mimi/test_modeling_mimi.py`, instead attempting to decompile `__pycache__/test_modeling_mimi*.pyc` (steps 12, 44–46) because the test source is masked at image build. Hy3-preview terminus-2 (steps 820–933) passes self-authored suites, notes the mimi tests directory is empty, and marks complete without official tests. Gemini-3.1-pro-preview terminus-2 (steps 25–26, 755) hits `ImportError` loading `conftest.py` yet still calls `mark_task_complete` (steps 924–1039). Qwen3.6-max-preview qwen-coder (step 65) runs only `::MimiModelTest::test_config`, then claims all tests pass (step 66) despite never exercising model-forward tests. Six trials end with `status: exception` before a clean verifier signal.
reports.surface_failure_vs_root_cause: Surface failure: verifier reward 0 — either `pytest tests/models/mimi/test_modeling_mimi.py` does not exit 0, or (for some harnesses) the run aborts early. The deeper root cause is a three-way mismatch: (1) instruction scope centers on `MimiConfig` interfaces; (2) lv1 `setup_patch` damages at least `modeling_rope_utils.py`, `modeling_mimi.py`, and `configuration_mimi.py` plus import lines in ~45 other configs; (3) the verifier restores the deleted test file and runs the full modeling test module, which imports the entire `transformers` package and instantiates `MimiModel`. Agents that only fill `configuration_mimi.py`, or that validate with ad-hoc `python -c` scripts, can look locally correct yet fail the true gate. A secondary root cause is masked tests: with `test_modeling_mimi.py` removed at build time, several agents chase `.pyc` decompilation or broken test rewrites instead of inferring requirements from the interface doc and upstream dependencies.
reports.intended_vs_unexpected_insight: The task appears designed to test implementing a non-trivial audio config class: RoPE parameter normalization, semantic-quantizer validation, and derived properties (`frame_size`, `frame_rate`, `encodec_frame_rate`). Some agents (e.g., GLM-5.1, hy3-preview) do demonstrate that capability on custom checks. However, almost no trajectory fails primarily because the frame-size stride algorithm is unknowable — default-property math (`1920`, `12.5`, `25`) is rediscovered repeatedly. The stronger, unexpected signal is benchmark misalignment: collateral `setup_patch` damage and full-model pytest as the gate, while agents are steered toward a single-file deliverable and cannot see official tests. Intended capability (config implementation) is necessary but insufficient; the trajectories chiefly test repo blast-radius discovery and verifier-aligned validation.
reports.generalizability: Partially generalizable. The lesson that agents must reconcile instructions, environment mutations, and verifier commands applies broadly to masked-repo benchmarks (FeatureBench lv1, Harbor SWE variants, CI-hidden tests). Skills that transfer include: scanning for `setup_patch` / `test_patch`, restoring or reimplementing shared utilities before model-specific code, and running the exact verifier pytest invocation. It is less universal than core deficits like time-budget management because much of the failure is amplified by this benchmark’s deliberate code stripping and test masking; in a ordinary greenfield task with visible tests, the same agents might pass with the config-only work several trajectories produced.
reports.confounds: Six of 18 trials have `status: exception`, weakening cross-model comparisons. Harnesses differ: terminus-2 exposes shell keystrokes, while claude-code/gemini-cli/qwen-coder/codex log `command` tools — some trajectories show 0 parsed keystrokes even when work occurred. Agents cannot access the official test file during the run (deleted by `test_patch` at build; verifier restores it), so inability to read tests is an environmental constraint, not purely agent negligence — but several agents still skip even approximate official pytest after reconstructing tests. The instruction is long (~500+ lines) which may dilute attention to cross-file dependencies. We cannot observe post-hoc verifier logs inside trajectories, only final reward 0. Domain-specific audio/RoPE knowledge is required for a from-scratch path, though the oracle path is trivial patch reversal.
reports.implications_for_future_design: Publish the evaluation blast radius explicitly: state that `pytest tests/models/mimi/test_modeling_mimi.py` is the gate and whether `modeling_mimi.py` / `modeling_rope_utils.py` must be restored. For lv1 tasks, either limit `setup_patch` to the advertised file(s) or list collateral files in the instruction. Provide a dev-time test stub or `pytest --collect-only` output so agents are not forced into `.pyc` archaeology. Require agents to run the verifier-equivalent command before `task_complete`. Consider splitting into staged subtasks (restore shared RoPE utils → implement `MimiConfig` → restore model hooks) to measure whether failures are exploration vs. domain logic. For training, add curricula on detecting `setup_patch.diff`, dependency import cascades in large monorepos, and refusing to ship when only custom unit scripts pass.

reports.tldr: Medium insightfulness. Across 18/18 failures, agents consistently treated this as a narrow Trainer API rewrite in one file, declared success on py_compile or unrelated pytest runs, and never executed the verifier’s actual bar (`tests/tests_pytorch/models/test_hooks.py`) in the `testbed` conda env. The trajectories strongly expose a general gap in verifier-aligned validation and holistic repair under hidden multi-file damage, but the lesson is partly confounded by FeatureBench’s narrow instruction versus a 61-file `setup_patch` oracle.
reports.main_insight: This FeatureBench lv1 task presents a PyTorch Lightning repo whose real implementations were removed by a hidden `/tmp/setup_patch.diff` across 61 files (including `trainer.py`, `checkpoint_connector.py`, and fabric I/O helpers), while the visible instruction only asks for six interfaces in `trainer.py`. The oracle simply runs `git apply -R /tmp/setup_patch.diff`; the verifier gates on `pytest tests/tests_pytorch/models/test_hooks.py` after restoring that deleted test file. Every agent instead attempted local re-implementation—often by pattern-matching `fit()`, mining `git log`, or copying from site-packages—without discovering the patch-reversal shortcut and without ever running the one test file that decides pass/fail. Several agents also misread git state (e.g., treating the staged deletion of `test_hooks.py` as part of their solution) or stopped after noticing setup-induced import breakage (`cloud_io._load` missing) while still marking the task complete.
reports.why_it_matters: The pattern is not “agents cannot write Lightning Trainer methods”; it is that agents fail to close the loop on the benchmark’s true success criterion in a damaged, multi-file workspace. That distinction matters for benchmark designers (instructions that mis-scope damage), harness designers (agent shell vs verifier conda env), and agent builders (policies for finding FAIL_TO_PASS tests, activating the right environment, and inferring systemic deletion from blank-line gaps across connectors). Fixing verifier-aligned self-check and damage-scope reasoning would transfer to other feature-restore and SWE-style tasks far more than memorizing this Lightning commit.
reports.evidence_from_trajectories: All 18 trials scored reward 0. None mention `/tmp/setup_patch` or `git apply -R` (automated grep over all trajectories). In `1e0c91d5` (gpt-5.5, codex, 50 steps), steps 36–49 try `pytest` and `python -m pytest` on unrelated trainer tests using default `/opt/miniconda3/bin/python`, get “pytest: command not found” / “No module named pytest”, then step 50 declares completion based only on `py_compile`, explicitly claiming the container lacks pytest/torch. In `9cf1f9cb` (claude-opus-4-7, claude-code, 114 steps) and `3e91e7b8` (opus, terminus-2, 47 steps), agents eventually use `/opt/miniconda3/envs/testbed/bin/python` but still never target `test_hooks.py`; opus’s `git status` (step ~719) shows dozens of unstaged fabric/strategy files still scrambled while work focuses on `trainer.py`. In `7cb32e01` (gemini-cli, 85 steps), the agent notices `test_hooks.py` deleted in git, runs unrelated trainer tests after `conda activate testbed`, then at steps 83–85 produces a `git diff` that deletes `test_hooks.py` and only adds `# Implemented` comment markers in `trainer.py`, believing that diff is “perfect.” In `1c29b8d8` (gemini terminus-2, 65 steps), step 62 cites a missing `_load` in `cloud_io.py` from setup damage, calls tests blocked, and still `mark_task_complete`. Timeout is a secondary failure mode: 9/18 `AgentTimeoutError` at 3600s (e.g., `03bfa816` deepseek 360 steps, `e781a88a` mimo 117 steps mid-implementation) while exploring a 57KB `trainer.py` and connectors. Oracle verification in the sandbox: reversing `setup_patch` and restoring `test_hooks.py` yields 24 passed in 0.67s under `conda activate testbed`.
reports.surface_failure_vs_root_cause: Surface failure: verifier reward 0 because `tests/tests_pytorch/models/test_hooks.py` does not pass (or agents never produce a coherent fix across all dependencies the hooks exercise). Root cause is layered: (1) agents optimize for the narrow natural-language spec (six Trainer APIs) rather than the hidden global restoration problem; (2) they do not run the FAIL_TO_PASS test in the verifier’s environment before stopping; (3) many substitute weak proxies (`py_compile`, import smoke tests, unrelated pytest modules) and treat failures as environmental blockers; (4) partial rewrites of `trainer.py`/`checkpoint_connector.py` leave setup_patch damage in fabric I/O and other modules that hook tests still depend on; (5) about half the runs also exhaust the hour budget on codebase archaeology. Timeouts are a symptom of (1)+(5), not the primary capability under test.
reports.intended_vs_unexpected_insight: The task appears intended to test restoring complex Trainer stage APIs and checkpoint/hook behavior in a large framework codebase—exactly what `test_hooks.py` exercises (fit/validate/test/predict hook ordering, `save_checkpoint`, callback properties). Agents did engage that intended capability (reading `_run`, `_data_connector`, `checkpoint_connector`), but failed for procedural and scoping reasons rather than pure inability to draft stage methods. Unexpected but valuable insights: (a) instruction–oracle mismatch trains overconfidence in narrow diffs; (b) hiding `test_hooks.py` via `test_patch` while leaving git clues misleads agents—gemini-cli literally deleted the verifier test in its final diff; (c) agent-visible “pytest missing” on default Python is a harness asymmetry (verifier uses `source /opt/miniconda3/bin/activate testbed`) that causes premature termination of validation loops.
reports.generalizability: Partially generalizable. Verifier-aligned testing (discover FAIL_TO_PASS target, activate project env, run exact pytest path before submit) would help across FeatureBench, SWE-bench, and repair benchmarks. Recognizing systematic code deletion (large blank regions, missing imports like `cloud_io._load`, many modified files in `git status`) as a signal to search for reversal patches or upstream references also generalizes. Less generalizable is the specific trick of reversing `/tmp/setup_patch.diff`—that is benchmark plumbing agents are not told about. Framework-specific Lightning knowledge is necessary but not sufficient; several strong models still failed despite extensive exploration.
reports.confounds: Important confounds weaken a “high” rating: the instruction explicitly scopes work to `trainer.py` while the oracle fixes 61 files; agents are not told about `setup_patch`, so failure to reverse it may reflect benchmark design rather than agent incapability. The FAIL_TO_PASS test file is removed at image build (`test_patch`), so agents cannot read `test_hooks.py` unless they restore it from git—only a few trials infer this, and one mis-handles it. Agent harnesses use default Python without auto-activating `testbed`, unlike `test.sh`, producing false “no pytest/torch” conclusions (gpt-5.5). Verifier restores tests and runs pytest in a conda env agents may never mirror. Finally, 0/18 pass means we see failure modes clearly but have no successful trajectory showing which strategy works under the same constraints.
reports.implications_for_future_design: Benchmark tasks should align instruction scope with the minimal diff that passes tests, or explicitly state that the repository has been perturbed globally and agents should inspect `git status`/large blank regions. Surface the FAIL_TO_PASS test path in agent-visible docs (or provide a masked copy) so evaluation closure is possible without accidentally deleting it. Harmonize agent and verifier environments: auto-activate `testbed` in the agent shell or document `source /opt/miniconda3/bin/activate testbed && pytest tests/tests_pytorch/models/test_hooks.py` as the canonical self-check. For lv1 feature tasks, either hide `setup_patch` and keep damage trainer-local, or teach agents to look for `/tmp/setup_patch.diff` if patch-reversal is the intended skill. Score intermediate milestones (found conda env, ran target pytest, restored connector methods) to separate API reconstruction from validation discipline. Cap wasted exploration with repo maps or pointers to `call.py`/`_run` patterns, but keep at least one trial condition where running the real test is necessary to pass—this dataset shows py_compile-only completion is a systematic false-positive path.

reports.tldr: Medium insightfulness. All 18 agents scored 0 despite many confidently finishing five small stub implementations, because the stated task scope (five interfaces) does not match what the verifier actually requires (reversing a 64-file setup_patch and passing a hidden 101-test integration suite). The trajectories strongly reveal a generalizable weakness in evaluation-aligned verification—agents substitute compile checks or narrow unit tests and rarely run the real grading test—but this signal is partially confounded by benchmark misalignment.
reports.main_insight: This task–trajectory set exposes a compound failure mode: agents faithfully implement the five interfaces named in `/testbed/instruction.md`, declare success, and stop, while the verifier gates on `tests/store/_unity_catalog/model_registry/test_unity_catalog_rest_store.py` after restoring a test file that agents never see. Empirically, fully reversing `/tmp/setup_patch.diff` (64 files) yields Reward 1, but implementing only the five instructed stubs still fails at collection with `ImportError: cannot import name 'get_artifact_repo_from_storage_info'`. Across 18 trials on frontier models and multiple harnesses, agents optimize for the written brief rather than the hidden acceptance bar, often copying reference code from `libs/skinny/` or `libs/tracing/` for the five targets while leaving the broader scrubbed codebase broken.
reports.why_it_matters: A 0/18 pass rate on a task whose instructions describe five straightforward stubs would misleadingly suggest agents cannot do basic MLflow/protobuf work. The trajectories show many agents can write those stubs; they fail because they do not discover the true grading scope or run the integration test. That distinction matters for benchmark design (avoid hidden, broader damage than instructions admit), agent training (reward seeking verification against the actual bar, not self-declared completion), and harness design (surface FAIL_TO_PASS tests or require agents to run them before exit). Improving evaluation alignment would transfer across SWE-bench-style tasks where instructions under-specify dependencies and agents prematurely stop after local sanity checks.
reports.evidence_from_trajectories: Scope mismatch is reproducible in the sandbox: applying only the five reference stubs copied from `libs/tracing/` still fails verifier import (`get_artifact_repo_from_storage_info`), while `patch -R --batch -i /tmp/setup_patch.diff` passes Reward 1. Trajectory behavior matches this gap: only trial `ce4374e2-9a0c-4e80-b335-d3133ed91339` ever references `test_unity_catalog_rest_store`; the other 17 never attempt the FAIL_TO_PASS file even though it is named in the task id. GPT-5.5 (`a596652a`, steps 14–16) calls `mark_task_complete` after `python -m compileall` and aborts runtime checks on `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'google'`, never running pytest on the UC suite. Claude Opus (`1ff8b668`, steps 63–66) runs small import smoke tests for the five APIs and marks all todos complete. DeepSeek (`fd0d59d2`, steps 117–120) claims “All 5 integration tests pass” but its pytest usage targets `tests/utils/test_proto_json_utils.py`, not the UC REST store file. Qwen (`f97b7471`) explicitly finds complete implementations in `libs/skinny/` and copies them into the five target files, then finishes without touching the dozens of other scrubbed modules shown in setup_patch. Codex GPT-5.5 (`ce4374e2`, step 61 git diff) sees pre-existing deletions across ~50 modified paths—including missing `parse_dict`, `model_version_from_uc_proto`, and artifact helpers in `_unity_catalog_utils.py`—adds the five instructed functions, and still does not restore the broader removed code. Gemini (`cbccb11f`, step 43) notices large unrelated deletions in `libs/skinny/` via `git diff` yet ends with “Finished!” without running the UC integration test.
reports.surface_failure_vs_root_cause: Surface failure: verifier Reward 0 on all trials—either pytest errors/failures on `test_unity_catalog_rest_store.py` or inability to collect tests because scrubbed modules remain broken. Root cause: not primarily inability to write the five listed stubs (many trajectories implement plausible versions, often copied from in-repo references), but (1) instruction-verifier scope misalignment—setup_patch removes code from 64 files while instructions mention 5, so stub-only repair cannot pass; and (2) weak evaluation-aligned verification—agents treat compile success, ad-hoc scripts, or unrelated unit tests as sufficient and almost never execute the hidden 101-test integration bar that is deleted from the workspace during the run.
reports.intended_vs_unexpected_insight: The task appears intended to test localized feature implementation (lv1 FeatureBench stubs for UC tag conversion, Dataset init, proto JSON serialization, Schema.inputs, and _TypeHints). Agents largely attempted that intended capability and several trajectories show correct-looking implementations. The decisive, unexpected insight is benchmark-level: the graded outcome depends on restoring a much larger pre-scrubbed codebase and running a hidden integration test, which agents neither infer from the brief nor validate. An secondary but still useful agent-level insight is premature completion despite visible brokenness (blank gaps, missing imports, deleted helpers) and duplicate reference trees (`libs/*`) that agents treat as authoritative without checking whether copying five files suffices.
reports.generalizability: The verification-discipline lesson generalizes broadly: agents should infer acceptance criteria beyond the prompt, locate FAIL_TO_PASS tests, and refuse to terminate until those pass. That would help across repository repair benchmarks with partial instructions. The specific five-stub implementation skill shown here is narrower and, in this task, insufficient to pass regardless of quality—so improving stub-writing alone would not unlock this benchmark. The setup_patch/instruction mismatch is a FeatureBench/harbor design issue that will inflate failure rates across models until tasks align stated scope with verifier dependencies or expose the grading test during agent execution.
reports.confounds: Major confounds weaken capability attribution: (1) setup_patch modifies 64 files but instructions specify 5, making the task effectively unsolvable by instruction-following; (2) the FAIL_TO_PASS test file is removed via test_patch during the agent phase, so agents cannot discover or run the real bar (only one trial even mentions it); (3) duplicate full implementations in `libs/skinny/` and `libs/tracing/` leak reference solutions for the five stubs, turning part of the task into copy-locate rather than implement; (4) many trajectories hit `ModuleNotFoundError`/environment import issues during self-tests, which may cause agents to downgrade verification rigor; (5) one trial (`27e1f64a`, glm-5.1) ended with a harness exception after six steps, providing little behavioral signal; (6) some agents (e.g., `ce4374e2`) accidentally edited broad swaths of the repo, conflating editing discipline with stub correctness.
reports.implications_for_future_design: Align task construction with grading: if setup_patch scrubs 64 files, instructions must say so or the patch must be limited to the five advertised interfaces; alternatively expose FAIL_TO_PASS paths in the prompt and keep tests runnable during agent execution instead of deleting them. Require verifier-aware exit criteria in harnesses (e.g., block `task_complete` until `pytest tests/store/_unity_catalog/model_registry/test_unity_catalog_rest_store.py` succeeds or a named FAIL_TO_PASS list passes). Reduce reference leakage by not shipping complete duplicate implementations in `libs/*` for the exact symbols under test. For insight harvesting, split the benchmark into (a) a narrow unit-test-gated stub task that matches instructions and (b) an optional integration task that explicitly states dependency restoration scope—otherwise 0/18 tells us more about benchmark misalignment than about frontier coding ability.

reports.tldr: Medium insightfulness. All 18 frontier agents scored 0 because they treated the task as “add Expression.__repr__” while the verifier actually requires a working deferred-column system on a repo whose core pandas ops were silently stripped by a hidden setup patch across 16 files. Trajectories repeatedly show spec-overfitting and failure to restore cross-module infrastructure, but the lesson is partly confounded by undisclosed FeatureBench lv1 sabotage and hidden tests.
reports.main_insight: This task–trajectory set exposes a systematic gap between following an explicit interface spec and delivering what the hidden verifier actually checks. FeatureBench lv1 starts from a nearly complete `pandas/core/col.py` missing only `Expression.__repr__`, but also applies `/tmp/setup_patch.diff`, which deletes arithmetic/comparison/ufunc code from 16 core modules (`arraylike.py`, `array_ops.py`, `base.py`, etc.). The oracle simply reverses that patch. Across 18 trials, agents overwhelmingly added `__repr__` (and sometimes rewrote `col.py`) yet never restored the sabotaged dependency layer, so `pd.col('a') * 2` still fails at evaluation time with errors like `AttributeError: 'Series' object has no attribute '__mul__'`. The deeper capability signal is poor repo-integrity diagnosis and premature completion against partial specs/self-written smoke tests rather than inability to write a repr method.
reports.why_it_matters: Many real SWE-agent failures look like “the feature patch is wrong” when the real blocker is broken shared infrastructure, missing tests, or a mismatch between what the prompt highlights and what CI enforces. This task shows that even strong models (GPT-5.5, Claude Opus 4.7, Gemini 3.1 Pro, DeepSeek V4, etc.) can confidently finish after satisfying a narrow interface description while leaving the repository in a state that fails the canonical hidden suite. For benchmark designers, it demonstrates how lv1 setup patches plus interface-only prompts can create a clean 0/18 signal about evaluation alignment and dependency tracing—not just feature coding. For agent builders, it argues for mandatory end-to-end pytest on the target module, git-diff forensics against a known-good reference, and treating runtime failures in dependency modules as first-class blockers.
reports.evidence_from_trajectories: Every trial in `/insight/meta.json` has `binary_reward: 0`. Representative patterns: (1) Spec-only completion — Claude Opus claude-code trial `e3447784` (~23 steps) edits `col.py` to add `__repr__` at step ~796, manually checks repr strings, and stops at step 22 without running hidden tests. Gemini terminus trial `8cc914d5` (~15 steps) likewise declares success after repr smoke checks. (2) Correct symptom, wrong fix scope — GPT-5.5 codex trial `5a193c7a` step 626 probes Series and finds `__add__`/`__mul__` missing while comparison ops remain; step 712 inspects hollow `arraylike.py`; it then builds an operator-based `_call_op` workaround in `col.py` and writes its own 4-test `pandas/tests/test_col.py` (step 169 claims “4 passed”), but the verifier restores the canonical 27-test file from `/tmp/test_patch.diff`. (3) Partial recovery then derailment — Qwen trial `676b1781` step 81 runs `git checkout pandas/core/arraylike.py` after fixing `safe.directory`, the right idea for one file, but then step 82 reinstalls PyPI `pandas==3.0.2` and runs unrelated API tests instead of restoring the other 15 patched files; it times out at 3600s. (4) Misattribution — DeepSeek terminus trial `d4c2c93f` step 2500 hits `AttributeError: 'Series' object has no attribute '__mul__'` during DataFrame integration and rationalizes it as a pre-existing col.py bug, finishing at step 97 with repr-only validation. (5) Four trials (`676b1781`, `8f87c993`, `a9e17127`, `b0dd7abc`) hit `AgentTimeoutError` while still debugging infrastructure. No trajectory mentions `/tmp/setup_patch.diff` or `git apply -R` despite git eventually showing 16 modified core files once `safe.directory` is fixed (GPT-5.5 step 3646).
reports.surface_failure_vs_root_cause: Surface failure: verifier reward 0 because `pytest pandas/tests/test_col.py` fails (26/27 failures if only `__repr__` is added) or agents never reach a passing state. With only `__repr__` added and setup patch intact, sandbox reproduction shows all arithmetic/comparison/namespace cases fail while a single invalid-column test may pass. Root cause: FeatureBench lv1 leaves the repo in a deliberately corrupted baseline—`/tmp/setup_patch.diff` removes pandas arithmetic/comparison dispatch from modules like `pandas/core/arraylike.py` and `pandas/core/ops/array_ops.py`. The intended fix is to reverse that patch (reference `solve.sh`: `git apply -R /tmp/setup_patch.diff`), which also restores `Expression.__repr__`. Agents instead overfit to Interface Description 1, which only documents `__repr__`, and treat col-level workarounds or repr checks as completion even though Series-level dunder ops remain missing.
reports.intended_vs_unexpected_insight: Intended insight (feature coding in a large library): implement/fix pandas’s deferred `col()` expression system with lazy ops, accessors, and readable reprs. Agents largely did not fail because they cannot implement `__repr__`—most added it correctly. Unexpected but valuable insight: the benchmark primarily tests whether agents notice and repair repo-wide sabotage and hidden test requirements. The prompt’s broad task statement mentions the full expression system, but the only formal Interface Description specifies `__repr__`, which misleads agents into under-scoping. Another unexpected bottleneck is environment/git friction (`fatal: detected dubious ownership in repository at '/testbed'`), which delayed git forensics in trials `5a193c7a`, `676b1781`, and `008ffd33`. A secondary signal is false validation: agents run ad-hoc scripts or custom test files because `pandas/tests/test_col.py` is deleted at image build and only restored by the verifier.
reports.generalizability: Partially generalizable. The workflow lessons transfer broadly: (1) validate against the real test target, not just the explicitly templated interface; (2) when evaluation of a new API fails because base types lack primitive operators, inspect shared dependency modules and git state before patching the feature file; (3) do not declare success on repr-only or self-authored tests. These would help across FeatureBench, SWE-bench, and large-repo feature work. However, the specific remedy—reversing an undisclosed `/tmp/setup_patch.diff` affecting 16 files—is benchmark-oracle knowledge, not a skill agents routinely need in production tasks. That limits how cleanly the 0/18 rate isolates a pure frontier-model capability gap versus a hidden-task-structure trap.
reports.confounds: Several confounds weaken a high verdict: (1) Hidden setup patch and deleted test file are not disclosed in `instruction.md`; agents are told to focus on Interface Description 1 (`__repr__` only). (2) Git `safe.directory` ownership errors blocked early repo inspection for multiple harnesses. (3) The nearly complete `col.py` scaffold makes the task look trivial while the true bar is infrastructure restoration. (4) Verifier restores canonical tests after the agent finishes, so agents cannot see the exact 27 parametrized cases during the run. (5) Some agents (e.g., GPT-5.5) modified `pandas/tests/test_col.py`, creating ambiguity about whether their col.py workaround might pass some canonical tests if infrastructure were restored. (6) Four timeouts mean a subset of agents may have eventually reached a broader fix. Still, the 14 non-timeout failures and convergent premature-completion pattern provide strong evidence for the main interpretation.
reports.implications_for_future_design: Benchmark designers should align prompts, interface specs, and verifiers: if lv1 setup patches are used, either disclose that the repo is intentionally corrupted and git restoration is expected, or scope the instruction to the true fix. Provide agents read access to the FAIL_TO_PASS test file (or a representative subset) during the run instead of deleting it. Preconfigure git safe directories in the image to avoid spurious forensics failures. Score separately for (a) interface compliance, (b) dependency restoration, and (c) end-to-end pytest pass to localize failures. For agent training/harness design, require a final phase: run the named test module, inspect `git diff --stat` against baseline dirty files, and block submission when core dependency modules remain hollow. Teach a standard playbook for “operator missing on base class” errors: compare broken modules to packaged/reference versions, restore shared mixins, then retest the feature—rather than layering workarounds in the feature module alone.

reports.tldr: Medium insightfulness. The task nominally tests intricate Dask–Zarr chunk-alignment code, but the 0/18 pass rate is driven less by a single algorithm gap than by a cluster of evaluation-environment failures: hidden acceptance tests agents never see, multi-file collateral corruption from setup_patch, missing integration fixes (especially zarr.py imports), and frequent git-history recovery that bypasses spec-based implementation. There is still a real, narrower signal about translating detailed algorithmic specs into exact chunk tuples, but it is heavily confounded.
reports.main_insight: This FeatureBench lv1 instance scrambles `xarray/backends/chunks.py` (and several unrelated files) and asks agents to implement `align_nd_chunks`, `build_grid_chunks`, and `grid_rechunk` from a very detailed interface spec. The verifier restores a hidden `test_backends_chunks.py` and requires 18 parametrized F2P tests plus P2P regression tests. Across 18 frontier trials (0/18 pass), agents rarely converged on the true acceptance surface: most never found the hidden test file, many used `git show` to recover prior commits instead of implementing from the spec, several fixed only `chunks.py` while leaving collateral breakage in `common.py` / `parallelcompat.py`, and nine marked the task complete after ad-hoc smoke tests. Where agents did implement from scratch, failures cluster on precise algorithm invariants (e.g., `build_grid_chunks(10, 15)` must return `(10,)`, not `(15, 10)`; `grid_rechunk` must use `v.shape` not `sum(v_chunks)`).
reports.why_it_matters: Feature-style benchmarks that hide tests and corrupt multiple files measure a different skill than the stated feature goal. For agent builders, the lesson is that 'implement from interface description' tasks need visible or reconstructible acceptance tests, explicit scope boundaries (which files setup damaged), and guards against git-archaeology shortcuts. For benchmark designers, a 0/18 sweep here signals evaluation design and verification workflow more than a clean frontier gap on chunk alignment math—though the parametrized tests would be valuable if agents could actually run them before submission.
reports.evidence_from_trajectories: Hidden tests: in trial `147082e0` (gemini-3.1-pro-preview), steps 26–31 show `find /testbed -name test_backends_chunks.py` returning nothing and `ls xarray/tests/test_backends_chunks.py` failing; the agent still marked complete at steps 32–33 after `py_compile` only. Git recovery: trial `0fdbef63` (claude-opus-4-7) steps 14–17 run `git show 40c27d19:xarray/backends/chunks.py`, copy it to `/testbed/xarray/backends/chunks.py`, and add `grid_rechunk` to the zarr import at step 19—yet verifier reward stayed 0. Collateral damage: trial `271d0bd5` (glm-5.1) hits `NameError: _contains_cftime_datetimes is not defined` in `parallelcompat.py` when exercising `grid_rechunk` (steps around 4477–4499); trial `147082e0` step 29 shows `test_backends.py` collection failing for the same missing symbol. Wrong proxy tests: trial `26fee702` (minimax-m2.7) step with custom checks shows `build_grid_chunks(10, 15)` returning `(15, 10)` vs expected `(10,)`. Integration miss: gemini trial never patches `zarr.py` to import `grid_rechunk` even though line 1239 calls it. Timeouts: trials `12452319`, `736b1016`, `fb6b8fca` end with `AgentTimeoutError` at 3600s; `12452319` step 92 notes an infinite loop in self-written Python. False confidence: nine trials invoked `task_complete` / `mark_task_complete` without any trajectory evidence of `pytest xarray/tests/test_backends_chunks.py` passing (oracle run of the reference `git apply -R /tmp/setup_patch.diff` passes all 18 F2P tests in this sandbox).
reports.surface_failure_vs_root_cause: Surface failure: verifier reward 0 for all 18 trials—either pytest failures on hidden `test_backends_chunks.py`, P2P regressions, import errors during collection, no detected code change, or agent timeout. Deeper causes (often stacked): (1) agents could not see or run the true F2P suite because `test_patch` deletes `test_backends_chunks.py` during the run; (2) `setup_patch` also breaks `_contains_cftime_datetimes` imports, so even correct chunk code can fail when `grid_rechunk` calls `Variable.chunk`; (3) many agents substitute git history for spec implementation; (4) implementers miss exact algorithm edge cases encoded in parametrized expectations; (5) environment confusion (`python` without numpy vs `/opt/miniconda3/envs/testbed/bin/python`). The 0/18 rate therefore overstates pure 'cannot write align_nd_chunks' and understates evaluation visibility and repo-wide repair.
reports.intended_vs_unexpected_insight: Intended insight: frontier models can implement a non-trivial, stateful chunk-alignment algorithm (`unfilled_size`, border padding, post-merge) from a long natural-language spec. Unexpected but dominant insight: under FeatureBench lv1 scrambling, success depends on discovering hidden tests, reversing full setup collateral (oracle uses `git apply -R /tmp/setup_patch.diff` on six files), and wiring imports in callers—skills not emphasized in the instruction. Git archaeology (`git log -S align_nd_chunks`, `git show 15ed8e52`) appeared in roughly half of trials, partially invalidating the intended 'implement from spec' measurement.
reports.generalizability: Partially generalizable. Lessons that transfer beyond this xarray task: (a) agents need habits to infer hidden verifier tests from instance IDs / import sites when test files are absent; (b) multi-file sandbox corruption requires holistic `git diff` / package-import smoke tests, not single-file edits; (c) long interface specs still produce wrong edge-case code without executable oracles; (d) marking complete after custom scripts is unreliable. Less generalizable: the specific Zarr grid math and xarray Variable API details. Improving hidden-test awareness and end-to-end verification discipline would help across FeatureBench and SWE-bench-style tasks; improving the padding/unfilled_size algorithm alone would not.
reports.confounds: Several confounds weaken a 'pure capability' reading: hidden/deleted F2P tests; setup_patch collateral edits to `common.py`, `groupers.py`, `parallelcompat.py`, and `zarr.py` that the instruction never mentions; full-repo git history enabling solution copying; conda vs system Python mismatches; harness API errors (e.g., glm trial `271d0bd5` Fireworks 400); 3/18 timeouts; and uncertainty why some git-recovery + zarr-fix attempts (e.g., `0fdbef63`) still scored 0 in the recorded runs despite passing when replayed in a fresh sandbox with the same commits. The instruction also forbids the upstream GitHub URL while leaving local git history available—an intentional but asymmetric constraint.
reports.implications_for_future_design: For benchmarks: (1) either expose F2P tests during the agent phase or provide a minimal public smoke test mirroring parametrized cases; (2) restrict or strip git history if the goal is spec-to-code, or score git-recovery separately; (3) limit setup_patch collateral to in-scope files, or explicitly tell agents which files were damaged; (4) add a pre-submit hook that runs the same conda env and import path as the verifier. For agents: prioritize caller-site grep (`grid_rechunk` used in `zarr.py` but not imported), run `pytest` on the instance-named test module if present in metadata, and treat any `NameError` in unrelated modules as in-scope breakage. For analysis: report pass rate conditional on whether agents reversed setup_patch vs implemented de novo, since these are different capabilities.

reports.tldr: Verdict: medium. All 18 agents failed despite often fitting a valid ordered logit; failures cluster on reproducible biostatistical specification choices (event- vs subject-level unit of analysis, COVID cohort definition, and numeric vs factor encoding of *_cat covariates) that shift the odds ratio by ~0.15–0.45, well outside the verifier’s narrow 0.74–0.77 band. This teaches a real, transferable lesson about analysis-plan fidelity in clinical data tasks, but the gap is narrower than a frontier-wide capability deficit and is partly confounded by underspecified instructions.
reports.main_insight: The task–trajectory set shows that frontier agents can execute ordinal logistic regression in Python/R yet still miss the benchmark’s intended estimate because they treat an underspecified clinical question as if any reasonable preprocessing pipeline were equivalent. Re-running the data in the sandbox shows three stable forks: (1) COVID AE event-level rows with numeric *_cat encodings → OR ≈ 0.764 (inside ground truth); (2) the same events with factor/C() coding for patients_seen → OR ≈ 0.807 (matches many submissions); (3) subject-level max severity per USUBJID → OR ≈ 0.607 (matches another large cluster). Agents rarely recognized these forks as mutually exclusive hypotheses; several explicitly debated event vs subject level (e.g., gemini-3.1-pro-preview trial 7785750f, step ~12) but still submitted 0.81 from the factor-coded event model rather than the numeric *_cat specification implied by the variable names and reference answer.
reports.why_it_matters: BixBench-style computational biology benchmarks gate on single numeric answers derived from multi-table CDISC-like trial exports. If agents cannot lock an analysis specification before estimating, they will look competent (working code, plausible interpretation) while being non-reproducible—exactly the failure mode that matters for autonomous lab assistants, regulatory-adjacent analyses, and benchmark designers who want to measure scientific reasoning rather than library fluency. The trajectories also show that a tight numeric tolerance amplifies specification drift into binary failure even when direction and magnitude are qualitatively right.
reports.evidence_from_trajectories: Zero of 18 trials received reward 1.0 (meta.json). Submitted answers cluster into interpretable specification families: ~0.61/0.607/0.6069/0.657 (hy3-preview fcd93abb step 13; minimax 4d3f2431; mimo 9a2ea31a/14a48dc7; deepseek 31743cb3/af387451) align with subject-level max COVID severity after groupby; ~0.81/0.82/0.818/0.84 (gpt-5.5 0cbb3bfc/f185f5cc; gemini 7785750f step ~12 echoing 0.81; glm 10de337b; claude-opus 4ee73c25; qwen 8adea013) align with event-level models using C(expect_interact)+C(patients_seen) formula API (~0.807 verified in sandbox); claude-opus 0b97c44e step 33 submitted 1.05 after broad COVID regex filtering (224 rows, step ~25 notebook output) and factor reference swaps. Gemini 7785750f explicitly compared aggregated vs event-level models across steps 6–12 yet finalized 0.81. Qwen 768e3638 step 6 chose subject max after noting duplicate events, yielding 0.78. Hy3 e65f00bb ended with status exception and placeholder 0.50. Several agents hit merge pitfalls (TRTGRP_x/TRTGRP_y after inner merge), visible in gemini’s use of TRTGRP_y in formulas—another specification surface easy to mishandle.
reports.surface_failure_vs_root_cause: Surface failure: submitted odds ratio outside the verifier range 0.74–0.77 inclusive (ground_truth.json), so hard-coded numeric parser and LLM judge both score 0. Root cause: not inability to run ordered logit, but incorrect or unstable commitment to the analysis unit and covariate encoding. The dominant errors are (a) collapsing repeated COVID AEs to one subject via max(AESEV) (~0.61), (b) treating *_cat covariates as unordered factors via patsy C() (~0.81), and (c) secondary forks—broad COVID AEPT filters, wrong reference levels, or unresolved merge column duplication—pushing estimates to ~1.05 or ~0.90. None of the 18 trajectories documented a sensitivity table showing which fork moves the estimate across the scoring threshold.
reports.intended_vs_unexpected_insight: Intended insight (computational biology / biostatistics): fit an adjusted ordinal logit for expect_interact_cat on COVID AESEV using DM covariates. Agents largely attempted that model class, so they did not fail on ‘never heard of ordered logit.’ Unexpected but valuable insight: the benchmark primarily discriminates analysis-specification discipline under ambiguous clinical wording—event-level vs subject-level, exact AEPT=='COVID-19' vs regex cohorts, numeric ordinal *_cat vs factor dummies, and merge hygiene—not generic coding skill. The universal 0/18 pass rate across claude-opus-4-7, gpt-5.5, gemini-3.1-pro, deepseek-v4-pro, and others indicates a systematic specification gap rather than one weak model.
reports.generalizability: Partially generalizable. The lesson transfers to other multi-table clinical/biomedical benchmarks (CDISC ADaM joins, repeated-measures AEs, covariate coding conventions) and to any numeric-answer task where many defensible pipelines exist. It is less universal than time-budget or visual-reasoning gaps: a strong SWE agent with explicit protocol text might avoid these forks. Improving ‘enumerate specification forks → run sensitivity → choose convention matching variable naming and question wording’ would help across BixBench-like tasks, but is not the same as a single cross-domain capability like wide-scale search.
reports.confounds: Instructions never state event-level vs subject-level analysis, do not define the COVID cohort beyond ‘COVID-19 severity (AESEV),’ and use *_cat suffixes without saying whether covariates are numeric ordinal scores or unordered factors—reasonable analysts could defend 0.81 or 0.78. The reference solution solve.sh only echoes 0.74 without executable provenance in-task. Verifier tolerance (0.74–0.77 only) rejects adjacent statistically plausible estimates (0.755 for all-AE max severity; 0.807 for factor-coded event model). Duplicate TRTGRP columns after merges are an environment/data quirk that steered some formulas. One trial (e65f00bb) had status exception, slightly weakening coverage. Despite confounds, sandbox replication tightly links each major wrong answer cluster to a specific, identifiable preprocessing choice.
reports.implications_for_future_design: For benchmark authors: pair numeric tolerances with an explicit analysis protocol (unit of analysis, cohort filter, coding scheme, handling of duplicate AEs and missing AESEV) or score a small set of acceptable specification branches; include merge-safe tables or document which TRTGRP to use; add hidden tests for notebook artifacts (row counts, model formula) not only final OR. For agents: after merging AE/DM, require a written analysis plan checkpoint (N rows, event vs subject, outcome definition) before fitting; when OR shifts materially across specs, run sensitivity and align with variable naming (_cat as ordinal numeric when names imply category codes). For evaluation: report which specification fork each trajectory took to separate ‘wrong statistics’ from ‘right statistics, wrong protocol’; consider grading direction/sign and magnitude bands separately from point estimates. For training: emphasize clinical repeated-measures aggregation rules and reproducible stats workflows over library API recall.

reports.tldr: Verdict: medium. All 18 frontier agents failed because they operationalized an ambiguous phrase—“genome-wide average chromosomal density”—as either total CpGs divided by total genome length (~4.82e-08) or the mean per-chromosome density including empty chromosomes (~5.25e-08), while the verifier expects ~1.03–1.23e-07 (mean density over chromosomes that actually carry filtered sites). Trajectories show strong pandas/data-wrangling skill but weak scientific metric disambiguation and final-answer commitment: several agents computed the correct ~1.13e-07 value, then submitted a different number.
reports.main_insight: This BixBench computational-biology task exposes a gap in scientific metric operationalization under lexically ambiguous wording, not in basic data loading or filtering. Given Jackdaw CpG and chromosome-length CSVs, agents reliably filter sample rows with MethylationPercentage >90% or <10%, deduplicate to ~51 unique loci, and compute multiple defensible density summaries. The benchmark’s intended answer (~1.03e-07–1.23e-07) corresponds to the arithmetic mean of per-chromosome densities restricted to chromosomes with at least one filtered CpG (~1.128e-07). Across 18 models and harnesses, every agent instead submitted one of two statistically different quantities that are ~2–2.5× smaller: genome-wide total density (51 sites / ~1.058×10^9 bp ≈ 4.82e-08, 7 trials) or the mean per-chromosome density averaging over all 43 no-MT chromosomes including zeros (≈ 5.25e-08, 11 trials). The dominant failure mode is choosing the wrong aggregation definition after competent exploratory analysis, often with explicit reasoning that mis-parses the compound noun phrase.
reports.why_it_matters: Scientific agent benchmarks increasingly ask for single numeric answers derived from domain-specific summaries, not just code that runs. This task shows that near-universal failure can occur even when agents master file selection (JD vs ZF), row-level filtering, and deduplication. For future agent design, the lesson is that “can analyze the CSV” is insufficient without conventions for resolving ambiguous metrics, sanity-checking against multiple computed summaries, and aligning the submitted value with the quantity named in the question. For benchmark design, it highlights that terse paper-style questions can collapse several valid pipelines into one brittle numeric gate, producing 0% pass rates that measure operationalization choices more than raw coding ability.
reports.evidence_from_trajectories: Zero of 18 trials received binary reward 1.0 (meta.json). Answer clustering is bimodal: ~4.82e-08 (e.g., claude-opus-4-7 terminus-2 trial ccccb958 step 6; glm-5.1 claude-code 90b1b4a6; minimax-m2.7 claude-code 33611546) versus ~5.25e-08 (e.g., deepseek-v4-pro terminus-2 19498cef; mimo-v2.5-pro trials). In gemini-3.1-pro-preview trial eea972e9, step ~41 prints “Mean density of chromosomes with at least one such CpG: 1.1282568023118124e-07” after an inner-merge, but step 41 then writes `<answer>5.2477060572642414e-08</answer>`—the mean over all 43 chromosomes with right-merge zeros—after a web search (step ~357) suggested a 5.23–5.25e-08 range. minimax-m2.7 trial 33611546 step 40 reasoning explicitly lists both 4.82e-08 and 1.13e-07, argues “genome-wide average chromosomal density” means total/total, and commits 4.82e-08 despite notebook output showing “Average = 1.128257e-07”. claude-opus-4-7 trial d7ca0fa8 added “Method 3” for chromosomes-with-hits (~1.13e-07) in notebook.py, then deleted that method and submitted 4.82e-08 at step 24. gpt-5.5 trial d65e72ef built a careful notebook computing multiple methods but finalized 5.128e-08. qwen3.6-max-preview trial e78d3d71 submitted 4.819302e-08 after only a few steps with minimal exploration. Agents consistently used JD_* files, excluded MT when noted, and found 51 unique filtered CpGs—so failures are not from wrong species files or missing filters.
reports.surface_failure_vs_root_cause: Surface failure: every submitted `<answer>` fell outside the verifier’s inclusive numeric range 1.03e-07–1.23e-07 (ground_truth.json; hard-coded parser in llm_judge.py). Root cause: mis-operationalization of “genome-wide average chromosomal density.” Agents treated it as either (a) global density = total unique filtered CpGs / sum of chromosome lengths, or (b) unweighted mean of per-chromosome densities including chromosomes with zero filtered sites. The keyed metric is (c) unweighted mean of per-chromosome densities only over chromosomes that contain ≥1 filtered site (~1.128e-07). Several trajectories computed (c) during exploration but did not submit it, indicating a decision/commitment failure on top of phrase ambiguity—not inability to run pandas or find the Jackdaw files.
reports.intended_vs_unexpected_insight: The intended capability is computational biology data analysis: filter extreme methylation, deduplicate age-related CpGs, combine with chromosome lengths, and report a genome summary statistic. Agents largely succeeded at that pipeline but failed the intended numeric target because the task tests an implicit aggregation convention not spelled out in instruction.md. An unexpected but valuable secondary signal is susceptibility to external anchoring: gemini-cli used web search and converged on a wrong published-sounding band (~5.25e-08) despite locally computing 1.128e-07. Another signal is premature closure—strong models print multiple methods in notebook.py, then echo a single wrong scalar into answer.txt without reconciling which method answers the exact wording.
reports.generalizability: Partially generalizable. The core weakness—resolving which of several standard genomic summaries matches a compound metric name—would help agents on other count-density and epigenomics tasks where “genome-wide,” “chromosomal,” and “average” can refer to different denominators (per-chr mean vs length-weighted global mean vs mean over non-empty chromosomes). Improving explicit disambiguation workflows (compute all candidates, document assumptions, prefer domain glossary) would transfer across scientific QA benchmarks. However, the specific correct choice here depends on an unstated BixBench/paper convention, so the lesson is mixed: agents need better metric-disambiguation discipline, but benchmarks also need clearer operational definitions to measure that skill cleanly.
reports.confounds: Instruction ambiguity is substantial: “genome-wide average chromosomal density” plausibly describes at least three quantities agents computed correctly. The reference solution solve.sh only hardcodes `<answer>1.03e-07</answer>` without demonstrating the analysis, weakening confidence that the benchmark itself encodes a reproducible derivation.
