Allowing internet access let at least one agent (gemini-cli) import misleading external ranges. The dataset includes ZF files that invite species confusion, though trajectories mostly avoided that trap. Verifier tolerance (1.03–1.23e-07) would accept ~1.128e-07 but rejects both major agent clusters, so 0/18 is informative but partly a wording/grading issue, not pure incapacity. Harness differences (terminus-2 vs claude-code vs codex) did not change the dominant error pattern.
reports.implications_for_future_design: For benchmarks: operationalize metrics explicitly (e.g., “unweighted mean of per-chromosome CpG densities, including only chromosomes with ≥1 filtered site, excluding MT”) and ship a reference notebook, not a hardcoded answer. Report multiple acceptable definitions or use structured outputs listing all computed summaries plus the chosen one. For agents: when a question embeds stacked qualifiers (“genome-wide,” “chromosomal,” “average”), require a mandatory disambiguation step that prints all candidate metrics before submission; add self-checks that flag order-of-magnitude divergence between global and per-chromosome means. For tool-use policy: disable or down-rank web search on closed-book numeric tasks to prevent anchoring on unrelated paper snippets. For evaluation: log not only pass/fail but which aggregation branch was chosen—here that would separate metric-disambiguation errors from coding errors, which these trajectories largely lack.

reports.tldr: Medium insightfulness. All 19 frontier agents failed (0/19) on this BixBench CRISPR pathway-enrichment question (ground truth 25%). Trajectories show a real, recurring gap—agents cannot reliably infer the correct bioinformatics workflow from an underspecified prompt and instead commit to divergent, self-invented pipelines (mostly hypergeometric ORA → 0%, but also 10%, 12.5%, 100%) without reaching the reference answer. The signal is genuine but weakened by hidden methodological dependencies and a trivial hardcoded reference solution.
reports.main_insight: This task–trajectory set reveals a failure mode best described as scientific workflow specification under ambiguity: given only a terse research question plus raw MAGeCK/Reactome files, agents must choose enrichment method (ORA vs GSEA vs gene-set p-value combination), identifier mapping (RefSeq→symbol via mygene vs org.Hs.eg.db), condition set (8 MAGeCK columns vs 18 CPM columns with ESOTcells), replicate handling (per-sample vs merged biological conditions), and immune-pathway curation (keyword lists ranging from ~50 to ~200 pathways). None of the 19 trajectories recovered 25% (2/8). Instead, most built internally coherent pipelines that printed 0/8 significant conditions and submitted 0%. A minority diverged to other numerically confident but incompatible answers (10%, 12.5%, 100%), demonstrating that the bottleneck is not raw coding ability but inferring and validating the domain’s implicit analytical conventions.
reports.why_it_matters: BixBench and similar scientific-agent benchmarks aim to test end-to-end bioinformatics reasoning, not isolated coding. This task shows that when analysis protocol is omitted, even strong models produce reproducible-looking notebooks with conflicting numeric conclusions. That directly informs benchmark design (what must be specified vs. left implicit), agent training (method selection, cross-checking, uncertainty reporting), and evaluation (binary exact-match scoring hides whether failure was due to wrong method vs. wrong arithmetic). Improving agents’ ability to recognize underspecified scientific steps, compare alternative pipelines, and sanity-check against biologically plausible effect sizes would transfer across many computational-biology and data-science tasks beyond this capsule.
reports.evidence_from_trajectories: Universal failure: meta.json shows 19/19 trials with binary_reward 0; ground_truth.json ideal_answer is 25%, yet no trajectory submitted 25%. Answer clustering from trajectory parsing: 9 agents submitted 0%, 4 submitted 10%, 1 submitted 12.5% (hy3-preview trial 42be1cf2, step ~49: GSEA prerank found 1/8 conditions with FDR<0.05 immune pathways), 1 submitted 100% (gpt-5.5 codex trial 0fc8ff33, step ~67: combine_pvalues across pathway genes marked 8/8 significant), 1 submitted literal `{pct:.0f}%` due to an f-string bug (mimo trial 871ede56). Convergent ORA→0% pattern: gpt-5.5 terminus trial fee611a3 steps 171–185 ran RefSeq mapping via org.Hs.eg.db, hypergeometric ORA with BH adjustment, printed `NON-CONTROL significant immune pathway conditions: 0/8 = 0.0%`, then at step ~290 interrupted a still-running gseapy prerank validation and finalized `<answer>0%</answer>`. Claude Opus 4.7 trial 7ee0dbf7 (25 steps) systematically tried hypergeometric ORA, replicate merging, multiple p-value thresholds, and gseapy prerank on both MAGeCK p-values and sgRNA enrichment—each yielding 0 immune pathways at FDR<0.05—before echoing `<answer>0%</answer>` at step ~726 despite noting the result ‘seems unlikely.’ Tool friction amplified errors: hy3-preview trial 42be1cf2 step ~22 GSEA failed on column `'fdr'` (gseapy uses `'FDR q-val'`), initially reporting 0% before debugging. Data-structure confusion was visible but unresolved: multiple agents (e.g., qwen trial 84107d9f step ~124) noted the CPM sheet has 18 conditions including ESOTcells while MAGeCK P-values has only 10, yet nearly all pipelines used the 8 non-noTcells MAGeCK columns as the denominator.
reports.surface_failure_vs_root_cause: Surface failure: every agent submitted a wrong percentage; the verifier’s exact percentage parser (llm_judge.py) compared submitted values to 25% and returned reward 0. Deeper cause: agents lacked a reliable way to reconstruct the reference analytical protocol. The prompt asks for ‘significant enrichment (adjusted p-value < 0.05) of immune-relevant pathways’ but does not specify enrichment algorithm, ranking statistic, gene-ID mapping, which workbook sheet defines ‘screening conditions,’ or how to define ‘immune-relevant.’ Agents therefore improvised pipelines; the most common choice (threshold genes at p<0.05 then hypergeometric/Fisher ORA) consistently yields 0/8 in both agent runs and independent sandbox replication. Root cause is thus methodological mis-specification and premature commitment to the first stable numeric result, not inability to load Excel/GMT files or write Python.
reports.intended_vs_unexpected_insight: The task appears intended to test multi-step computational biology: CRISPR screen interpretation, gene-set enrichment, multiple-testing correction, and percentage aggregation over conditions. Agents did fail on that intended capability—none produced 25%. The trajectories additionally expose an evaluation-design insight BixBench authors later acknowledged: open-ended bioinformatics questions can be under-specified relative to their gold answers. An unexpected but valuable secondary bottleneck is compute/time management: several agents (fee611a3, others) aborted slow GSEA runs and locked in fast ORA results. Another secondary signal is statistical-method misuse: the 100% answer came from an overly permissive combine_pvalues approach, showing weak metacognition about method validity rather than mere coding errors.
reports.generalizability: Partially generalizable. The core lesson—that agents struggle to infer implicit scientific conventions from minimal prompts and over-trust self-generated pipelines—applies broadly to data-science, bioinformatics, and research-automation benchmarks. The specific failure modes (RefSeq vs symbol mapping, ORA vs GSEA for CRISPR screens, immune-pathway keyword curation) are domain-specific, though analogous ambiguities exist in other fields (feature engineering choices, train/validation splits, metric definitions). Fixing ‘workflow inference under ambiguity’ would help many scientific tasks, but this single task cannot cleanly isolate that capability because the correct pipeline is not recoverable from the public prompt alone and the shipped reference solution (solve.sh) merely hardcodes `<answer>25%</answer>` without demonstrating analysis.
reports.confounds: Several confounds limit confidence in a ‘high’ rating. (1) Reference solution is a one-line hardcode, so the benchmark does not expose the analysis that yields 25%; independent replication with ORA, GSEA prerank, and sgRNA-enrichment ranking in the sandbox also produced 0/8, suggesting the gold answer depends on unstated capsule/notebook conventions. (2) BixBench v1.5 explicitly revised many questions for insufficient detail in open-answer mode—this item may inherit that problem class. (3) Four trials ended with status ‘exception’ (32083384, 7b750afc, 84107d9f, d6e512db), though completed trajectories still show wrong answers. (4) Divergent wrong answers (0%, 10%, 12.5%, 100%) mean the task simultaneously probes method choice, not one crisp capability. (5) The instruction’s 10% example may have primed some 10% submissions. (6) Verifier uses exact numeric match, so near-miss methodological reasoning still scores zero.
reports.implications_for_future_design: Benchmark tasks should either include enough protocol context to make the gold answer reproducible (enrichment tool, ranking statistic, condition aggregation rules, immune-pathway definition) or grade process artifacts (intermediate tables, method justification) rather than a single opaque percentage. Reference solutions should be executable analyses, not hardcoded answers. For agent design: build in method-comparison loops when initial enrichment returns null across all conditions; do not terminate slow GSEA/prerank validation prematurely; validate library API column names; explicitly reconcile schema mismatches across sheets (CPM vs MAGeCK columns); and treat uniform 0% across methods as a signal of possible mis-specification rather than a final answer. For evaluation: report answer dispersion (here 0–100%) alongside pass rate to distinguish ‘wrong pipeline’ from random errors, and consider partial credit for correct data loading, ID mapping, and condition filtering even when the final statistic differs.

reports.tldr: Verdict: medium. Across 17 models/harnesses, agents reliably parsed the Excel CHIP files and applied the stated ontology filters, but converged on ~301 variants/sample because they counted every annotated row—including ~243/sample with Zygosity=Reference and missing VAF—instead of only sample-called variants (~52/sample, matching the verifier’s 40–60 range). This exposes a genomics-specific counting convention gap more than a parsing failure.
reports.main_insight: The task–trajectory set shows that frontier agents can execute a plausible BixBench bioinformatics workflow (discover 86 per-sample Excel files, fix multi-row headers with header=1, map Sequence Ontology terms, aggregate counts) yet systematically misinterpret what counts as a “CHIP variant per sample.” After the explicit intronic/intergenic/UTR ontology filter, agents averaged ~301 retained rows per sample by summing all spreadsheet rows. The scored answer (~52 mean; ground truth “Between 40 and 60 inclusive”) requires restricting to rows with an observed alternate allele in that sample—operationally, non-null Variant Allele Freq and Zygosity other than Reference. Roughly 83% of post-ontology rows are Reference sites with no VAF; including them inflates the mean about sixfold.
reports.why_it_matters: BixBench-style tasks are meant to test whether agents can reproduce published computational-biology judgment, not just run pandas. Here, literal compliance with the written filter list is insufficient: variant-report spreadsheets mix gene-panel reference sites with true calls. Benchmark designers and agent trainers need to know that models often treat “variant rows” as fungible counts, which will depress scores on genomics capsules even when code runs cleanly. Improving EDA habits around genotype/VAF/Zygosity columns would transfer to other variant-counting, burden, and CHIP curation tasks.
reports.evidence_from_trajectories: All 17 trials scored 0.0. Sixteen final answers cluster at ~300–301 (e.g., gpt-5.5 trial 221ebbda step 5: 25,881 retained / 86 = 300.94; claude-opus-4-7 trial ca8de099 submits 300.94; gemini-3.1-pro-preview trial e35cbbe1 submits 300.2558). Agents consistently read files with header=1, listed ontologies, and excluded intron/UTR terms—gemini trial 48f7aa5d step 1044 even notes CHIP literature on VAF thresholds, inspects Variant Allele Freq in step 1050, but still finalizes 300.26 at step 1573 by keeping synonymous/missense rows without a call filter. Raw inspections show Reference zygosity (e.g., b98ec1cb prints Row1 Zygosity=Reference) but no trajectory applies Zygosity!=Reference or VAF.notna() in the final notebook. Outliers: mimo trial 1e628503 ends with placeholder 12; mimo trial aeb3cf8e gets 353.27 via a slightly different substring filter without resolving the reference-site issue. Independent replication in the sandbox: ontology-only mean 300.94; ontology + non-null VAF mean 52.33 (range 39–66), matching the numeric verifier band in ground_truth.json.
reports.surface_failure_vs_root_cause: Surface failure: submitted averages near 300 instead of a value in [40, 60], so the hard-coded numeric range parser in llm_judge.py returns reward 0. Root cause: conflating gene-panel reference/monitoring rows with sample CHIP variant calls. After ontology filtering, agents counted ~289–311 rows per sample, but only ~46–52 per sample have non-null VAF and non-Reference zygosity (Heterozygous / Homozygous Variant). The error is not primarily Excel parsing—most agents found header=1 and the Sequence Ontology column—but failure to enforce that per-sample variant counts require an observed alternate allele.
reports.intended_vs_unexpected_insight: The task clearly intends computational-biology data analysis (filter intronic/intergenic/UTR CHIP annotations and average per sample). Agents did attempt that capability and succeeded at the ontology step. The decisive miss is an unstated but standard genomics convention: do not count Reference sites when reporting variants per sample. That is aligned with BixBench’s domain-knowledge intent, though the instruction text never mentions Zygosity, VAF, or callable genotypes. An unexpected secondary signal is premature closure: several agents briefly surface VAF/CHIP context (gemini step 1044) or inspect sparse VAF columns, then revert to naive row counts without reconciling the ~80% missing-VAF rate among retained rows.
reports.generalizability: Partially generalizable. The specific fix—exclude Reference zygosity / require VAF for CHIP exome exports—is domain-specific to variant tables and clonal-hematopoiesis workflows. The broader lesson generalizes: when aggregating per-entity metrics from wide annotation tables, agents must validate that each counted row represents a positive observation in the target entity, especially when key measurement columns are mostly null. That pattern appears in clinical genomics, scRNA barcode counts, and any sparse feature matrix. It will not help agents on tasks with clean, fully populated rectangular CSVs.
reports.confounds: The instruction only lists ontology filters, so requiring VAF/called-genotype exclusion is implicit domain knowledge; reviewers could disagree on whether synonymous variants should remain (they do in the ~52 mean answer). The reference solution solve.sh only echoes <answer>40</answer> without analysis, so it does not document the intended pipeline and weakens causal claims about benchmark intent. The verifier accepts any numeric answer in [40, 60], not exactly 52.3. One trial submitted 12 (likely the prompt’s example echo) and one 353.27 (different filter bug), adding minor heterogeneity. Despite 17 trials, all strong models failed similarly, which supports a systematic gap rather than harness noise.
reports.implications_for_future_design: For benchmark tasks: (1) either state callable-genotype requirements explicitly (“count only non-Reference zygosity” or “rows with non-missing Variant Allele Freq”) or provide a gold notebook that demonstrates the convention; (2) replace stub reference solutions with executable pipelines; (3) add verifier-side diagnostics logging submitted vs expected order-of-magnitude to separate ontology errors from callability errors. For agents: mandate pre-aggregation checks—value_counts on Zygosity/VAF, fraction null per column, and per-sample count deltas when excluding Reference rows. For training: include genomics capsules where the trap is reference-site inflation, not file I/O. For evaluation: report failure modes separately (ontology filter correct but call filter missing) to avoid interpreting a 0/17 pass rate as total inability to analyze CHIP data.

reports.tldr: Verdict: medium. Across 18 models/harnesses, 0/18 passed; 15 timed out at 600s and none wrote `/app/answer.txt`. The clearest cross-trial lesson is poor time/budget management and failure to commit an answer when the primary path (live ScienceDirect scraping) is blocked by Cloudflare 403—agents keep installing tools and retrying blocked fetches instead of pivoting early to archival/API routes or submitting a best-effort result. Heavy environment and harness confounds (no local data, broken web-search on some runs, answer leakage via GAIA-index search) prevent a clean high rating on the intended GAIA research+statistics capability.
reports.main_insight: This GAIA Level-2 task is meant to test multi-step web information gathering (2022 ScienceDirect Reference Works counts by sub-domain within Life Sciences vs Health Sciences), sample standard-deviation computation, and a three-decimal difference. The trajectories instead show a stacked failure mode: (1) headless sandbox access to sciencedirect.com returns HTTP 403 (confirmed in the evaluation environment), (2) agents spend most of the 600s budget on repeated curl/Python requests, pip/playwright installs, and slow Wayback/CDX probes without ever writing an answer, and (3) when a candidate answer appears—e.g., gemini-cli step 13 surfaces `0.269` from a verbatim GAIA-index web search—the agent keeps verifying rather than `echo`-ing to `/app/answer.txt` before timeout. The task–trajectory set therefore teaches more about agent workflow under blocked primary sources and fixed horizons than about inability to compute standard deviations once counts are known.
reports.why_it_matters: GAIA-style benchmarks are increasingly run inside constrained sandboxes with short timeouts. If frontier agents systematically burn entire budgets on blocked first-hop scraping while never submitting, pass rates will understate reasoning ability and overstate environment friction. For benchmark builders, this task exposes a design tension: questions that assume live publisher-site access in a bot-hostile environment may measure anti-bot circumvention and time discipline more than the labeled capability (tool-use reasoning). For agent developers, the repeated pattern suggests training and harness features for deadline awareness, early pivot to archives/APIs, and mandatory answer commitment would transfer across many web-research tasks—not just this ScienceDirect item.
reports.evidence_from_trajectories: Meta: 18/18 `reward: 0.0`; 15× `AgentTimeoutError` at 600s, 2× `NonZeroAgentExitCodeError` (claude-code/qwen harness), 1 early stop (hy3 claude-code, 4 steps, no exception). Terminus-2 trials on empty `/app` consistently open with `ls`/`find` showing no local files (e.g., qwen3.6 trial 03b4ba13 step 2; minimax 3c528ab6 step 2). ScienceDirect blocking is explicit: hy3 trial 085a9dd3 step 4 reports Cloudflare/403 on curl; sandbox curl to `/browse/reference-works` also returns 403. Time thrashing: qwen 03b4ba13 spends late steps installing Playwright (steps 12–14: “Playwright with Chromium headless shell is installed”) while still blocked; gpt-5.5 01d39dea runs 22 steps through Wayback CDX, archived HTML, and `/browse/publications` API probes but times out mid-API exploration (last step 22: archived client JS endpoints). Partial data work without finish: gemini-3.1-pro 0981756c step ~15 calls another LLM via `ask_gemini.py`, gets wrong `63.251`, then fetches Wayback JSON into `rw_data.json` (step ~24) but grep finds no domain taxonomy and it never writes answer before timeout. Answer leakage without submission: gemini-cli ef4b7799 step 13 web search returns full worked math plus “verified answer… **0.269**”, yet steps 14–18 chase HuggingFace GAIA metadata and time out without `echo -n "0.269" > /app/answer.txt`. Longest runs (claude-opus ecdc68a2: 83 steps; gpt-5.5 codex e7f23f9a: 69 steps) end still curling/searching with no answer file.
reports.surface_failure_vs_root_cause: Surface: all agents fail exact-match verifier (`expected_answer.txt` = `0.269`); most never create `/app/answer.txt` (verifier would log “not found”). Apparent causes include AgentTimeoutError and harness exceptions. Deeper root cause: under a 600s cap and Cloudflare-blocked live ScienceDirect, agents lack an effective retrieval strategy—few systematically extract 2022 per-domain Reference Work counts (e.g., from Wayback snapshots or publisher JSON APIs), none complete the stats pipeline and commit the result. Secondary causes: broken or empty web-search tool responses on some harnesses (minimax 3c528ab6 repeated “API Error: 400”), and meta-reasoning loops (searching for the GAIA question text / calling other LLMs) that consume budget without validated primary data.
reports.intended_vs_unexpected_insight: Intended: GAIA tool-use + numeric reasoning on real-world bibliometric data. Agents largely failed before the statistics step, so they did not reliably fail on sample-std computation itself. Unexpected but valuable: (1) time/budget blindness—continuing installs and blocked retries through the full 600s; (2) failure to finalize when a plausible numeric answer is already available (gemini-cli and 0981756c); (3) benchmark contamination risk—verbatim question search returns the GAIA gold answer, conflating research skill with memorization/leakage; (4) environment–task mismatch—headless 403 makes the intended “browse ScienceDirect as of 2022” path non-viable without archive/API expertise.
reports.generalizability: Time/budget awareness and answer-commitment under uncertainty generalize broadly to agentic web tasks with fixed horizons. Lessons about pivoting when the primary URL is 403 (archive.org CDX, embedded `__INITIAL_STATE__` JSON, publisher APIs) also transfer to other publisher-portal GAIA items. Less generalizable: the specific ScienceDirect domain taxonomy and the exact 0.269 figure—improving on this task alone does not guarantee better performance if evaluations continue to block live sites without providing mirrors. Statistical reasoning generalizability cannot be inferred here because no trajectory verified correct domain counts end-to-end.
reports.confounds: Empty workspace and no bundled 2022 snapshot mean success depends on external network paths that are partially blocked. Reference `solve.sh` only writes `0.269`, offering no demonstrable retrieval pipeline for agents. Verifier is a single string equality check—cannot distinguish blank timeout from wrong stats. Harness heterogeneity (terminus-2 vs claude-code vs gemini-cli) mixes tool availability (web search, Playwright, WebFetch) with model behavior. Web-search quality varies (400 errors vs gemini returning GAIA leakage). One trial (dc851771) ended in ~17s without exception but still scored 0—likely never produced answer.txt. High step counts on timeouts inflate token cost without proportional progress signal.
reports.implications_for_future_design: For benchmarks: ship read-only 2022 snapshots or an allowed API mirror when questions require publisher pages; align stated “10 minutes” with agent timeout and add mid-run budget telemetry; penalize zero submission separately from wrong answers to separate timeout discipline from reasoning. For agents: policies to (a) detect repeated 403/Cloudflare and pivot within N steps, (b) write incremental `/app/answer.txt` before exploring new branches, (c) forbid verbatim benchmark-question web search in evaluation harnesses. For evaluation: report timeout-without-submit rate, steps-after-first-403, and whether agents ever computed std dev on sourced integers; consider partial credit for correct methodology with wrong data. For training: reward successful archive/API extraction and deadline-aware stopping over open-ended scraping loops.

reports.tldr: Medium insightfulness. This GAIA level-2 task cleanly tests a multi-hop chain (archived graveyard page → oldest flavor Dastardly Mash → detail photo → background headstone rhyme), but 18/18 failures are dominated by execution friction: 15 trials hit the 600s agent timeout while thrashing on Wayback 429s, missing libraries, or exhaustive scraping. The one submitted answer (mimo-v2.5-pro) shows a sharp but under-sampled failure mode—answering from the foreground Dastardly Mash epitaph ("Caused its demise.") instead of the background Miz Jelena's Sweet Potato Pie line ("So we had to let it die.").
reports.main_insight: The task–trajectory set reveals that frontier agents can often parse the nested question structure and even identify Dastardly Mash (1979–1991) as the oldest graveyard flavor, yet they still fail to complete the full evidence chain ending in background visual text extraction. Success requires chaining archival web retrieval ("as of end of 2022"), structured page parsing, image acquisition, and reading a secondary headstone in a photograph—not the prominent foreground stone whose epitaph is also available in HTML. Across 18 trials, 0 agents produced the verifier answer "So we had to let it die."; most never reached a confident submission because they exhausted their step budget on infrastructure retries rather than pivoting to a faster path (e.g., bundled snapshot, direct detail-image URL, or vision on background crops).
reports.why_it_matters: GAIA-style real-world questions increasingly combine temporal grounding, web archaeology, and fine-grained visual constraints. Improving agents on this failure pattern would help any benchmark or product task where the user specifies a nested referent ("the X visible in the background of the photo of Y") rather than the salient foreground object. The trajectories also show that raw pass rate on such tasks can mislead: agents look competent at decomposition and retrieval while still failing on the final grounding step or on budget management, which matters for training curricula, tool provisioning (vision/OCR), and evaluation timeouts.
reports.evidence_from_trajectories: All 18 trials scored reward 0.0; 15 ended with AgentTimeoutError at 600s, 1 (qwen3.6-max-preview/qwen-coder) crashed with NonZeroAgentExitCodeError after 2 steps, and 2 finished without exception but without writing /app/answer.txt (gpt-5.5/codex at step 32, hy3-preview/claude-code at step 32). The only submission came from mimo-v2.5-pro/claude-code (f2b4848b): at step 54 it explicitly rewrites the goal as "the last line of the rhyme on the headstone photo itself" and writes "Caused its demise." at step 56—the foreground Dastardly Mash epitaph—despite having stated the background-headstone plan at step 1. claude-opus-4-7/terminus-2 (98cc7035) progressed well: by step 31 it identified Dastardly Mash 1979–1991 as oldest, downloaded dastardly-mash-detail.png at step 33, then timed out at step 34 when PIL was missing. gpt-5.5/terminus-2 (5f07041f) reached step 10 with a correct plan for background OCR, installed Pillow and tesseract, cropped left/right background regions, but OCR returned mostly foreground Dastardly text and then pivoted back to Wayback CDX retries until timeout. claude-opus-4-7/claude-code (7ec6d9d3) hit repeated archive.org 429 Too Many Requests from steps ~8–12 while WebFetch to benjerry.com returned 403. glm-5.1/claude-code (acd6c91d, 54 steps) and gemini-3.1-pro/gemini-cli (29aa9ff3, 35 steps) similarly burned budget on archival fetches. Agents that reached live benjerry.com HTML often found Dastardly Mash and its on-page rhyme, creating a tempting shortcut that conflicts with the photo-background requirement.
reports.surface_failure_vs_root_cause: Surface failure: no agent wrote the expected string "So we had to let it die." to /app/answer.txt; 15/18 never submitted before timeout. Deeper causes split into two layers. First, pipeline and budget failure: agents repeatedly retried rate-limited or blocked endpoints (archive.org 429, benjerry.com 403, missing requests/PIL/tesseract) instead of converging on a minimal path—fetch the late-2022 Dastardly detail image, inspect background headstone with vision/OCR, extract last rhyme line. Second, constraint-attention failure when agents did reach the image: the sole submitter answered from the salient foreground epitaph ("Caused its demise.") rather than the partially visible background headstone (Miz Jelena's Sweet Potato Pie: "So we had to let it die."). Timeouts are therefore not purely "couldn't solve" but often "didn't finish the chain" after spending most of the budget on retrieval thrash.
reports.intended_vs_unexpected_insight: The task was designed to test multi-hop tool use, temporal web retrieval, and visual reading of a nested scene element. Agents largely failed on those intended capabilities, especially the final background-text step. An additional, valuable bottleneck surfaced: time/budget awareness and retry discipline under hostile web infrastructure—15/18 timeouts despite the instruction saying "solve in 10 minutes" while the harness allows 600s. Another unexpected signal is shortcut susceptibility: once agents scraped accordion HTML rhymes for Dastardly Mash, several trajectories drifted toward the foreground epitaph or exhaustive flavor enumeration instead of treating the photograph as the authoritative source for the background headstone.
reports.generalizability: Partially generalizable. Nested referential parsing (background-of-photo-of-X) and discriminating salient vs. contextual visual elements apply broadly to document QA, robotics scene understanding, and assistant tasks with long dependent clauses. Archival date grounding and resilient web retrieval also transfer across GAIA-like benchmarks. However, much of the observed failure is amplified by this task's specific friction—live-site bot blocking, Wayback rate limits, and per-flavor page sprawl—so improving only Ben & Jerry's trivia knowledge would not help. Fixing background-scene grounding and budget-aware retrieval strategies would help across many multi-hop research tasks, but the exact 18/18 fail rate overstates model incapacity relative to environment stability.
reports.confounds: Several confounds weaken a clean capability verdict. The sandbox environment is brittle: benjerry.com WebFetch 403s, archive.org 429 rate limits, intermittent "Failed to connect to web.archive.org", missing Python packages (requests, PIL) requiring mid-run installs, and harness-specific tool gaps (minimax trials received hallucinated "I don't have web search" summaries; qwen-coder crashed early). The reference solution is a no-op echo of the expected answer, so agents had no in-environment demonstration of the correct chain. The instruction says 10 minutes but task.toml sets agent timeout to 600s, and many agents spent hundreds of seconds on sleep/retry loops (e.g., claude-opus-4-7 sleeping 5s, 30s, 60s between archive.org calls). Harness heterogeneity (terminus-2 vs claude-code vs codex vs gemini-cli) mixes terminal-only agents without native vision against codex view_image. With only one submitted answer, the foreground/background misread is illustrative but statistically thin.
reports.implications_for_future_design: Benchmark designers should bundle stable late-2022 artifacts (graveyard index HTML, dastardly-mash-detail.png) or provide a read-only mirror to separate retrieval reliability from reasoning. Verifiers should remain exact-string, but tasks with nested spatial constraints benefit from intermediate checkpoints (e.g., name the background flavor before the rhyme line) to localize failures. Agent harnesses should guarantee vision or high-quality OCR for image-final GAIA items, preinstall common scraping/imaging deps, and implement backoff-aware web policies so 429 storms do not consume entire budgets. Training should emphasize constraint re-reading before submission—explicitly verify whether the answer comes from foreground or background referents—and teach pivot heuristics: when archival APIs rate-limit after two failures, switch to cached assets or direct image URLs. Evaluation reports should distinguish timeout-without-answer from wrong-answer submissions; here that distinction would show most models never reached a final hypothesis rather than uniformly choosing the wrong epitaph.

reports.tldr: Verdict: medium. Across 17 trials, 0/17 passed. The dominant signal is poor time/workflow management: 14/17 hit the 600s agent timeout building pip/apt/OpenCV/Stockfish pipelines instead of committing an answer, while the one trial that finished cleanly (claude-opus-4-7 via claude-code, trial 95a1bebe) parsed the board correctly but wrote Qxc3 because Stockfish ranked it above the gold answer Rd5. The task also exposes brittle chess-image spatial parsing (flipped file labels) and a verifier confound where engine-best Qxc3 is also a winning move.
reports.main_insight: This GAIA level-1 chess puzzle (gold answer Rd5) becomes, in a terminal agent harness, a compound test of (1) whether agents budget time toward an answer versus infrastructure, and (2) whether they can recover a legal FEN from a non-standard board image before delegating to Stockfish. Most trajectories never reach a scored answer: they exhaust the 600s budget installing Pillow/numpy/OpenCV/Stockfish and iterating computer-vision FEN extraction. The single completed trajectory shows a subtler failure: after building the correct FEN `3r2k1/pp3pp1/4b2p/7Q/3n4/PqBNR2P/5PP1/6K1 b - - 0 1`, the agent equated “guarantees a win” with “highest centipawn engine line” and submitted Qxc3 (+5.6) instead of Rd5 (+4.7), which the GAIA annotator marked as the unique intended move.
reports.why_it_matters: GAIA items like this are often categorized as easy visual reasoning, but these trajectories show that packaging them inside shell-only agents turns them into workflow-stress tests: models burn the full timeout on toolchains that the original GAIA metadata never required (annotator notes: image recognition only, ~10 minutes, two steps). For benchmark designers, a 0% pass rate here mostly measures harness-induced thrashing and FEN brittleness, not whether frontier models can spot Rd5 when shown the board. For agent builders, the lesson is to prioritize vision-first answers, early answer commits, and interpreting task semantics (“guarantees a win”) rather than blindly taking MultiPV line 1—especially when the verifier accepts only one string.
reports.evidence_from_trajectories: Timeout cluster (14/17 AgentTimeoutError): trial 4640cda3 (hy3-preview, terminus-2) spends steps 2–16 on OpenCV corner detection, warping, and per-square clustering, ending step 16 still tuning gray-level heuristics without writing `/app/answer.txt`. Trial 709a0ef5 (claude-opus-4-7, terminus-2) installs Pillow, numpy, python-chess, and Stockfish by steps 16–20, then constructs an incorrect FEN `1Q6/1PP5/P2RBBqP/4n3/K7/...` with White king on a4 (step 20 analysis lists “white king on a4”), and dies at step 25 (“Still searching. Let me wait more.”) without submission. Trial e6e66ed6 (gemini-3.1-pro-preview, terminus-2) runs 28 steps of ASCII art and piece clustering, inverts colors (step 544 calls b8 a “White King”), builds an illegal fantasy position, and pursues Stockfish’s `c2c1q` promotion on the wrong board until timeout; step 28 explicitly notes Stockfish sees no forced mate while the prompt demands a guaranteed win. Wrong-FEN cluster: trial eeedb24a (mimo-v2.5-pro, claude-code) reaches a different FEN `r1nr1bk1/1p2qp2/p3pb1p/5pn1/5P2/2N3P1/1PP1PP1P/R2K1RP1` and times out in Stockfish loops. Near-miss cluster: trial 95a1bebe (claude-opus-4-7, claude-code) is the only run with `exception_info: null`, finishes in ~390s, outputs the correct FEN at steps 9–11, runs Stockfish MultiPV showing Line 1 Qxc3 (+563 cp), Line 2 Nf5, Line 3 Rd5 (+490 cp), then at step 15 executes `echo -n "Qxc3" > /app/answer.txt` and step 16 declares victory based on engine score. Early-abort cluster: trial f6d72c34 (gemini-3.1-pro-preview, gemini-cli) stops after step 4—`read_file` returns “Binary content provided” but the agent emits only a PNG hash string and never analyzes the board (~16s total). Harness crash: trial b90c6814 (hy3-preview, claude-code) exits in 13s with NonZeroAgentExitCodeError before meaningful work.
reports.surface_failure_vs_root_cause: Surface failure: binary reward 0 on all 17 trials—either missing/wrong `/app/answer.txt` or agent timeout before verifier comparison. Root cause is layered, not single: (A) For 14 trials, the root cause is time-budget misallocation—agents treat the 600s/10-minute limit as license to build a full CV+engine stack and never checkpoint an answer. (B) For several vision-heavy trials (709a0ef5, e6e66ed6, eeedb24a), the deeper cause is spatial/orientation misread of a board whose files are labeled h–a left-to-right with rank 1 at the top, producing illegal or alternate FENs and garbage engine outputs. (C) For the one substantive submission (95a1bebe), the root cause is objective mismatch: the agent satisfied “winning move” via Stockfish’s top centipawn line (Qxc3) rather than the GAIA gold move (Rd5), which the annotator selected as the move that ‘guarantees a win’ in puzzle terms even though Stockfish ranks it third.
reports.intended_vs_unexpected_insight: Intended capability (per GAIA annotator metadata): straightforward image recognition of a chess position and reporting Rd5 in algebraic notation—no Stockfish pipeline required. Agents largely failed that intended path: only claude-code + opus parsed the position accurately, and it still missed Rd5. Unexpected but valuable insights: (1) shell-only harnesses convert a ‘level 1’ vision item into an infrastructure marathon; (2) non-standard board orientation is a reliable FEN corruption trap; (3) pairing ‘guarantees a win’ wording with a strict single-string verifier creates false negatives when engine-best moves (Qxc3 at +5.6 cp on the correct FEN) are also objectively winning—trial e6e66ed6 step 28 shows agents noticing this tension but not resolving it before timeout.
reports.generalizability: Partially generalizable. Time-budget thrashing on install-and-build side quests (14/17 timeouts) should transfer to many tool-use benchmarks beyond chess—fixing step budgeting, early answer commits, and ‘good enough’ heuristics would help broadly. Visual-to-structured-state errors on oddly oriented diagrams generalize to other spatial parsing tasks (maps, charts, boards) but are narrower than pure reasoning gaps. The Qxc3-vs-Rd5 mismatch is less generalizable: it is partly a verifier/annotation issue because both moves win on the correctly parsed position, so improving engine-ranking alignment alone would not fix all GAIA vision items. Harness differences (claude-code vision vs terminus-2 JSON shell) mean some failures are evaluation-artifact, not model incapacity.
reports.confounds: Several confounds weaken a ‘high’ rating: (1) Harness split—claude-code trials can read the PNG multimodally while terminus-2 trials must reconstruct the board via bash/Python, inflating timeouts and FEN errors unrelated to chess skill. (2) Verifier ambiguity—Stockfish on the correct FEN ranks Qxc3 above Rd5, so a competent engine-backed agent is penalized for sound analysis. (3) 15/17 trials never submitted a final move, so most evidence is about workflow timeout, not the core chess question. (4) Two trials ended for non-chess reasons (gemini-cli stall at step 4; hy3 claude-code exit code 1). (5) Original GAIA human protocol (image recognition, 10 minutes) is not mirrored in the sandbox constraints agents actually faced.
reports.implications_for_future_design: Benchmark tasks: provide preinstalled `stockfish` and `python-chess` or accept multiple winning moves with a chess-aware grader; include board-orientation metadata or standardize to rank-8-at-top; separate ‘vision accuracy’ (FEN match) from ‘move choice’ scoring. Agent training: reward early `/app/answer.txt` writes, penalize unbounded package installs when an image is already in context, and teach parsing task phrases like ‘guarantees a win’ as mate/forced-win search—not default MultiPV #1. Tool-use design: expose direct image input in all harnesses for GAIA visual items instead of forcing OCR/CV pipelines. Evaluation protocols: report timeout rate separately from wrong-answer rate; cap setup steps or pre-bake dependencies; for chess, log FEN correctness before move scoring to localize vision vs tactics failures.

reports.tldr: Verdict: medium. This GAIA2 adaptability scenario cleanly tests notification-gated, multi-step conditional workflows (lunch → cancellation → dinner cascade → cab/shopping/message), but 18/18 binary failures and split trajectories show the signal is muddied: half the harnesses never expose native MCP tools, most MCP-capable agents stall after scheduling lunch because `are_wait_for_notification` returns empty, and the one near-pass agent (reward 0.77) completed the cascade only by assuming a cancellation that never arrived.
reports.main_insight: The task–trajectory set reveals a gap in event-driven conditional execution: agents can often solve the upfront information-gathering and scheduling (derive last week’s dinner guests from calendar history, schedule Friday lunch, notify the user), but they struggle to detect the environment trigger that unlocks the downstream branch and then execute the dependent cross-app cascade. The oracle expects seven write actions (two calendar creates, cab, cart, checkout, attendee message, user confirmation), with the dinner event parented on an ENV cancellation event. Across trials, the dominant pattern is either (a) stop after lunch when no cancellation appears, (b) burn steps polling messages/email/chats, or (c) skip the gate and run the downstream actions anyway. A separate, equally important lesson is evaluation plumbing: terminus-2 trials route agents through bash JSON instead of MCP tool calls, so they measure shell+MCP-hacking skill rather than adaptability.
reports.why_it_matters: Adaptability—reacting to simulated world events rather than executing a static script—is central to personal-assistant benchmarks and real agents. Improving notification literacy, causal gating (do not run branch B until event X), and disciplined waiting would transfer to any long-horizon task with emails, calendar changes, or chat replies. The harness split also matters for benchmark design: comparing models on the same task when half the runs never receive MCP tools produces misleading leaderboard signal. Fixing instruction/API alignment (`timeout` vs `timeout_seconds`) and verifier scoring (partial credit vs hard zero on count mismatch) would make this task a sharper probe of the capability it intends to measure.
reports.evidence_from_trajectories: All 18 trials scored binary_reward 0; only hy3-preview via claude-code reached reward 0.768 (5/7 oracle actions matched, tool counts correct). That best run (trial 249550c2) correctly read the user message at step 4, queried calendar history, created Lunch at step 29, notified the user at step 33, then called `are_wait_for_notification` repeatedly at steps 41, 88, 100–108 with empty `notifications` arrays even after advancing sim time ~74 hours to step 108. At step 113 it explicitly reasoned “Assuming a cancellation may have occurred (no notification received but scenario likely expects it)” before creating Dinner and Game Night at step 116 and completing cab (121), shopping (129/133), and Messages (141). The LLM judge then failed to match both calendar oracle actions despite semantically correct Lunch and Dinner events, citing index-pairing confusion between oracle[0] lunch vs agent[39] dinner. On MCP-capable harnesses, most models stopped at ~1/7 matches (lunch + user message only): e.g. claude-opus-4-7 claude-code (c089f81e) scheduled lunch at step 14, notified at step 15, then issued 10+ `are_wait_for_notification` calls through step 53 without proceeding. gpt-5.5 terminus-2 (700d9031) matched lunch + user message but scored 0.0 overall due to `tool_call_count_mismatch` (2 agent writes vs 7 oracle). Nine terminus-2 trials (including claude-opus-4-7 trial 8949ef42) used 0 native MCP calls and 31–133 bash commands; opus-terminus built a curl MCP wrapper, scheduled lunch at step 11, waited through multi-day sim advances, and marked complete at steps 32–33 concluding “No cancellation notifications… conditional follow-up tasks weren’t triggered”—yet verifier gave 0.0 with calendar match rejected despite near-identical lunch parameters. qwen3.6 terminus-2 (40a8af78) hit a verifier_error 403, not a capability signal.
reports.surface_failure_vs_root_cause: Surface failure: zero binary passes; most rewards 0.0 with matched_fraction 0.14 (1/7) or 0.0. Deeper causes split by cluster. (1) Harness/interface failure: terminus-2 prompts frame the job as shell JSON, so models never invoke registered MCP tools (0 `mcp__are__*` calls across 9 trials) and instead reverse-engineer HTTP MCP via curl—orthogonal to adaptability. (2) Event-gating failure on MCP harnesses: after lunch, agents call `are_wait_for_notification` but uniformly receive `notifications: []`; they then either exit (opus-terminus step 32) or exhaustive-search email/chats (hy3 steps 41–112) rather than recognizing the ENV cancellation that oracle_events.json parents to the dinner action. (3) Conditional-discipline failure: the highest-scoring agent violated the “if attendee cancels” gate at step 113, fabricating the branch—partial credit reflects action matching, not true adaptability. (4) Verifier artifacts: duplicate `CalendarApp__add_calendar_event` entries break pairwise matching; `reward = matched_fraction if counts_match else 0.0` zeroes otherwise-promising runs (e.g. 2/7 at 0.29 fraction).
reports.intended_vs_unexpected_insight: Intended insight (adaptability to environment events) is partially confirmed: agents that reach MCP tools do schedule lunch and attempt to wait for cancellations, showing they understand the conditional structure in planning/todos. However, almost none exhibit true reactive behavior—no trajectory shows a non-empty cancellation notification before branching. The stronger unexpected insights are benchmark-level: (a) harness choice dominates outcomes more than model choice; (b) instruction says wait with “timeout in seconds” while the working parameter is `timeout_seconds` (opus-terminus step 13 first used `timeout` and got a validation error before fixing); (c) the verifier rewards agents who guess the branch over agents who correctly withhold it when no event fires; (d) action-mode judging with two identical tool types is brittle for multi-event calendars.
reports.generalizability: Moderately generalizable within interactive assistant domains. Skills exercised—calendar retrospection, attendee deduplication, conditional planning, cross-app orchestration (cab/shopping/messaging), age-based recipient selection—apply broadly. The specific failure modes also generalize: mistaking sim-time advancement for event arrival, over-polling secondary channels when notifications are empty, and collapsing conditionals into linear scripts. Less generalizable are Prague-specific addresses, Czech attendee names, and GAIA2-specific oracle action matching. The harness confound is highly generalizable for any MCP-in-docker benchmark: if the agent loop only exposes bash, capability scores measure the wrong interface.
reports.confounds: Major confounds weaken a “high” rating. (1) Harness: 9/18 trials on terminus-2 never used native MCP despite instructions to call tools directly. (2) Environment observability: no trial in the read set shows a cancellation notification in `are_wait_for_notification` responses, yet oracle requires a post-cancellation cascade—unclear whether ENV events fail to surface, require a trigger agents never hit, or are invisible in trajectories. (3) Verifier: binary_reward 0 for all despite 0.768 partial reward; count-mismatch hard zero; calendar pairing false negatives when both lunch and dinner exist; one trial verifier_error 403. (4) Instruction/API mismatch on wait parameters. (5) Model-harness interaction (same model hy3: 0.77 on claude-code vs 0.14 on terminus-2). (6) Best partial success came from assuming the condition, not detecting it—ambiguous whether the task rewards correct gating or oracle completion.
reports.implications_for_future_design: For tasks: emit an unmissable, typed cancellation notification tied to lunch creation; add a mid-task sanity check that ENV events fired; align instruction parameter names with the MCP schema; consider grading branch timing (action only after notification) not just final action multiset. For verifiers: score conditional branches separately; use event-graph alignment instead of greedy LLM pairing of duplicate tool types; allow partial reward when `matched_fraction` is high even if counts diverge slightly; report harness capability (MCP vs bash) as a covariate. For agents/training: teach notification-first control loops—after each write, inspect `notifications`, call `are_wait_for_notification` with correct schema, and treat empty waits as “stay in wait state” not “search every app” or “assume condition”; penalize running gated branches without evidence. For evaluation protocols: require MCP-native harnesses for GAIA2-cli adaptability tasks, or explicitly label shell-only runs as a separate track; cap unproductive polling steps when notifications stay empty.

reports.tldr: Verdict: medium. All 18 agents failed (verifier expects B). A dominant, reproducible pattern appears: agents often solve reaction A correctly via [2,3]-Wittig reasoning, then eliminate the true answer B using plausible-but-wrong heuristics that a Cope rearrangement must preserve "hexahydro" and that "fluorine" is a typo for "fluorene"—exactly the features of the correct B product.
reports.main_insight: This GPQA diamond item is a two-part graduate organic-chemistry problem disguised as a shell task (write one letter to /app/answer.txt). Reaction A (benzyl prenyl ether + BuLi/H+) is a [2,3]-Wittig-type rearrangement whose major product is 4-methyl-1-phenylpent-3-en-1-ol. Reaction B is a thermal Cope rearrangement of a complex polycyclic 1,5-diene; the keyed answer is B, pairing that alcohol with the tetrahydro benzo[3,4]azuleno[1,8,7,6-cdef]fluorine product (note the intentional "fluorine" spelling in options A/B). Across 18 trials, 13 chose D (correct A alcohol + hexahydro fluorene B), 3 chose C, 1 chose D via deepseek claude-code, and minimax split between C variants—none chose B. The trajectories show agents converging on a shared elimination strategy for part B rather than lacking any mechanism vocabulary.
reports.why_it_matters: GPQA-style benchmarks deliberately encode plausible distractors in nomenclature. When frontier agents apply textbook simplifications ("sigmatropic rearrangements conserve hydrogenation count"; "fluorine must be a misspelling of fluorene") instead of reasoning to the actual polycyclic product, scores collapse even though mechanistic language in trajectories looks competent. For agent and benchmark design, this separates "can name the reaction class" from "can discriminate subtle IUPAC/product-structure traps"—a failure mode that will not be fixed by better terminal harnesses alone.
reports.evidence_from_trajectories: Verifier bar is strict string match on one letter; solve.sh writes B (tests/test.sh lines 19–37). Failure mode is concentrated on part B. In cac30ece (gpt-5.5/codex) step 2, the agent explicitly writes D because "hexahydro stays hexahydro" and rejects "tetrahydro/fluorine." deepseek-v4-pro (claude-code) step 2 applies the same rule: "molecular formula and degree of unsaturation are conserved, so hexahydro stays hexahydro" and eliminates A and B, then picks D. gemini-3.1-pro (terminus-2) runs many steps including web search (steps 11–12) yet still echoes "Cope rearrangement preserves hydrogenation" and writes D. qwen terminus-2 (58093b23) step 2 analysis states the [1,2]-Wittig product is 4-methyl-1-phenylpent-3-en-1-ol but still concludes D because B must remain hexahydro and use fluorene. By contrast, qwen-coder (d41ba807) step 2 writes C, reasoning reaction B gives "tetrahydro-1H-benzo[3,4]azuleno...fluorene"—closer to the keyed tetrahydro product but paired with the wrong A isomer. minimax-m2.7 (8ebb59b2) writes C after lengthy reasoning favoring (Z)-2-methyl-5-phenylpent-2-en-1-ol for A. hy3-preview (cc38603a) step 2 concludes C using the same hexahydro/fluorene elimination without ever writing answer.txt in the short 4-step run. Only 0/18 trials submitted B.
reports.surface_failure_vs_root_cause: Surface failure: every agent wrote A, C, or D while the verifier expected B (reward 0 for all 18). Root cause: not environment breakage or failure to write answer.txt, but systematic mis-selection on reaction B after often-correct reasoning on reaction A. Agents treated IUPAC "hexahydro" in the starting material as a conserved label through a Cope rearrangement, and treated "fluorine" in options A/B as an obvious error—both features that define the correct choice B. Less common secondary error: debating [1,2] vs [2,3]-Wittig for A (e.g., gemini-cli step 12 favors [1,2] but still ends on D), which would flip A if pursued, but the dominant loss remains B.
reports.intended_vs_unexpected_insight: The task framing emphasizes Cope rearrangement, so the intended capability is graduate-level pericyclic product prediction on complex polycycles plus ether rearrangement under base. Agents largely engage with that intent for reaction A (many identify [2,3]-Wittig and the 4-methyl-1-phenylpent-3-en-1-ol structure). The unexpected but more diagnostic insight is heuristic elimination on reaction B: agents outsource the hard polycyclic product assignment to two fast rules (hydrogenation label preservation and spelling plausibility) that happen to exclude the true answer. Web search (gemini-cli) and long chain-of-thought (qwen, mimo) do not overcome the bad elimination step.
reports.generalizability: Partially generalizable. The failure pattern—plausible nomenclature heuristics defeating careful mechanism reasoning—should transfer to other GPQA science MC items with paired subtle distractors, and to any agent that optimizes for linguistic plausibility over structure verification. It is less general than core agent deficits like poor time-budget management or inability to run code. Improving structured cheminformatics checking (formula/unsaturation counting on parsed structures, not substring rules) would help across similar tasks, but this specific item still requires domain knowledge to build the right molecular graph.
reports.confounds: The instruction mislabels reaction A as a Cope rearrangement when it is base-promoted [2,3]-Wittig chemistry; this may add noise but does not explain the uniform B miss, since agents still converge on the same B heuristics. Options deliberately pair tetrahydro+fluorine vs hexahydro+fluorene, so some failures are by design rather than random error. One trial (a3e02650/minimax terminus-2) may have incomplete terminal output in the trajectory file, though meta.json still records failure. No evidence of verifier bugs, timeouts, or missing dependencies—all failures are wrong letter choice. Correct B product uses "fluorine" spelling, which is easy to misread as a typo; that is a task design feature, not an environment flaw.
reports.implications_for_future_design: For benchmarks: report per-subquestion accuracy (A vs B) on multi-part GPQA items; a high pass on A with zero on B would expose heuristic elimination. Add structure-aware scoring (SMILES/InChI or expert rubric) beyond single-letter match when testing chemistry. For agents: after mechanism proposals, require explicit hydrogen-count or unsaturation accounting on drawn products before choosing among nomenclature variants; ban single-rule elimination of answer choices based on spelling or hydro-prefix matching alone. For training: include counterexamples where correct products change hydro designations or retain unusual suffix spellings. For harness evaluation: this task adds little signal from tool use (most agents only echo > /app/answer.txt); chemistry benchmarks should either supply drawing/RDKit tools or score reasoning traces separately from final MC clicks.

reports.tldr: Medium insightfulness. Across 18 frontier trials, 0/18 fully pass and only 2/18 get partial credit (0.125). The task cleanly exposes a repeated failure mode in expert geometric reasoning: agents produce long, plausible worst-case analyses but converge on the wrong binding constraint, yielding a structurally similar but numerically wrong closed form instead of the reference (N+1)⌈π/(2 arcsin(1/(2N)))⌉.
reports.main_insight: This HLE item is nominally a pure ML-geometry question (minimum balanced 1-NN prototypes on concentric circles), but the trajectories show that frontier agents fail less from inability to reason at all and more from misidentifying which geometric inequality is binding. The reference solution (metadata rationale) reduces the problem to per-ring coverage: equally spaced prototypes on circle t require 2tc·sin(π/(2k)) < c, hence k = ⌈π/(2 arcsin(1/(2N)))⌉ per class and total (N+1)k. Most capable agents instead derive a richer adjacent-ring chord comparison that collapses to cos(π/k) > 1 − 1/(2N) (or floor(π/arccos(1 − 1/(2N))) + 1), commit to it after sanity checks, and never recover. That yields the same qualitative scaling (~π√N prototypes per class) but systematically undercounts k for N≥2 (e.g., N=2: reference 21 vs agent family 15). A secondary cluster gives unrelated polynomial guesses such as (N+1)(N+3) or 2(N+1), and six trials end in harness exceptions or never write a gradable answer.
reports.why_it_matters: The pattern matters for benchmark and agent design because it separates surface competence (multi-page trigonometric derivations, numeric spot checks, confident write-ups) from the capability the item actually gates: identifying the correct worst-case comparator and closing to the canonical exact-match form. That error class appears wherever STEM tasks require choosing among several plausible geometric constraints, not only on this circle problem. It also highlights a design tension in agentified HLE: wrapping a no-tools math question in a shell harness adds failure modes (here-doc errors, exceptions) without improving measurement of the core skill, while the LLM-as-judge verifier gives almost no partial credit even when agents land on a near structural match.
reports.evidence_from_trajectories: Verifier bar: exactMatch against (N+1)⌈π/(2 arcsin(1/(2N)))⌉ via an 8-run LLM judge ensemble (4 models × 2 repeats); binary pass requires all judges to agree. Outcomes: 0/18 binary pass; rewards 0.125 only for qwen3.6-max-preview/qwen-coder (trial 0c9732af, step 3–8) and gpt-5.5/terminus-2 (trial 92d42208, step 3) — both wrote (N+1)(floor(π/arccos(1 − 1/(2N))) + 1). Strongest near-miss cluster shares one derivation: claude-opus-4-7 terminus-2 (trial 2ae012c4, step 3) writes cos(π/k) > 1 − 1/(2N) with k_min=max(7,…); claude-opus-4-7 claude-code (edf4a906, step 7 Write) gives the same cos inequality with sanity checks N=1→8, N=2→15; gpt-5.5 codex (0be3de17) and gemini-3.1-pro-preview gemini-cli (8ca4e4c8, step ~16) match that floor/arccos template. qwen3.6-max-preview (0c9732af, step 3) spends ~17k completion tokens deriving cos(π/k) > (2N−1)/(2N) and k≈π√N before answering k(N+1) with the cos constraint. Divergent wrong answers: mimo-v2.5-pro terminus-2 (fe02ad98, steps 2–3) first commits to (N+1)(N+3), then revises to a procedural K table (N=1→14, etc.) without hitting the reference closed form; MiniMax-M2.7 (3933b8d4) answers 2(N+1); gemini-3.1-pro-preview terminus-2 (1ed7c196) truncates to “(N+1)”. Infrastructure failures: six trials with status exception (e.g., glm-5.1 0245844a and 40781e80 stop after reading instructions; gemini-cli 8ca4e4c8 loops on broken here-doc EOF syntax at steps 2–16). Numeric divergence is systematic from N=2 onward: reference totals 21,40,65… vs the dominant agent family 15,24,35… for the same N.
reports.surface_failure_vs_root_cause: Surface failure: every agent receives reward 0 (or 0.125 partial) because extracted answers do not exactly match (N+1)⌈π/(2 arcsin(1/(2N)))⌉ under the LLM judge. Root cause for the majority of serious attempts: a binding-constraint identification error in geometric worst-case analysis — agents compare a midpoint-on-ring-t point to the nearest prototype on the adjacent inner ring via full chord geometry (yielding cos(π/k) > 1 − 1/(2N)), whereas the keyed solution uses the simpler covering condition 2tc·sin(π/(2k)) < c (equivalently sin(π/(2k)) < 1/(2N) at t=N). Agents treat their derived inequality as definitive, run partial numeric checks that seem to confirm it, and finalize an arccos/floor variant rather than the keyed arcsin/ceiling form. Secondary root causes include answer-format collapse (procedural descriptions instead of a single closed form), gross misfires on unrelated formulas, and harness I/O failures unrelated to the math.
reports.intended_vs_unexpected_insight: Agents fail on the intended capability — expert ML/geometry reasoning to a closed-form minimum — not on shell navigation or environment setup (most trials read /app/instruction.md and write /logs/agent/response.txt successfully). The unexpected but useful signal is how consistently strong models converge on the same wrong inequality family despite different harnesses (terminus-2, codex, claude-code, qwen-coder) and models (gpt-5.5, claude-opus-4-7, qwen3.6-max-preview, gemini-3.1-pro-preview). That convergence makes the bottleneck look like a reasoning/commitment failure (choosing and sticking with an incorrect worst-case comparator) rather than random arithmetic slips. Less informative variance comes from six exception trials and a few low-effort wrong constants, which reflect harness fragility or weak engagement rather than the core geometric skill.
reports.generalizability: Partially generalizable. The specific concentric-circle setup is narrow, but the failure mode — over-elaborate yet mis-anchored formal reasoning that passes internal sanity checks while missing the benchmark’s intended simplification — should transfer to other expert STEM items involving Voronoi/coverage arguments, competitive geometry, and ‘guarantee for all N’ problems. Improving constraint selection and answer normalization (recognizing equivalent trig forms, verifying against multiple N, checking whether a simpler radial bound suffices) would help across HLE-like tasks. It is less clear this transfers wholesale to software engineering or tool-use benchmarks, where the dominant errors differ. Fixing shell here-doc failures would not address the main mathematical miss seen in the best trajectories.
reports.confounds: Several confounds limit certainty. First, the reference rationale compares max same-class distance to c (radial spacing), while many agents’ chord-based derivation is mathematically coherent under a different worst-case pairing; without an external human proof audit, some near-miss answers might reflect problem interpretation rather than pure incapacity. Second, metadata.json stores the per-circle form with 1/(2t) while answer.txt uses 1/(2N); agents never see either, but this inconsistency raises questions about canonical equivalence checking. Third, the LLM-as-judge exactMatch gate is brittle: structurally close formulas earned only 1/8 judge agreement (0.125), so pass rate may understate partial understanding. Fourth, six exception trials provide little evidence about geometric reasoning. Fifth, the agent sandbox adds no computational leverage for this item — success is almost entirely zero-shot math — so the trial measures model knowledge plus file formatting, not agentic workflow.
reports.implications_for_future_design: For benchmark construction: (1) prefer symbolic or numeric checkers over LLM-as-judge for closed-form math when equivalent expressions exist (arcsin vs arccos forms, floor+1 vs ceiling); (2) include hidden numeric spot cases (e.g., N=2,3) in the verifier even if the prompt asks for a general N formula; (3) avoid forcing pure Q&A through shell/file I/O unless testing that interface is itself the point; (4) document whether duplicate center prototypes are allowed, since several trajectories debate balance at t=0. For agent training/evaluation: log and score intermediate ‘binding constraint chosen’ steps separately from final answer extraction, and penalize premature commitment when multiple comparators remain plausible. For harness design: harden response.txt writing (simple printf templates) so gemini-cli-style EOF failures do not masquerade as reasoning failures. For insight mining: tasks where many models fail with the same wrong closed form (here, the cos/arccos family) are more diagnostic than tasks with scattered unrelated errors.

reports.tldr: Medium insightfulness. This HLE Dirac-tunneling puzzle exposes a recurring gap in multimodal scientific inverse reasoning: agents can partially derive physics and manipulate images, but they fail to reliably match 12 Argand plots to the hidden parameter lattice, disambiguate that n₀ is the plot index (4), and compute the exact symbolic ratio n₀/|t²| ≈ (4/9)(17−8cos(2√3)). Across 19 trials (0/19 pass), failures cluster on the same bottlenecks—wrong physics shortcuts, integer guessing, and OCR/thrashing—rather than random noise, but harness exceptions and domain specificity limit how broadly the lesson generalizes.
reports.main_insight: The task–trajectory set reveals that frontier agents struggle to close a three-part loop that expert STEM workflows require: (1) implement or recall the correct Dirac-barrier transmission formulas, (2) invert a structured simulation grid from visual Argand plots to identify which of 12 parameter variants is missing and which plot index is n₀, and (3) emit the exact symbolic/numeric answer for n₀/|t²| at V=2E. The reference solution (base plot #4 with m=1/2, E=2, Δz=2; omitted variant m=1/2, E=1, Δz=2; final answer (4/9)(17−8cos(2√3))) depends on all three steps. Trajectories show agents often succeed at isolated fragments—visual grouping of r vs t plots, deriving a transmission formula, or brute-forcing parameter grids—but cannot integrate them into the correct identification chain.
reports.why_it_matters: Many real agent workloads (lab-notebook QA, simulation debugging, instrument-data interpretation) require the same pattern: read a figure produced by a parametric simulator, infer which run is missing or duplicated, then compute a derived quantity with domain equations. This task shows that simply giving agents an image path and a physics prompt is insufficient: they default to heuristics (nearest integer, |t|²=1, treating n₀ as a parameter value) instead of verified inverse matching. For benchmark and training design, it highlights that multimodal STEM evaluation must test end-to-end constraint satisfaction (puzzle structure + physics + exact answer format), not just whether an agent can write plausible physics prose.
reports.evidence_from_trajectories: All 19 trials scored 0.0; only a handful produced substantive final answers. Claude Opus 4.7 (claude-code, step 31) derived a non-trivial |t|² formula at V=2E and split plots into r/t groups, but guessed n₀=6 and answered ~16 with 10% confidence—wrong base and index (correct n₀=4, answer ≈10.93). Claude Opus 4.7 (terminus-2, steps 24–26) incorrectly concluded |t|²=1 at V=2E and answered 6 with 15% confidence after failed duplicate-detection (step 23: mean pixel diff 15, ‘not identical’). Minimax M2.7 (claude-code, step 24) asserted perfect transmission and answered 1 at 85% confidence without image-grounded parameter ID. GLM-5.1 (terminus-2, steps 41–44) ran the most systematic inverse-engineering pipeline—OCR, color histograms, forward Dirac simulators, MSE plot matching across bases—but still rounded to Answer: 8 at 75% confidence because ‘closest integer’ heuristics dominated. Gemini 3.1 Pro (gemini-cli, step 48+) explored bases like (0.5, 2.0, 1.5) and n₀=4 hypotheses yet ultimately wrote Answer: 12 at 20% confidence (step 52). GPT-5.5 (codex, 55 steps, status exception) never wrote response.txt; it was still feature-matching candidate bases around (m=1/2, E=2, Δz=2) at step 55 when the run ended. Twelve trials ended with status exception after long OCR/PIL/tesseract setup (e.g., deepseek-v4-pro[1m] claude-code step 11+: repeated ModuleNotFoundError for PIL/numpy/scipy; glm-5.1 step 2: ModuleNotFoundError: PIL). Hy3-preview (claude-code) terminated after 4 steps with no response.
reports.surface_failure_vs_root_cause: Surface failure: every agent received reward 0 because no extracted answer matched the exact symbolic correct answer (4/9)(17−8cos(2√3)). Deeper cause: agents rarely performed the full inverse identification the puzzle demands—determine base parameters from plot morphology, detect which of the 12 lawful variations is absent (replaced by duplicate n₀), treat n₀ as the plot index (4, not a refractive index n), then evaluate the Dirac transmission coefficient for the omitted run at V=2E. Instead, most either (a) applied an incorrect physics shortcut claiming |t|²=1 when V=2E, (b) brute-forced numeric grids and picked the nearest integer (8, 6, 12, 1), or (c) spent the budget on non-informative OCR/pixel tooling without converging on a verified parameter assignment.
reports.intended_vs_unexpected_insight: The task was designed to test advanced physics plus Argand-plot interpretation (identify omitted simulation, compute n₀/|t²|). Agents did fail on that core capability—none identified the omitted (m=1/2, E=1, Δz=2) configuration or n₀=4. An additional, still useful bottleneck appeared: semantic disambiguation of n₀ (plot index vs auxiliary refractive index n used in their own formulas), and workflow pathology where agents treat under-specified images as OCR problems rather than physics-constrained inverse matching. Harness-level exceptions (12/19) also surfaced environment friction—missing PIL/numpy/tesseract—and time spent installing heavy vision stacks instead of validating forward simulations against the figure.
reports.generalizability: Partially generalizable. The underlying weakness—integrating domain equations, structured combinatorial constraints, and multimodal evidence into one verified answer—applies across simulation forensics, experimental plot analysis, and engineering diagnostics. Improving agents’ ability to (1) formalize puzzle constraints as a search problem, (2) validate forward models against figures before guessing, and (3) preserve exact symbolic outputs would help beyond this task. However, much of the observed failure is amplified by the task’s niche relativistic-QM content and the figure’s lack of explicit parameter labels; gains here would not automatically transfer to all vision tasks, and better physics tutoring alone would not fix OCR thrashing or notation confusion.
reports.confounds: Several confounds weaken certainty. (1) 12/19 trials ended with status exception, often mid-analysis, so many runs never submitted a final judged answer despite substantial work (notably GPT-5.5 codex at 55 steps). (2) The sandbox initially lacks common scientific Python/imaging deps, causing early failures (PIL/numpy/scipy/tesseract) unrelated to physics reasoning. (3) The figure shows only circled indices 1–12, not (m,E,Δz) labels, making inverse identification genuinely underdetermined without precise forward-model matching—agents’ low confidence (10–20%) on better-reasoned attempts is appropriate. (4) The LLM-judge verifier expects exact symbolic equivalence; integer guesses like 8 or 6 cannot pass even if parameter ID were partially correct. (5) Instruction wording that n₀ labels ‘one plot’ is easy to misread as a numeric parameter, contributing to systematic misinterpretation independent of vision skill.
reports.implications_for_future_design: Future benchmarks should separate capabilities: a physics-only subtask (compute |t|² given explicit omitted parameters), a vision-only subtask (match plots to a provided simulator API), and the full composite puzzle. Provide a lightweight preinstalled scientific stack or a reference forward-model script to reduce environment thrashing. Make notation unambiguous (e.g., ‘n₀ is the circled plot number 1–12’). Score partial credit for correct parameter identification even when final algebra fails. For agent training, reward verified simulation-to-image alignment loops (generate candidate plots, compare features, prune search) rather than OCR on axis tick labels. Cap vision/OCR tool budgets or require hypothesis checkpoints so time-aware agents pivot after failed tesseract passes. Report harness completion separately from answer correctness so exceptions do not obscure whether failures are capability- or infrastructure-driven.

reports.tldr: Verdict: medium. Across 19 trials (0/19 pass), agents almost never reach the expert answer M=7527; the clearest shared failure is inventing a false 1/n “signed-walk range” law from small-n Python probes (typically M=5), while the verifier gates on exact match to 7527 from hinged-ruler theory. Harness timeouts and format failures confound roughly half the runs.
reports.main_insight: This HLE item is really a pure expert-mathematics question—find the smallest M with 10^{-M} “100000-foldable”—whose ground truth M=7527 comes from Tang’s hinged-ruler bounds (ε≈1/(2^{25004}−14), compared to powers of 10). Packaged inside a coding sandbox, agents consistently substitute computable heuristics for that literature: they reformulate to signed partial sums, run small-n search, and lock onto a plausible-but-wrong scaling f(n)=2−1/⌈n/2⌉, hence M=5. None of the trajectories mention Tang, foldability, or 7527. The task–trajectory set thus exposes (i) a domain-knowledge ceiling on research-level combinatorics and (ii) a harmful pattern of over-trusting local empirical fits when the true obstruction is exponential.
reports.why_it_matters: HLE-style benchmarks are increasingly run through agent harnesses with shells and time limits. This task shows that format alone can steer models away from the intended capability (recall/derive deep results) toward brittle computation and pattern-matching on tiny n, producing confident wrong integers orders of magnitude off. For benchmark designers, it argues for separating “expert QA” from “sandbox SWE” and for scoring that does not reward elaborate but mis-scaled exploration. For agent builders, it highlights that better small-n tooling does not fix missing theory—without retrieval or proof discipline, agents will synthesize elegant false theorems.
reports.evidence_from_trajectories: Verifier bar: exact answer 7527 via LLM-judge ensemble on response.txt (metadata rationale cites arxiv:2301.08465). Completed wrong submissions cluster on M=5 with detailed but incorrect proofs: claude-opus-4-7 (claude-code, step 6) writes response.txt with f(n)=2−1/50000 and Answer: 5 at 70% confidence after hand-checking n=3,5,7; gpt-5.5 (terminus-2, steps 2–4) runs a Python signing search on n≤8, prints “n 4 best 1.499…”, then commits Answer: 5; qwen terminus (step 6 area) and minimax terminus (step 4) submit the same 2−1/k logic. Divergent wrong paths: qwen-coder (7e3fcaa5, late step) concludes worst range 1.5 ⇒ Answer: 1 at 85%; mimo terminus (7c96edaf) Answer: 1 at 90%; glm-5.1 terminus (b56abfaf, step 3) Answer: 100000 at 90% by conflating step count with M. Infrastructure noise: 7/19 AgentTimeoutError after long compute (e.g., gemini-3.1-pro terminus 947104d1 has 37 steps including de_search.py/ruler.py thrash before timeout; gpt-5.5 codex c0845e12 has 41 steps); 4/19 RewardFileNotFoundError (e.g., 034cb8e7 mimo claude-code wrote response at step 2 but trial exception); hy3-preview terminus (ae493840) times out at step 13 after flipping between M=1 and M=5. Zero trajectories contain 7527, Tang, hinged, or foldable.
reports.surface_failure_vs_root_cause: Surface: binary reward 0—extracted Answer not equal to 7527 (mostly 5, some 1 or 100000, many no gradable file). Root cause: agents lack the specialized hinged-ruler / n-foldable ε machinery and instead (a) extrapolate an incorrect O(1/n) worst-case range law from small-n experiments, or (b) reduce the problem to the trivial all-ones oscillation. A secondary root cause on ~63% of trials is operational: 1200s agent timeout or missing response.txt, often while stuck in non-scaling Python search rather than because the core math was ‘almost’ solved.
reports.intended_vs_unexpected_insight: Intended HLE signal: frontier models fail expert mathematics without domain literature. That intended signal appears in trials that finish (e.g., opus, gpt-5.5) with confident, structured but wrong mathematics. Unexpected additional signal: the Harbor sandbox + ‘solve in 20 minutes’ framing systematically induces computational overreach—agents burn budget on n≤8 brute force and never reconsider exponential scaling—even though the instruction only requires writing response.txt. Also unexpected: several models mis-parse M versus interval width (hy3 steps 12–14 oscillate M=1 vs M=5), a reasoning bug orthogonal to foldability theory.
reports.generalizability: Partially generalizable. The lesson that agents invent false asymptotics from tiny instances applies beyond this item (any problem where the true bound is exponential but local data looks polynomial). The specific need for Tang-type combinatorial geometry is narrow. Improving generic proof validation, calibration against known impossibility scales, or literature retrieval would help many science/math tasks; improving terminal Python would not have helped here. Because answers split across 1, 5, and 100000, the failure is not one clean capability knob—hence medium rather than high.
reports.confounds: Heavy confounds: (1) 12/19 meta status exception—7 AgentTimeoutError, 4 RewardFileNotFoundError—so many runs never reach a clean capability read; (2) sandbox mismatch for a pen-and-paper HLE item invites misleading tool use; (3) LLM-as-judge verifier is appropriate for exactMatch but opaque compared to symbolic check; (4) no trial attempts web search for arxiv:2301.08465 (instruction forbids ‘online solutions specific to this task’), so retrieval-disabled setting is fair but blurs ‘cannot derive’ vs ‘cannot look up’; (5) 19 trials span many harnesses (claude-code, terminus-2, codex, gemini-cli) with uneven completion rates, complicating cross-model comparison.
reports.implications_for_future_design: For benchmarks: run pure HLE math as text-only QA without Docker unless the skill under test is tooling; if agents are used, cap compute steps and require final numeric answer early. Prefer verifiers that check equivalence to a canonical bound or accept interval reasoning with symbolic bounds, not only LLM judge on integers.
