For agents: when n is huge (100000), treat small-n curve-fitting as hypothesis generation only; explicitly test exponential/ruler constructions before committing M; add a ‘scale sanity’ check (|M−log10(n)|) before writing response.txt. For evaluation protocols: separate scores for (i) answered vs timed out, (ii) answer magnitude bin (within orders of 10^k of truth), to avoid conflating timeout with ignorance; report whether wrong answers share the same false lemma (here 2−1/⌈n/2⌉) to measure systematic bias.

reports.tldr: Verdict: medium. Across 18 trials (0 passes), agents repeatedly fail on expert algebraic-geometry facts—especially that the Picard stack X₃ is universally closed but not separated—because they apply coarse heuristics (non-proper stack ⇒ not uc) instead of the valuative criterion. The bottleneck is real and well-evidenced, but it is narrow to research-level math rather than a broadly transferable agent capability.
reports.main_insight: This HLE task asks for a compact property profile of three categories fibered in groupoids (Hilbert scheme, weighted quotient, Picard stack). The trajectories show that frontier agents can often identify the right objects and even compute dimensions, but they systematically mishandle subtle moduli-theoretic flags—above all universal closedness for the non-rigidified Picard stack X₃. Fifteen of eighteen trials produced a formatted Answer line; none matched the reference [S,s,irr,33] [S,s,irr,3] [A,uc,6]. The dominant shared error is omitting uc on X₃ (0/15 correct on that tag) while explicitly reasoning that X₃ is not universally closed. A secondary cluster misclassifies X₂ as a DM quotient stack rather than an algebraic space/scheme after stabilizer analysis, and a smaller cluster misstates Hilb¹¹(𝔸³) reducibility using folklore about Iarrobino rather than the task’s intended irreducibility result.
reports.why_it_matters: HLE-style benchmarks are meant to measure expert knowledge, not coding skill. This task–trajectory set shows that current agent stacks (multiple models, claude-code/terminus/codex harnesses) can produce fluent, structured mathematical prose yet still encode wrong theorems with high confidence. For benchmark designers, it demonstrates that a single multi-part question can localize failure to specific expert lemmas (valuative criterion for stacks, trivial stabilizers on an open quotient, Hilbert-scheme irreducibility thresholds). For agent builders, it argues that math agents need verification hooks (literature lookup, formal checklists per property) rather than longer chain-of-thought alone.
reports.evidence_from_trajectories: Verifier bar: exact profile strings judged by an LLM ensemble (test_judge.py) against answer.txt [S,s,irr,33] [S,s,irr,3] [A,uc,6]; metadata rationale confirms X₃ is non-separated but satisfies the existence part of the valuative criterion (universally closed), dim Pic(C)+dim B𝔾_m=6. Automated extraction of final Answer lines: 8/15 trials submitted [S,s,irr,33] [S,s,irr,3] [A,6]—correct on X₁ and X₂ tags, missing uc on X₃; 0/15 had [A,uc,6]. claude-opus-4-7 (trial 087fd783, steps 6–7): writes a careful stabilizer proof for X₂ (free ℂ*-action ⇒ scheme) yet for X₃ states “It is not universally closed: the disjoint union over ℤ-many components Pic^d is not quasi-compact” and outputs Answer [A,6]; step 7 summary explicitly lists “not universally closed, reducible” for the Pic stack. gpt-5.5 (6fe13ca3, step 2): similarly concludes X₃ is “not separated, not irreducible, not universally closed” while answering [A,6]. hy3-preview (bb5fa5bd) revises toward [A,uc,7] at step 4—shows uc is guessable—but keeps coarse dimension 7 instead of 6. claude-opus-4-7 via terminus (fa10e5c2, steps 1–2): gets X₂ wrong as [DM,s,irr,3] after claiming finite cyclic stabilizers remain, and X₁ as [S,s,33] without irr based on Iarrobino reducibility at n≥8. Three trials (06004f09 glm-5.1, 1c43df62 mimo-v2.5-pro, e95d9147 deepseek-v4-pro) ended with status exception before a final Answer line. Per-component rates among answered trials: X₁ 11/15, X₂ 9/15, X₃ 0/15 on the uc tag.
reports.surface_failure_vs_root_cause: Surface failure: binary reward 0 on all trials because the extracted Answer profiles do not match [S,s,irr,33] [S,s,irr,3] [A,uc,6] under LLM-as-judge exactMatch-style grading. Root cause: not harness I/O (most agents wrote /logs/agent/response.txt correctly) but incorrect expert reasoning. The clearest root cause is a domain-knowledge/heuristic gap on algebraic stacks: agents treat universal closedness as synonymous with properness, quasi-compactness, or separatedness, and infer “infinitely many Pic^d components ⇒ not universally closed,” whereas the reference solution uses the valuative criterion—X₃ is universally closed despite being non-separated and reducible. Secondary root causes include incomplete stabilizer bookkeeping on weighted quotients (X₂) and outdated or misapplied Hilbert-scheme reducibility lore (X₁).
reports.intended_vs_unexpected_insight: The task is designed to test advanced algebraic geometry (CFG type, separated/uc/irr, dimension). Agents largely attempted that capability: they name Hilbert schemes, quotient stacks, and Picard stacks and debate properties in explanations. They fail on the intended capability—especially the non-obvious uc flag for X₃—rather than on an unrelated bottleneck. An unexpected but valuable secondary signal is split competence: several models nail X₂’s free-action argument and dimensions yet still fail the global score, showing that partial correct subproofs do not propagate to the final tagged answer. Another unexpected signal is overconfident revision without external checks (e.g., hy3 adding uc with wrong dimension).
reports.generalizability: Improving universal-closedness reasoning for non-separated moduli stacks would help on research-math and formal-moduli tasks, but it will not materially help typical software-engineering agents. The lesson generalizes within expert STEM evaluation and training: models need better calibration on counterintuitive definitions (uc ≠ proper, stacks can be uc but not s). It does not generalize as strongly as cross-domain agent skills (time budgeting, wide search, performance optimization). The repeated X₃ uc miss across models and harnesses is informative for math-benchmark design, but the overall task family remains niche.
reports.confounds: The sandbox adds almost no computational affordance—agents cannot run CAS or search papers—so failure blends pure parametric knowledge with reasoning under format constraints. LLM-as-judge ensemble grading may add variance, but agent answers are wrong on their face (e.g., missing uc) before judge ambiguity matters. Three exception trials reduce coverage slightly. Multiple distinct error modes (X₁ irr folklore, X₂ DM vs S, X₃ uc, occasional dim 7 vs 6) mean the task tests several lemmas at once, not a single atomic skill. Reference rationale cites a specific irreducibility paper for X₁ that agents rarely retrieve. Harness differences (claude-code vs terminus) do not explain the unified X₃ uc omission.
reports.implications_for_future_design: For benchmarks: tag multi-part math items by sub-skill (stack uc, quotient stabilizers, Hilbert irreducibility) and report partial credit to avoid conflating ‘almost right’ with total failure; include rationale links or allowlisted references when folklore thresholds matter. For agents: add property-check workflows (explicit valuative-criterion checklist for uc; verify stabilizers on each stratum for quotients; separate ‘not proper’ from ‘not uc’). For evaluation: HLE harbor tasks should report per-component accuracy; this task would show a sharp cliff on X₃ uc. For training: prioritize counterexample-rich stack geometry (uc without separatedness) rather than more terminal formatting practice—the agents already comply with response.txt structure.

reports.tldr: Verdict: medium. The task targets expert alkaloid identification from a small 2D structure GIF (ground truth: Sophoridine). Across 18 trials, 0 passed. Agents with native vision often converge on the wrong close stereoisomer Matrine with high confidence, while terminal-only harnesses produce unrelated guesses or time out after OCR/PIL thrashing—revealing both a narrow biochemistry discrimination gap and strong evaluation/harness confounds, but not one clean frontier-wide capability failure.
reports.main_insight: This HLE biology/medicine item tests whether agents can name a specific alkaloid from a 107×99 pixel chemical-structure GIF. The trajectories split into three regimes: (1) vision-enabled harnesses (Codex view_image, Claude Code Read on image.gif, Gemini CLI read_file binary) that usually recognize a tetracyclic quinolizidine lactam scaffold but name Matrine instead of Sophoridine; (2) Terminus-2 runs without base64 image injection that reconstruct the GIF via PIL/tesseract/ASCII art and then guess unrelated alkaloids (Nicotine, Noribogaine, Caffeine, Quinine, Berberine, Tropinone); and (3) nine AgentTimeoutError trials that never write response.txt after long tool loops (PIL installs, OCR, PubChem fetches). The deepest intended signal is fine-grained medicinal-chemistry naming among matrine-type stereoisomers; the strongest unintended signal is that Harbor-style terminal agents are poorly matched to image-native HLE items unless vision is wired through.
reports.why_it_matters: HLE is used to measure expert knowledge, but Harbor adapters often run models in shells where image understanding is optional or absent. This task shows that pass rate can collapse for reasons unrelated to the biochemistry being tested—modality, timeout thrashing, and stereoisomer ambiguity—so benchmark designers must separate 'can the model see the structure?' from 'does it know Sophoridine vs Matrine?' Training and evaluation teams should not interpret 0/18 here as pure ignorance of alkaloids; they should audit harness vision paths, image resolution/stereochemical cues, and whether the item is even discriminable from a flat 2D diagram before using it to rank frontier models.
reports.evidence_from_trajectories: Ground truth and verifier bar are exact-match LLM judge against 'Sophoridine' (tests/answer.txt, test_judge.py ensemble). Completed wrong answers: trial 693a9a4d (claude-opus-4-7, claude-code, step 8) Read image.gif as base64 then wrote 'Answer: Matrine' at 92% confidence; trial 0f1d8ffb (gpt-5.5 codex, step 7) used view_image on /app/image.gif then submitted Matrine at 78%; trial c783b55d (gemini-3.1-pro-preview, gemini-cli, steps 3–24) got 'Binary content' from read_file on the GIF, built PubChem ASCII overlays, and submitted Matrine at 99% claiming connectivity 'perfectly matches' Matrine vs Lupanine/Aphylline. Terminal misreads: trial 1a94db88 (terminus-2 opus, step 13) ASCII-from-pixels → Nicotine 70%; trial 3713fc7f (gemini terminus-2, step 14) → Noribogaine 80%; trial 4c334bd0 → Caffeine; trial 828d8ed2 → Quinine; trial b9d8c503 → Berberine; trial d14644e7 (claude-code mimo) → Tropinone. Timeout pattern: trial d7ae34c7 (terminus-2 minimax, 24 steps) installed tesseract, printed ASCII art of '@' atoms, never created response.txt before AgentTimeoutError at 1200s; similar for trials 29d3d882, 2a3e8efa, 4ea8c3cd, 6bf812e0, 9778de71, b1434567, cdb837ea (all exception status in meta.json).
reports.surface_failure_vs_root_cause: Surface failure: binary reward 0.0 on all trials because extracted answers (Matrine, Nicotine, etc.) do not match Sophoridine under the LLM judge. Deeper causes differ by cluster: for vision agents, misidentification of a matrine-type stereoisomer (Sophoridine is (5β)-matridin-15-one / allomatrine, same C15H24N2O scaffold as Matrine but different bridgehead stereochemistry) despite confident reasoning; for Terminus-2, lack of reliable image perception forces lossy ASCII/OCR pipelines on a 107×99 GIF, producing arbitrary alkaloid families; for nine trials, time/tool budget exhaustion (installing Pillow/tesseract, repeated OCR, PubChem API calls) without submitting an answer—an agent workflow failure layered on top of the knowledge task.
reports.intended_vs_unexpected_insight: Intended: expert biochemistry—name a specific alkaloid from its 2D structure (metadata category Biology/Medicine, raw_subject Biochemistry). Agents partially hit the intended skill (quinolizidine lactam recognition) but fail the exact name, most often naming the better-known stereoisomer Matrine. Unexpected but valuable: (1) harness modality gap—terminus-2 trials show vision_b64=False while claude-code/codex show vision; (2) overconfidence on wrong close answers (78–99% for Matrine); (3) half of trials timing out on tooling rather than answering; (4) possible item ambiguity—flat 2D line drawings may not encode stereochemistry needed to distinguish Sophoridine from Matrine, so even capable vision models default to the canonical name.
reports.generalizability: Partially generalizable. The lesson that terminal agents need explicit multimodal image delivery for HLE image items transfers to any vision-QA benchmark run in Harbor/Daytona shells. The Matrine-vs-Sophoridine confusion generalizes within medicinal chemistry and stereoisomer naming but not broadly across agent tasks. Timeout/tool thrashing generalizes as poor time-and-deliverable awareness when the core answer could be committed earlier. It does not generalize like a single missing algorithmic skill—failure modes are too heterogeneous (random alkaloids vs near-miss stereoisomer vs no submission).
reports.confounds: Multiple confounds weaken a high insightfulness rating: (1) harness heterogeneity (codex/claude-code/gemini-cli vs terminus-2) mixes vision and non-vision paths in one task score; (2) 9/18 AgentTimeoutError trials provide no final chemistry answer; (3) tiny GIF (107×99, ~2 KB) may omit stereochemical wedges needed to separate Sophoridine from Matrine; (4) sparse sandbox (no PIL initially, missing file/hexdump/strings) pushes agents into long install side quests; (5) LLM-as-judge exact match may be correct for benchmark fidelity but offers no partial credit for matrine-type scaffold; (6) some agents used external PubChem/network calls despite 'do not cheat' wording—uneven compliance. The 0/18 sweep is therefore overdetermined by setup as well as knowledge.
reports.implications_for_future_design: For benchmark tasks: tag HLE image items with required modalities and reject or adapt items where the reference stereoisomer cannot be distinguished from common confusers on the provided asset; provide higher-resolution structure images with explicit stereochemistry when testing isomer names. For agent harnesses: ensure image.gif is always passed to the model via native vision (base64 Read, view_image) rather than terminal pixel hacks; cap tool-install loops or pre-bake Pillow in the image for chemistry tasks. For evaluation protocols: report stratified metrics (vision vs non-vision harness, submitted vs timeout); consider structured outputs (SMILES/InChI) plus synonym-aware judging for stereoisomer families. For training: calibrate confidence when distinguishing congeners (matrine, sophoridine, oxymatrine) from Sophora alkaloids; teach agents to commit an answer before exploratory OCR/PubChem spirals exhaust the 1200s budget.

reports.tldr: Verdict: medium. This HLE runology item cleanly tests expert identification of a specific Ingvar runestone (Ög 155) from an inscription fragment; all 18 trials scored 0. Trajectories show agents can sometimes transcribe runes or build clever retrieval pipelines, but they systematically fail to map evidence to the correct specialist catalog ID—defaulting to famous stones (Sö 179), confabulating corpus facts (Vs 19 for a hælfningi inscription), or accepting false-positive computer-vision matches (Sö 96). The lesson is real and transferable to other expert-ID benchmarks, but failure modes are heterogeneous and partly domain-narrow.
reports.main_insight: The task–trajectory set reveals a gap between surface-level humanities competence and authoritative specialist identification. Agents know what Ingvar runestones are, can discuss Rundata-style IDs, and sometimes read visible Younger Futhark bands, but they do not reliably retrieve the exact corpus entry (Ög 155) from a ~26-stone specialist set with near-duplicate formulae. The strongest signal is a near-miss: one agent correctly read þurfriþ × risti … × hilfniki—the signature phrase of Ög 155—yet answered Vs 19 with 100% confidence, misattributing a rare lexical marker (hælfningi) that in fact appears only on Ög 155 and Ög 145. Other agents skipped careful reading entirely and anchored on the most famous exemplar (Gripsholm, Sö 179) or on heuristic style cues (RAK → Sö 131).
reports.why_it_matters: HLE-style benchmarks increasingly mix multimodal expert QA with exact-match grading. This task shows that raising agent scores on such items is not mainly about better terminal tooling or longer search loops; it requires structured access to specialist references (e.g., Samnordisk runtextdatabas / Rundata), disambiguation among near-duplicate catalog entries, and calibration when evidence is partial. That matters for training (teach retrieval over confabulation), for agent design (when to query authoritative databases vs. Wikipedia), and for benchmark construction (items that punish popularity bias and reward corpus-level precision).
reports.evidence_from_trajectories: Across 18 trials, binary reward was 0 for every model/harness pair (meta.json). Seven trials completed without harness exceptions; nine hit AgentTimeoutError after spending many steps on pip installs, OCR, and OpenCV pipelines (e.g., trial c74e43c9 glm-5.1 terminus-2 timed out at 1200s while installing Pillow/Tesseract). Completed wrong answers cluster into three patterns: (1) Popularity/default-exemplar guessing—claude-opus-4-7 claude-code (68cdf4b2, step ~7) wrote Sö 179 claiming visible "haraltr" and "bruþur" matching Gripsholm; gpt-5.5 codex (321664ab, step ~14) gave Sö 179 at 90% confidence with the same phantom "bruþur Ingvars" reading; claude-opus-4-7 terminus-2 (c5e02102, step ~17) admitted OCR failed but still answered Sö 179 at 15% as the "most famous" Ingvar stone. (2) Partial transcription + wrong catalog lookup—gemini-3.1-pro-preview gemini-cli (bb8c6f54, steps 12–16) meticulously traced þurfriþ × risti and hilfniki/hælfningi, then concluded Vs 19 at 100% confidence even though hælfningi is the discriminant for Ög 155 in the specialist literature. (3) Overconfident heuristic/vision pipelines—gemini-3.1-pro-preview terminus-2 (674db0b2, step ~22) installed OpenCV, scraped Wikipedia Ingvar-stone images, ran SIFT, and reported 133 feature matches for Sö 96 with "Confidence: 100%"; MiniMax-M2.7 claude-code (bb46fa1c) chose Sö 131 from RAK style heuristics at 85% despite Ög 155 also being RAK-class. No trajectory mentioned Ög 155.
reports.surface_failure_vs_root_cause: Surface failure: every agent submitted an incorrect exact-match answer (or no gradable answer after timeout/exception), so the LLM-as-judge ensemble in test_judge.py returned reward 0 against ground truth "Ög 155" from answer.txt. Deeper cause: not a single bug or format error, but failure to perform specialist corpus disambiguation—turning partial visual/textual evidence into the correct Rundata ID among confusable Ingvar stones. Sub-mechanisms include (a) salience bias toward famous stones, (b) confabulated rune readings that match well-known inscriptions, (c) incorrect expert-memory lookup after otherwise-accurate transcription, and (d) false-positive feature matching when agents substitute generic web corpora for authoritative runological databases.
reports.intended_vs_unexpected_insight: The task was designed to test hard expert humanities knowledge with an image (HLE Runology category; has_image=true in metadata.json). Agents did fail on that intended capability—none identified Ög 155. The unexpected but valuable secondary insight is architectural: terminal-first agents often cannot reliably see /app/image.png, so they burn budget on OCR/pip installs (9/18 timeouts) or guess from priors; and tool-augmented agents can look highly competent (SIFT pipeline, detailed rune tracing) while still being wrong with extreme confidence. The Gemini CLI near-miss is especially informative because it separates perception from specialist retrieval—the model read the right words but picked the wrong stone.
reports.generalizability: The core pattern—accurate partial analysis plus failure to disambiguate among near-duplicate entries in a specialist catalog—generalizes beyond runology to taxonomy keys, manuscript sigla, legal citation IDs, artifact accession numbers, and other expert QA where many items share formulaic text. Improving structured retrieval and verification against authoritative databases would help across those domains. Generalizability is capped because the item also requires Younger Futhark literacy and Ingvar-corpus knowledge; popularity bias toward Sö 179 is partly task-family-specific; and terminal vision limitations confound some harnesses, so not every failure is purely "missing runology."
reports.confounds: Several factors muddy a single-capability story: (1) 9/18 trials ended with AgentTimeoutError, often mid-setup (installing Pillow, Tesseract, OpenCV) rather than at a clear reasoning impasse; (2) 2/18 had NonZeroAgentExitCodeError from the claude-code harness before grading; (3) terminus/codex agents in a text-only shell may have weaker or indirect image access than claude-code/gemini-cli Read tools, inflating OCR/guessing failures; (4) the instruction forbids "online solutions" but some agents still scraped Wikipedia for SIFT—unclear how much external retrieval was available or intended; (5) diverse wrong answers (Sö 179, Sö 96, Sö 131, Vs 19, U 439) mean reviewers must attribute failures by trajectory, not by a single shared mistake; (6) LLM-as-judge scoring adds variance, though here all answers were clearly mismatched with Ög 155.
reports.implications_for_future_design: For benchmarks: keep exact-match expert-ID items like this—they discriminate well—but report failure typology (transcription vs. retrieval vs. timeout) and consider providing or requiring a curated specialist index when the learning target is catalog lookup, not memorizing ~26 stones. For agents: when a question asks for a corpus ID, prioritize querying structured databases (Rundata/Skaldic) over Wikipedia popularity; after reading distinctive n-grams (e.g., hilfniki), verify uniqueness before answering; treat high-confidence vision matches as hypotheses to confirm textually. For harness design: ensure reliable multimodal access to task images early, cap setup thrashing (preinstall OCR/vision deps in the image), and separate grades for "read inscription" vs. "map to ID" to localize errors. For evaluation: items where rare lexical markers discriminate among similar entries (Ög 155 vs. Ög 145) are more diagnostic than items solvable by naming the most famous example.

reports.tldr: Verdict: medium. Across 18 trials (0/18 pass), agents repeatedly fail on fine-grained Hebrew manuscript verse localization and on resisting the BHS→Tiberian stereotype, even when they read the visible shelfmark L-G Bib. 7.37. The task cleanly separates “generic Genizah parchment” reasoning from the exact four-field answer (babylonian 10-16 parchment 1chr.004:009), but the lesson is partly confounded by harness timeouts and narrow paleographic domain scope.
reports.main_insight: This HLE image-QA task targets expert multimodal humanities reasoning on a Cairo Genizah bifolium (Lewis-Gibson L-G Bible 7.37). The trajectories show a layered failure mode: many agents answer coarse metadata correctly (parchment; plausible 9th–16th-century spans) but systematically miss the discriminating subskills—(1) identifying Babylonian (supralinear) vocalization rather than defaulting to Tiberian because the prompt mentions BHS, and (2) mapping faded two-column layout to the precise BHS citation 1chr.004:009. Strongest runs (e.g., claude-opus-4-7 trial 0946c35e, gemini-3.1-pro trial c8c97df6) read the label and infer Babylonian vocalization yet still hallucinate plausible biblical references (gen.036:031, lev.008:028) instead of Chronicles 4:9. A second, cross-cutting pattern is operational: Terminus-style agents without reliable native vision spend hundreds of steps on OCR/thresholding pipelines and often hit the 1200s AgentTimeoutError before submitting any answer.
reports.why_it_matters: The task exposes where “looks like expert reasoning” stops being verifiable: agents can narrate paleographic features and Genizah context while still being wrong on the exact string the LLM judge requires. For benchmark design, it shows that composite HLE items mixing catalog metadata, script tradition, and verse indexing need sub-score reporting or staged gates; otherwise pass rate collapses to zero without telling you which capability failed. For agent improvement, it highlights two trainable gaps—ground answers in retrievable authority when identifiers are visible, and calibrate confidence when OCR is poor—that matter beyond this single manuscript, though less universally than core coding or math skills.
reports.evidence_from_trajectories: Ground truth from tests/answer.txt and metadata: babylonian 10-16 parchment 1chr.004:009; the public CUDL record for MS-LG-BIBLE-00007-00037 lists Babylonian vocalisation, 10th–16th century, parchment, and 1 Chronicles 3–4 content. Of 18 trials, 8 produced a four-token Answer line; none matched fully. Partial scoring on those 8: parchment 8/8; date exactly 10-16 only in trials b769592e and 384e3ef3; vowel babylonian in 0946c35e, c8c97df6, b769592e; tiberian wrongly chosen in 25dbbb62 (step 50: “tiberian 09-15 parchment 1kin.003:001” with claimed Hebrew “vayitchatten shelomoh”), be849c21, 384e3ef3 (gen.001:001). Trial 0946c35e (claude-opus-4-7, 65 steps) correctly cites label “L-G Bib. 7.37” and Babylonian supralinear marks at step 64 but answers gen.036:031 at 35% confidence—wrong book/chapter. Trial c8c97df6 (gemini-cli, 21 steps) web-searches “L-G Bib. 7.37” (steps ~13–20), concludes babylonian and parchment, yet asserts lev.008:028 at 99% confidence—clear overconfidence on unread text. Trial f395f18e (gpt-5.5 terminus, 22 steps) ends mid OCR connected-components loop (step 22) and times out with no Answer. Trial 9f27010c (deepseek, 97 steps) performs extensive WebSearch on Lewis-Gibson fragments but its synthesis incorrectly generalizes “Tiberian vocalisation” for the collection and never submits 1chr.004:009. Ten trials never reach a graded answer: ten AgentTimeoutError (e.g., f395f18e, d78044ba), two NonZeroAgentExitCodeError (b1252e39, b769592e), one RewardFileNotFoundError—showing harness/time limits are a major secondary failure channel.
reports.surface_failure_vs_root_cause: Surface failure: all 18 binary_reward=0 outcomes under the LLM-as-judge exactMatch bar in test_judge.py (extract Answer: line, compare to babylonian 10-16 parchment 1chr.004:009). Root cause is not random formatting: the decisive miss is Q4 verse identification from a degraded bifolium—agents substitute familiar citations (gen.001:001, lev.008:028, 1kin.003:001) or mis-read list context (gen.036:031 after seeing “אלוף”). A secondary root cause on Q1 is stereotype substitution: “BHS” in the prompt triggers Tiberian assumptions despite visible supralinear pointing (gpt-5.5 step 50; deepseek step ~4286 reasoning). A tertiary root cause is failure to close the loop from visible shelfmark to authoritative catalog (gemini finds 7.37 in search but does not ground Q4 in CUDL’s “1 Chronicles … 4:12” range). Timeouts are a separate root cause for terminus agents that treat terminal OCR as a substitute for vision rather than budgeting toward lookup or submission.
reports.intended_vs_unexpected_insight: Intended insight (per metadata rationale): combine OCR/visual analysis of faded ink with specialist knowledge of Babylonian vocalization and BHS verse numbering; reverse image search to Cambridge CUDL is an expected solution path for dating/material/tradition. Agents did fail on that intended stack—no trial reached 1chr.004:009. Unexpected but valuable secondary insights: (1) BHS mention in the question actively harms Q1 by pulling models toward Tiberian; (2) reading the shelfmark is insufficient without fetching MS-LG-BIBLE-00007-00037 metadata; (3) high stated confidence (gemini 99%) decouples from verification; (4) ~56% of trials fail operationally (timeout/crash) before judgment, which inflates apparent “inability” versus “wrong but gradable” answers.
reports.generalizability: Moderately generalizable lessons: (a) when an artifact exposes a stable identifier (library shelfmark, DOI, accession), agents should prioritize authoritative retrieval over speculative OCR narratives—a pattern that applies to museum specimens, lab notebooks, and legal exhibits; (b) prompts that include domain shorthand (BHS) can cause harmful prior injection unless agents verify against the artifact’s actual tradition; (c) under degraded inputs, agents should lower confidence and seek external grounding rather than fabricating verse text. Less generalizable: the specific skill of mapping Genizah column layout to BHS verse boundaries is niche humanities paleography; improving it helps manuscript/digital-humanities agents more than typical software engineering agents.
reports.confounds: Several confounds limit a “high” verdict: (1) exact four-field string grading with no partial credit—trials with 3/4 correct fields still score 0; (2) anti-cheat wording (“Do not cheat by using online solutions”) may discourage web lookup even though metadata says reverse search is valid; (3) harness heterogeneity—terminus agents lack the same native image tools as claude-code/gemini-cli, biasing toward OCR thrashing and timeouts; (4) 10/18 trials end with AgentTimeoutError or agent exit before response.txt, mixing capability failure with time-budget failure; (5) example formats in the prompt include 2kin.020:007 and psa.100:025, which may anchor wrong guesses (b769592e answered 2kin.020:012); (6) century span off-by-one (09-15 vs 10-16) is ambiguous relative to catalog “10th–16th century” wording.
reports.implications_for_future_design: Benchmark tasks should (1) report per-question rewards (vowel, date, material, verse) to localize failures; (2) either supply vision-native tooling in all harnesses or explicitly allow catalog lookup when shelfmarks are visible, clarifying that institutional metadata retrieval is not “cheating”; (3) avoid or disambiguate BHS shorthand if the tested tradition is non-Tiberian; (4) cap OCR preprocessing steps or provide a lightweight IIIF/metadata API hook for Genizah-class items so agents test identification rather than terminal image hacking; (5) require confidence calibration tied to evidence (e.g., cite catalog URL or transcribed line); (6) set agent timeouts with reference to the 20-minute instruction or add early-exit heuristics when label text is extracted. For training, prioritize workflows: read identifier → fetch authority record → only then attempt fine OCR for fields not in metadata (here, column-level verse boundary within a known chapter range).

reports.tldr: Verdict: medium. Across 18 frontier-model trials on this HLE art-history attribution item, agents almost uniformly answered Marc Chagall instead of the ground truth Eduardo Chillida. The pattern cleanly shows stereotype-driven plausibility matching (blue/yellow, Christian resonances) beating exact source verification, and web search often reinforced the wrong celebrity attribution—but the lesson is largely confined to obscure expert-trivia retrieval rather than a broad agent-workflow gap.
reports.main_insight: This task–trajectory set shows that when asked to attribute an obscure literary-theological quote to a 20th-century artist, agents do not perform careful provenance checking; they perform feature-to-famous-name matching. The prompt’s cues (Christian resonances, blue and yellow, wonder at creation) map almost deterministically to Marc Chagall in parametric memory, and agents treat that fit as if it were identification. Even agents that run DuckDuckGo scrapes (e.g., gemini-3.1-pro via terminus-2) search within a Chagall/Kandinsky/Rouault hypothesis set, interpret noisy snippets as confirmation, and submit Chagall at 90–100% confidence. Zero trajectories mention Eduardo Chillida, the Basque sculptor named in metadata as the Spanish source (Escritos, La Fábrica, 2005). The intended HLE capability—precise expert knowledge / exactMatch attribution—is what fails; the unexpected secondary signal is that retrieval can worsen accuracy by locking in a famous wrong answer.
reports.why_it_matters: HLE-style benchmarks increasingly place agents in sandboxes with tools and anti-cheating language, assuming failures will reveal whether agents can *find* expert facts rather than merely *guess* them. This item shows a common failure mode for attribution and citation tasks: conflating thematic plausibility with verified authorship. That matters for benchmark design because a 0/18 sweep can look like a hard knowledge gap when it is partly a reasoning-and-search strategy gap (never querying Spanish text, never considering sculptors vs painters, never treating Chagall as a hypothesis to falsify). For agent improvement, it suggests training and tool policies that require primary-source or multi-query disconfirmation before high-confidence submission on quote-ID tasks—not just more art-history facts in pretraining.
reports.evidence_from_trajectories: All 18 trajectories contain “Chagall” in the serialized trace; automated extraction of final `Answer:` lines shows Marc Chagall in 16 runs, Georges Rouault once (b0d3125e, claude-opus-4-7 terminus-2, step 4 writes Rouault at 45% confidence then deliberates but never updates the file to Chillida), and placeholder text in exception-partial runs. Representative moments: (1) gpt-5.5 codex trial 4ff5c1ee step 7 writes `Answer: Marc Chagall` with `Confidence: 90%` from pure parametric reasoning, citing stained glass and crucifixion scenes with no search. (2) claude-opus-4-7 claude-code trial c05a4ac0 step 7 explicitly says the quote “points strongly to Marc Chagall” because of blue/yellow and Christian works, then step 8 writes `Answer: Marc Chagall` at 65% confidence with zero `web_search_requests`. (3) gemini-3.1-pro terminus-2 trial 150af2db steps 2–4 run DuckDuckGo scripts (`search.py`, `search2.py`) but only query Chagall/Kandinsky/Rouault; step 5 concludes snippets “clearly associate” the quote with Chagall; step 6 writes `Answer: Marc Chagall` at `Confidence: 100%` despite never searching “Chillida” or the Spanish original. (4) deepseek-v4-pro terminus-2 trial db165dea step 2 writes Chagall at 90% from memory; step 3 reasoning mentions Gorky/Blake as doubts but still submits Chagall. (5) b0d3125e step 4 is the only substantive alternative (Rouault) but still wrong vs Eduardo Chillida. Thirteen trials completed verification with `reward: 0.0`; five had infrastructure exceptions (three `AgentTimeoutError`, two `RewardFileNotFoundError`) but still produced Chagall answers in trajectories before failure.
reports.surface_failure_vs_root_cause: Surface failure: every judged trial receives binary reward 0 because the LLM-as-judge ensemble (`test_judge.py`, comparing extracted answer to `answer.txt` “Eduardo Chillida.”) marks “Marc Chagall” incorrect. Root cause: agents lack the obscure fact (Chillida’s Spanish aphorism in Escritos) in usable form and substitute the most semantically aligned famous artist. Deeper mechanism: (a) cue-driven stereotype completion toward Chagall; (b) no falsification loop or language-variant search (metadata rationale gives Spanish: “Cómo es posible sin Dios…”); (c) when search is used, confirmation bias toward the prior celebrity (150af2db escalates confidence to 100% after weak DuckDuckGo snippets). This is not primarily a formatting, timeout, or verifier bug for the 13 completed runs—the agents chose the wrong entity with high stated confidence.
reports.intended_vs_unexpected_insight: Intended: HLE exactMatch expert knowledge in Art History—identify the precise author of a rare quote (Eduardo Chillida). Agents failed exactly on that capability across models and harnesses (codex, claude-code, terminus-2, gemini-cli, qwen-coder). Unexpected but valuable: tool-using agents that *do* search still fail, and search appears to *increase* overconfidence in the wrong answer (Chagall at 100% after HTML scraping) rather than correct toward Chillida; also, the uniform wrong answer despite one agent briefly considering Rouault shows the item functions as a structured distractor trap, not random error.
reports.generalizability: Partially generalizable. The habit of mapping quote imagery to the most famous matching artist will recur on other attribution, provenance, and “who said/wrote this?” benchmarks, especially when prompts include superficial cues aligned with a well-known figure. Improving disconfirmation search (alternate languages, exact-phrase queries, sculptor vs painter category checks) would help quote-ID and scholarly Q&A beyond this item. However, knowing that Chillida wrote this specific passage is a narrow fact unlikely to transfer to coding, math, or systems tasks; fixing it alone would mostly raise HLE humanities scores, not agent competence broadly. Thus the insight is real but narrower than top-tier cross-benchmark capability gaps like time-budget management or systematic wide-source reconciliation.
reports.confounds: Several confounds limit strength: (1) The English prompt hides that the canonical text is Spanish (per `metadata.json` rationale), so failure may reflect translation/corpus coverage, not only reasoning. (2) Sandbox DuckDuckGo HTML scraping is brittle—agents may miss Chillida even if retrievable with better APIs or Spanish queries (attempts in this environment returned zero snippets for Chillida queries). (3) Outer instruction says “Do not cheat by using online solutions,” which may suppress search in some harnesses while others still scrape the web, creating harness heterogeneity. (4) Five of 18 trials ended in `AgentTimeoutError` or `RewardFileNotFoundError`, so not all failures are capability failures (e.g., glm-5.1 terminus-2 trial af4bcdab timed out after 1200s with 18 steps). (5) LLM-as-judge scoring adds variance, though here the wrong name is unambiguous. (6) 0/18 pass rate could partly reflect memorized Chagall misattribution in training data rather than agent-specific workflow flaws—though trajectories still show explicit stereotype reasoning, not random guesses.
reports.implications_for_future_design: For benchmarks: include items where thematic cues deliberately mislead (Chagall trap vs Chillida truth) to separate plausibility reasoning from verified attribution; report whether agents search, in which languages, and whether they test rival hypotheses; provide optional metadata hooks (original language, medium/sculptor) without giving the answer. For agents: on quote-ID tasks, mandate a checklist—exact phrase search, source language query, list ≥3 candidates, require disconfirming evidence before >80% confidence; treat famous-name matches as hypotheses, not conclusions. For harnesses: distinguish “no web cheating” from “no verification”; offer reliable citation tools instead of ad-hoc HTML scrapers that amplify SEO noise. For evaluation: log extracted `Answer:` and confidence separately from judge ensemble (`JUDGE_MODELS` with repeats) to diagnose overconfidence on wrong entities. For training: emphasize primary-source attribution and penalize confident misattribution to celebrity figures when exactMatch is required.

reports.tldr: Verdict: medium. All 18 agents failed this HLE physics item (0% reward), but trajectories show a structured split: many hallucinate generic shock profiles (tanh/sech/logistic), while several that correctly invoke Becker shock theory still botch the Mach √3 closure—wrong exponential prefactors (3 or 8 instead of 2), sign flips, or coordinate-origin choices. That is a real, cross-model lesson about unreliable completion of rare closed-form STEM derivations, but it is narrower than a frontier-wide capability gap because the task is intentionally niche expert trivia.
reports.main_insight: This task–trajectory set shows that frontier coding agents, when forced through a Harbor sandbox to answer a rare fluids closed form, do not fail uniformly at “never heard of shocks.” A large fraction correctly compute Rankine–Hugoniot jumps (ρ₂/ρ₀ = 2 for γ = 5/3, M = √3) and name Becker’s Pr = 3/4 structure, yet still submit wrong density profiles. The dominant error is not missing the problem class but (a) substituting stereotyped shock-structure ansätze (tanh, sech², logistic rational forms) that satisfy boundary ratios but are not the Johnson (2014) inversion, or (b) carrying a Becker ODE through integration and then making Mach-specific algebra mistakes—especially the prefactor inside the exponential (2 vs 3 vs 8) and the sign of x in exp(±4x/(3L)). The reference answer 1 + 1/√(1 + 2 exp(−4x/(3L))) comes from Johnson’s closed-form shock family; agents almost never cite that paper and instead re-derive, then assert high confidence.
reports.why_it_matters: HLE-style benchmarks are used to measure expert knowledge and calibration. These trajectories show that agent harnesses plus strong models can produce fluent, physically plausible derivations that are still wrong on exactMatch grading—useful for evaluation design (need symbolic equivalence or literature-grounded rubrics, not just RH limits) and for agent training (verification of closed forms, not just setup of governing ODEs). The near-miss cluster (correct −4x/(3L) scaling but wrong inner coefficient or sign) is especially informative: it suggests scoring and training should target algebraic completion and normalization conventions, not only whether the model knows “Becker shock.”
reports.evidence_from_trajectories: Unanimous 0.0 reward across 18 trials (meta.json). Wrong-profile hallucinations: minimax-m2.7 terminus (trial 146a9a46, step 4) writes ρ/ρ₀ = 1 + (1/2) sech²(3ξ/4); minimax claude-code (91be7cce, step 32) finalizes ρ/ρ₀ = 3/2 + (1/2) tanh(x/L) at 85% confidence; mimo terminus (4e6aa5ed) gives ρ/ρ₀ = 1 + 1/(1 + exp(−x/L)); opus terminus (2d6cc6b6, step 6) uses a rational (1 + e^{x/L})/(1 + 0.5 e^{x/L}) form. Becker-aware near-misses: claude-opus-4-7 (0e744168, steps 7–8) derives dv/dx = (4/(3L))(1−v)(1/2−v)/v and answers ρ/ρ₀ = 1 + [1 + 3 exp(−4x/(3L))]^(−1/2) with 100% confidence; qwen-coder (dc42e096, steps 4–9) similarly ends at 1 + [1 + 3 exp(−4x/(3L))]^(−1/2); gpt-5.5 codex (1b423bab, step 14) writes 1 + 1/√(1 + exp[4(X−X₀)/3])—correct structural family but wrong sign and missing factor 2. Sign-only near-miss: gemini-3.1-pro terminus (52387152, step 2 bash) outputs 1 + 1/√(1 + 2 exp(4x/(3L))}—right prefactor 2, wrong exponent sign. Coefficient slip: mimo claude-code (e8cc2e1b) uses factor 8 inside the exponential. Non-answers: hy3-preview (72c28f85) stops after step 2 (“Let me read the instruction file”) with no response.txt; six trials have status exception / missing verifier reward file (e.g. 0fdf27bc, 290b2452, 4e6aa5ed, af20f8d2 per result.json). No trajectory retrieves Johnson (2014) despite metadata rationale pointing there.
reports.surface_failure_vs_root_cause: Surface failure: every agent receives binary reward 0 because the LLM-judge ensemble (test_judge.py, exactMatch against answer.txt) rejects their written Answer line. Root cause is not file-format noncompliance—most trials do write Explanation/Answer/Confidence to /logs/agent/response.txt. The deeper cause is incorrect expert physics: either inventing a familiar shock profile that matches ρ: 1→2 asymptotics, or executing a Becker reduction but failing the Mach √3 specialization and ρ(η) inversion that yields the Johnson closed form 1 + 1/√(1 + 2 exp(−4x/(3L))). Near-misses (3 vs 2, + vs − in the exponent) look like integration-constant / midpoint-normalization algebra errors, not random noise.
reports.intended_vs_unexpected_insight: Intended insight (HLE expert physics): agents lack the specific closed-form density profile for viscous shocks at Pr = 3/4 and M = √3—confirmed, 0/18 pass. Unexpected but valuable nuance: failure is bifurcated. Roughly half the trajectories never reach Becker–Johnson at all and instead emit tanh/sech/logistic templates with high confidence after correct RH arithmetic. The other half demonstrates partial mastery (Becker enthalpy trick, correct downstream ratio) yet still fails exactMatch due to coefficient/sign slips—suggesting the benchmark also probes unreliable symbolic completion and overconfidence, not only absent domain knowledge. The agent sandbox (CPU, shell) is largely irrelevant; no trial meaningfully uses computation to verify the formula against the ODE.
reports.generalizability: Partially generalizable. The lesson “do not trust a fluent derivation of a rare closed form—verify against literature or limiting cases” applies across expert STEM, law, and medicine QA, not only shock physics. The specific gap (Johnson 2014 Table 1 at M = √3) does not transfer broadly: fixing it mainly helps similar HLE physics items and other citation-locked formula recall tasks. The more portable sub-lesson is calibration: models assign 85–100% confidence to wrong tanh/sech answers and to near-correct exponentials. Improving general symbolic verification (check ρ(−∞)=1, ρ(+∞)=2, and ODE consistency) would help more tasks than memorizing one formula.
reports.confounds: Six of 18 trials ended with harness/verifier exceptions (no reward.txt), so some failures are infrastructure noise, not model capability. The task forbids “online solutions,” which may block the natural fix (fetch Johnson 2014) even though the benchmark rationale assumes that paper—agents are pushed to re-derive. LLM-as-judge exactMatch may be strict on equivalent forms (e.g. implicit η–f relations vs explicit ρ(x)), though here errors are substantively wrong functions, not notation. Coordinate-origin choices (midpoint at ρ = 3ρ₀/2 vs 4ρ₀/3) appear in agent text and could confuse graders even when physics is equivalent; in practice agents used genuinely different formulas, not equivalent reparameterizations. The sandbox agent setting adds steps (read instruction.md, mkdir, heredocs) unrelated to the tested knowledge.
reports.implications_for_future_design: For benchmarks: keep such items to test expert recall, but report subtags (profile family wrong vs Becker near-miss vs incomplete) because aggregate 0% hides diagnostic structure; consider symbolic equivalence checking or allowing literature retrieval when the rubric cites a specific paper. For agents: add a mandatory verification pass for closed-form PDE/shock answers (asymptotic limits + differentiate implied ODE) before writing 100% confidence; discourage default tanh/sech shock templates when Pr = 3/4 Becker reduction is invoked. For harness design: pure-QA HLE items need not spawn full terminal agents—reducing unrelated tool steps would sharpen measurement. For evaluation: ensemble LLM judges are appropriate given answer format diversity, but near-miss exponentials (2 vs 3) show why human or CAS adjudication matters for scientific benchmarks.

reports.tldr: Verdict: medium. This HLE geography item cleanly exposes two separable agent weaknesses: (1) terminal harnesses without reliable vision burn the full 1200s on forensic shell pipelines and often never answer, and (2) vision-capable agents usually get the Pacific Northwest but anchor to a famous wrong city (Seattle, Port Angeles, Vancouver) or hallucinate entirely different scenes. Zero of 18 trials answered Tacoma; the signal is real but split across modality mismatch and hyper-local geolocation error rather than one frontier-wide capability gap.
reports.main_insight: The task asks for exact city identification from a low-light Titlow Beach (Tacoma, WA) shoreline photo with only generic cues (chain-link fence, curved pebble beach, Puget Sound sunset, distant treeline, beach fire). Across 18 trials, failures cluster into two populations. Roughly half of runs (10/18) are Terminus/Codex-style shell agents that never establish reliable visual access and exhaust the 1200s budget on OCR, metadata mining, ASCII pixel dumps, or downloading/running CLIP/VQA models that hallucinate bridges and dogs. The other half produce answers but almost never Tacoma: they either correctly localize to the Pacific Northwest then default to a more salient city (Seattle at 95% in trial 05c9af39, Port Angeles at 45% in ac9e8760) or confabulate unrelated geographies (Bergen marina in 125d79ec, Dubai/Burj Khalifa from ASCII art in c0f8a98e, Beijing, Lisbon, Page AZ). No trajectory mentions Titlow Beach. The task therefore measures fine-grained visual geolocation plus benchmark harness alignment more than generic reasoning.
reports.why_it_matters: HLE items are increasingly deployed inside autonomous coding agents, not standalone VQA APIs. These trajectories show that packaging a pure image-QA problem in a shell-first harness can make failure look like incompetence when the root issue is missing modality. Separately, even strong vision models exhibit metropolitan anchoring and overconfident landmark fabrication—failure modes that break trust calibration in expert-QA benchmarks and any agent workflow that must commit to a precise entity (city, file, CVE) from weak evidence. Both lessons inform how to design tasks, timeouts, and scoring for multimodal agent evals.
reports.evidence_from_trajectories: Reference answer is Tacoma (metadata rationale: Titlow Beach; chain-link fencing, shoreline curvature, foliage). Completed wrong answers: 05c9af39 (gemini-cli, step ~17) writes Seattle at 95% citing invented Golden Gardens bonfire/fence details after briefly listing Tacoma as a candidate; 5ef145b3 (claude-opus-4-7, step 7) reads the image natively, notes PNW cues, but answers Seattle at 25%; ac9e8760 (qwen-coder, steps 3–21) runs multiple GPT-4o vision calls and converges on Port Angeles, Washington at 45%; 125d79ec (glm-5.1, step ~14) describes a Norwegian marina with boats and mountains—nothing like the actual dusk beach; c0f8a98e (claude-opus-4-7 terminus, steps 24–26) admits it is working from ASCII thresholding without seeing the image and answers Dubai/Burj Khalifa. Timeout/no-answer cluster: ed8b21df (deepseek-v4-pro terminus, 32 steps) loops on LSB steganography, grep for city names in PNG bytes, and OCR; 8d4d3f46 (gemini-3.1 terminus, 30 steps) installs ViLT/CLIP, gets hallucinated Golden Gate Bridge/dog outputs, pivots to Vancouver at 95%, then times out while chasing bridge-explosion hypotheses; 0d6de001 (hy3-preview terminus, 31 steps) installs Pillow/CLIP but never writes response.txt before AgentTimeoutError. Harness exceptions: 10/18 AgentTimeoutError or NonZeroAgentExitCodeError vs 8/18 completed submissions, all reward 0.0 under exactMatch LLM-judge ensemble.
reports.surface_failure_vs_root_cause: Surface failure: binary reward 0 on all 18 trials—wrong city string or no gradable response before timeout. Deeper causes are bifurcated. For Terminus/Codex runs, the root cause is modality/harness mismatch: agents treat /app/image.png as a forensic file to decode rather than an image to perceive, so they never reach a grounded hypothesis and burn the full agent timeout (1200s). For claude-code/gemini-cli/qwen-coder runs with image access, the root cause is hyper-local geolocation discrimination failure plus reasoning pathology: correct regional priors (Puget Sound, conifers, inlet water) followed by anchoring to the most famous nearby city or overfitting spurious features into named landmarks (Golden Gardens, Strait of Juan de Fuca) instead of the ground-truth Tacoma beach. A minority root cause is outright visual confabulation (Bergen marina, Dubai tower) where the model invents scene elements absent from the photo.
reports.intended_vs_unexpected_insight: The task was designed to test expert visual/geographic knowledge (HLE subject: Geography; exact city from a 2022 photo). Agents did fail that capability—none identified Tacoma—but the trajectories also reveal an unintended, equally important bottleneck: deploying image QA inside terminal agents without guaranteed vision produces 20-minute tool thrashing unrelated to geography knowledge. Among vision-capable failures, the intended gap (fine-grained city ID from subtle shoreline cues) appears as metropolitan anchoring within the correct region rather than random global guesses, which is closer to what the benchmark author likely targeted. Unexpected insight: secondary tool pipelines (CLIP, ViLT, ASCII rendering) systematically hallucinate structure (bridges, dogs, explosions) and can override or derail otherwise competent models.
reports.generalizability: Moderately generalizable. Modality-aligned harness design (ensure native multimodal input before shell tooling) would improve many vision-in-agent benchmarks, not just HLE geo items. Metropolitan/default-entity anchoring when evidence only supports a region applies beyond geography—to library selection, cloud region choice, and any disambiguation among similar candidates. Confident fabrication of supporting details (Golden Gardens bonfires at 95%) is broadly toxic for agent trust. Less generalizable is the specific Tacoma-vs-Seattle discrimination: it depends on obscure local geography and may be unsolvable without web search (explicitly discouraged) or training memorization. Improving hyper-local geo alone helps GeoGuessr-like tasks but not most coding agents.
reports.confounds: Task difficulty: the image lacks iconic landmarks; even humans may struggle without prior knowledge of Titlow Beach. Scoring is strict exactMatch on city name—Seattle and Tacoma are distinct despite geographic proximity. Instruction says 20 minutes but agent timeout is 1200s, encouraging over-long forensic loops. Anti-cheating text forbids online reverse image search, which is how many humans would solve this. LLM-as-judge adds variance though all failures here are clearly wrong answers. Model/harness heterogeneity (gemini-cli vs terminus-2 vs claude-code) mixes capability with infrastructure, making a single root cause harder to attribute. One glm-5.1 run may reflect weak vision on that stack rather than universal model limits. No trajectory found Titlow Beach, so we cannot tell if any model was close but mislabeled.
reports.implications_for_future_design: For benchmark authors: tag tasks with required modalities; do not place raw image-VQA items in shell-only harnesses without a first-class image tool path; consider tiered scoring (region correct, metro correct, exact city) for geo items to separate partial competence from total failure; cap or penalize tool loops when OCR/metadata yield nothing after N steps. For agent builders: short-circuit to native vision before ASCII/CLIP/OCR pipelines; when confidence is low, avoid inventing named landmarks; calibrate confidence (95% Seattle here is miscalibrated). For evaluation protocols: report failure mode taxonomy (timeout vs wrong-region vs wrong-city vs hallucination) per harness; align stated time budget with enforced timeout; optionally allow constrained retrieval if the construct of interest is visual reasoning rather than memorization. For training: emphasize disambiguation among geographically proximate entities and penalize confabulated evidentiary details in explanations.

reports.tldr: Medium insightfulness. The task is a LabBench FigQA item (count voltage steps in panel D where ASAP2f R414Q beats the triple mutant); the verifier gates on letter-mapped numeric answer "2". Across 17 trials, 0/17 passed: 10/17 hit AgentTimeoutError after spending most of the 300s budget installing Pillow/OCR tooling instead of answering, while finishers submitted scattered wrong counts (0, 1, 3, 4, 5, 6) via domain guessing, bar-chart hallucinations, or brittle pixel pipelines. The clearest general lesson is workflow mismatch—evaluating a vision-native scientific QA item inside a shell agent without pre-provisioned vision tools—plus secondary FigQA errors in panel localization and comparison semantics.
reports.main_insight: This LabBench FigQA task exposes two coupled failure modes when ported into Harbor terminal agents. First, most trajectories never reach a graded answer because the agent treats "read figure.jpg" as a systems problem: pip-install Pillow/matplotlib/pytesseract, apt-install tesseract-ocr, quadrant OCR, and slow per-pixel scans on a 4026×3134 JPEG until the 300s agent timeout fires (10/17 trials). Second, agents that do submit an answer rarely perform reliable panel-D trace comparison; they hallucinate the wrong plot type (bar chart with S1–S5 instead of paired fluorescence time traces), substitute ASAP2 domain priors without visual evidence, or debate whether "greater response" means algebraic ΔF/F or absolute magnitude—yielding counts of 0, 1, 3, 4, 5, or 6 against the gold count of 2.
reports.why_it_matters: LabBench and similar benchmarks are increasingly run inside general coding-agent harnesses, not dedicated multimodal chat UIs. These trajectories show that a 0% pass rate can reflect evaluation plumbing (no vision path, no imaging libraries, tight timeout) as much as model reasoning. For benchmark designers, that separates "cannot read the figure" from "cannot finish the harness workflow"; for agent builders, it motivates first-class image tools, preinstalled scientific-Python stacks, and early submission policies on short MCQ tasks. For training, it highlights that scientific FigQA needs grounded visual grounding (correct panel, legend colors, step boundaries) rather than OCR text dumps or paper-level priors.
reports.evidence_from_trajectories: Verifier bar: test.sh maps the agent's [ANSWER] letter through /app/.letter_mapping.json to the ideal text "2" from choices.json; all 17 trials scored reward 0. Timeout cluster (hy3-preview terminus-2 trial 1b5a8881 steps 4–12): after PIL import fails, the agent runs `pip install pillow matplotlib`, then `pip install pytesseract` plus `apt-get install tesseract-ocr`, runs full-image OCR, and quadrant OCR on a presumed 2×2 A–D grid—never writing answer.txt before AgentTimeoutError at step 12. Similar pip/OCR thrashing appears in gpt-5.5 terminus-2 (f65923c6, step 8: `pip3 install numpy matplotlib pytesseract`) and qwen terminus-2 trials. Completed wrong answers: claude-opus-4-7 (6be57bb8, steps 8–10) installs PIL, crops quadrants, then admits it cannot view the image and writes `[ANSWER]E[/ANSWER]` (0 steps) from ASAP2 paper priors. gpt-5.5 codex (b12dc99f, steps 6–38) installs Pillow, iteratively recrops panel D, runs purple/black pixel median scripts, concludes "four larger-magnitude responses" and writes `[ANSWER]D[/ANSWER]` (value 4 in its shuffle). gemini-cli (d416f834, step 5): multimodal reasoning counts 3 steps with black-line greater magnitude, writes `[ANSWER]E[/ANSWER]` (mapped to 3). minimax claude-code (32a5a858, step 13) describes panel D as a bar graph with S1–S5 and answers `[ANSWER]C[/ANSWER]` (1)—a figure-type hallucination inconsistent with the actual time-series panel D. glm claude-code (9414234a, step 257) likewise claims five bar-chart steps and answers D (5).
reports.surface_failure_vs_root_cause: Surface failure: binary reward 0 for every trial—either AgentTimeoutError with no answer.txt, or a submitted letter mapping to an incorrect count (0, 1, 3, 4, 5, or 6 instead of 2). Root cause is layered: (1) harness/workflow—terminal agents without native vision or preinstalled imaging libs default to expensive OCR/pip detours and exhaust the 300s budget; (2) scientific visual reasoning—even vision-capable harnesses misidentify plot geometry (bars vs traces), mislocalize panel D, or misinterpret "greater response" across signed ΔF/F steps; (3) fallback to domain knowledge (opus guessing 0 from ASAP2s > R414Q lore) instead of grounded measurement from the figure.
reports.intended_vs_unexpected_insight: Intended: LabBench FigQA capability—locate panel D, align legend colors (black = ASAP2f R414Q, purple = L146G S147T R414Q), count voltage steps where the black trace shows a greater stimulus response. Agents did fail this capability in every graded submission, but often never reached the test. Unexpected but valuable: the dominant terminus-2 bottleneck is time/budget misallocation on infrastructure (pip, apt, OCR) for a 5-minute MCQ; and a recurring secondary failure is figure-type hallucination (bar charts) even when models claim to "see" the image, which is a benchmark-design signal that CLI FigQA tasks need explicit vision tooling rather than emergent OCR hacks.
reports.generalizability: Partially generalizable. The timeout/workflow lesson transfers to any vision or document QA task run in shell-only agents without bundled multimodal tools—fixing it (vision API, preinstalled Pillow, crop-and-ask pattern, submit-early on MCQ) would help broadly, not only this item. The scientific-comparison errors (panel ID, trace vs bar, signed vs magnitude) generalize within FigQA and chart-QA families but are narrower than core coding-agent skills. Less generalizable: answer-choice shuffling and letter mapping are task-format specifics, though mapping numeric conclusions to shuffled letters is a recurring MCQ harness requirement.
reports.confounds: Several confounds limit a "high" verdict. (1) Harness heterogeneity: terminus-2 trials lack native vision and drove most timeouts; claude-code/gemini-cli/codex can view images yet still failed for different reasons, so pass rate mixes workflow and reasoning. (2) Environment: minimal base image (no PIL until pip), 1 CPU / 2 GB RAM, and 300s timeout encourage long installs on a 1 MB figure. (3) Instruction semantics: "greater response to stimulus" is debatable for bidirectional ΔF/F traces (gemini explicitly toggled algebraic vs |ΔF/F|), which may widen answer dispersion without proving uniform inability. (4) Anti-cheating shuffle: per-run letter mapping is correct for evaluation but adds a mapping step unrelated to FigQA. (5) 0/17 pass rate with spread wrong answers makes it hard to claim one crisp capability gap—timeouts, hallucinations, and pixel-misread are distinct mechanisms.
reports.implications_for_future_design: Benchmark tasks: For FigQA in agent sandboxes, either provide a native image-read tool in the harness, or ship Pillow/matplotlib in the base image and state that OCR is unnecessary; consider separate scores for "answered" vs "correct" to distinguish timeouts from reasoning failures. Keep timeouts aligned with stated "5 minute" guidance and cap setup work (discourage apt/pip chains via prebuilt deps). Agent design: On MCQ+image tasks, prioritize one vision call or targeted crop over full-document OCR; write answer.txt early with a best-effort letter, then refine if budget remains. Evaluation protocols: Report failure mode tags (timeout, no submission, wrong count, figure-type error) per harness; run at least one vision-enabled baseline when scoring LabBench-in-Harbor. Training: Emphasize scientific figure schemas (multi-panel labels A–E, time-series vs bar charts) and grounded counting with explicit step boundaries rather than domain priors from paper titles.

reports.tldr: Medium insightfulness. The task targets scientific-figure visual QA (read gene count from a specific panel); four agents finished but all chose wrong counts (6–9 vs. correct 7), while 14/18 timed out after spending the budget on Pillow/Tesseract setup and OCR rather than direct vision. The lesson is real—multimodal figure localization plus terminal-agent workflow mismatch—but timeouts and mixed failure modes keep it below a clean, high-confidence capability isolation.
reports.main_insight: This LabBench FigQA item tests whether agents can localize panel I in a dense biology composite figure and read a quantitative value: how many differentially expressed genes are in the "negative regulation of protein metabolic process" pathway (verifier ideal: 7). Agents that completed the run did engage vision (Read tool or image input) but systematically misread the graphic—interpreting bar lengths, volcano/dot-plot gene lists, or dual-axis orange dots—and mapped them to nearby distractors (6, 8, or 9). A larger share never reached a graded answer because terminal-first agents defaulted to installing Pillow and Tesseract and running full-page OCR on a 3584×5476 image until the 300s harness timeout.
reports.why_it_matters: Scientific agents must combine panel localization with precise numeric extraction from charts, not just OCR text. The trajectories show two separable gaps worth designing for: (1) visual grounding in multi-panel figures (which subplot, which axis, bar vs. dot count), and (2) agent harness efficiency on image tasks (avoid spending the entire step budget on environment setup when native image tools exist). Improving either would transfer to other FigQA, lab automation, and paper-reading benchmarks beyond this single MCQ.
reports.evidence_from_trajectories: Verifier bar: ideal answer "7" in /insight/task/solution/choices.json; agents must write [ANSWER]X to /app/answer.txt per test.sh. Completed wrong answers: trial 38ccf90e (mimo-v2.5-pro, claude-code) step 4 Read on /app/figure.jpg, step 8 Write [ANSWER]D — rationale counts nine gene names (Nfkb1, Nfkbia, …) on a dot plot; correct is 7. Trial 42181995 (glm-5.1, claude-code) step 8 Write [ANSWER]C — claims Panel I bar chart shows 8 genes. Trial ee17b3af (gemini-3.1-pro-preview, gemini-cli) step 7 echo [ANSWER]D — describes panel "l" (LPS LD-high vs LD-low pathway enrichment), orange dot halfway between 8 and 10 → 9. Trial c21b3e2a (MiniMax-M2.7, claude-code) step 9 message answer (D) 6 from volcano plot gene list. Timeout pattern (14 trials, AgentTimeoutError): e.g. trial 0e84554d (glm-5.1, terminus-2) steps 2–9 install pip Pillow, apt-get tesseract-ocr, pytesseract full-image OCR and crops searching for panel I — timed out at step 10 without answer.txt; mirrored in trials 2363710f, e1196732 (claude-opus-4-7), b15c68bc (gpt-5.5), and 10+ others.
reports.surface_failure_vs_root_cause: Surface: 0/18 binary reward; missing or wrong answer.txt, or AgentTimeoutError after 300s. Root cause splits two ways. (A) Visual reasoning errors among finishers: wrong subplot or encoding (dot-plot gene enumeration vs. pathway bar gene count), misread axis scale (gemini-cli inferring 9 from a dot between tick marks 8 and 10), or off-by-one neighbor distractors. (B) Workflow/time-budget failure among timeouts: agents treat figure.jpg as a text-extraction problem (OCR pipeline) instead of using available multimodal Read early, consuming most steps on apt/pip installs and slow OCR on a very large JPEG—so the harness never tests whether they could read the chart correctly given more time.
reports.intended_vs_unexpected_insight: Intended insight: scientific figure visual QA—find panel I and report the gene count for a named GO pathway. Agents that finished did attempt that capability but failed on accurate quantity and panel grounding (not random guessing). Unexpected but prominent insight: terminal-OCR workflow and 300s budget awareness dominate the dataset—most runs never submit an answer despite frontier models, which looks like total capability failure but is largely setup/timeout. Secondary unexpected signal: Roman numeral I vs. letter l confusion (gemini-cli explicitly labels panel "l").
reports.generalizability: Partially generalizable. Panel localization and quantitative chart reading are core skills for scientific agents, paper QA, and lab automation; improving multimodal grounding and teaching agents to read the correct visual variable (bar length, legend, axis) would help broadly. The OCR-install timeout pattern generalizes to any vision task run in text-only terminal harnesses without prebuilt image deps—but is as much a benchmark/harness design issue as a model capability gap. Less generalizable: this specific GO pathway name and distractor cluster (6/7/8/9).
reports.confounds: Heavy timeout confound: 14/18 trials end with AgentTimeoutError, so the pass rate mainly reflects workflow/time, not a clean vision score. Harness heterogeneity: claude-code/gemini-cli trials use native image Read; terminus-2 trials often lack that path and default to OCR. No preinstalled Pillow/Tesseract in the sandbox increases setup overhead. Panel label "I" may be ambiguous vs. lowercase "l" in OCR output. c21b3e2a may not have persisted answer.txt (final message only). Cannot verify ground-truth panel location from trajectories alone without independent figure inspection. Mixed failure modes reduce single-root-cause clarity.
reports.implications_for_future_design: For benchmarks: preinstall minimal image stack (Pillow, tesseract optional) or require multimodal Read in the harness spec; separate vision accuracy tasks (short timeout, must submit answer) from optional workflow stress tests; report whether answer.txt exists separately from correctness. For agents: on image MCQs, open figure with vision first, identify panel label and chart type before OCR; cross-check numeric answer against axis ticks and legend, not gene-name lists from adjacent panels. For LabBench FigQA specifically: include panel-crop images or explicit panel bounding hints in ablations to measure pure reading vs. localization; use distractors that are not all adjacent integers to reduce lucky guesses. For evaluation: flag trials that spend >N steps on apt/pip without answer.txt as workflow failures distinct from visual errors.

reports.tldr: Verdict: medium. This LabBench FigQA item cleanly tests scientific-figure reading, but the 0/18 outcome mixes three separable failures: (1) terminal harnesses without image input substitute paper priors or build OCR stacks until timeout; (2) vision-enabled agents still misread panel c (often guessing Posterior instead of Right); (3) one vision trial reasoned correctly but never wrote answer.txt. The lesson generalizes to benchmark harness alignment and agent workflow discipline more than to a single model blind spot.
reports.main_insight: The task–trajectory set shows that FigQA in a shell sandbox is not a pure vision benchmark unless the agent harness actually delivers figure.jpg as perceptual input. When it does not (terminus-2), agents explicitly abandon figure reading and answer from parametric biology knowledge—often incorrectly. When it does (claude-code/codex with Read-on-image), agents still frequently mis-localize the requested panel/metric (e.g., conflating heatmap intensity with bar-chart maxima, or posterior vs right sections) and pick the wrong letter. A secondary but repeated pattern is operational: many agents spend the full 300s installing Pillow/tesseract/apt packages and running OCR grid searches on a 2772×2738 JPEG instead of committing an answer, and at least one agent produced the correct semantic choice in chat without creating the graded artifact.
reports.why_it_matters: LabBench-style FigQA is meant to measure whether agents can extract quantitative claims from real publication figures—a capability needed for scientific assistants. These trajectories show that reported failure rates can be dominated by evaluation stack choices (text-only terminal vs multimodal IDE harness) and by agent workflow failures (timeouts, missing answer.txt) rather than by figure comprehension alone. For benchmark builders, that means aggregate scores can mis-rank models unless harness, timeout, and deliverable requirements are held constant; for agent builders, it highlights that scientific MCQ success requires aligned vision channels, panel-aware quantitative reading, and hard submission discipline under tight budgets.
reports.evidence_from_trajectories: Across 18 trials, reward was 0.0 for all; 13 ended with AgentTimeoutError at 300s (meta.json). Completed runs: claude-opus-4-7 / terminus-2 (27935e1a) at step 8 states it "can't actually see the image," cites Andalman et al. 2019 from memory, and writes [ANSWER]A[/ANSWER] for Posterior—even though its shuffle mapped Right to letter C (step 4 showed mapping A=Posterior, C="Right "). claude-opus-4-7 / claude-code (98320f5c) Read figure.jpg with base64 vision at step 4, then at step 6 claims the "most intense red signal" in shocked panel C is posterior and writes [ANSWER]C[/ANSWER] to answer.txt (correct letter was D=Right ). glm-5.1 / claude-code (c0c3fc0d) also receives the image but concludes posterior and writes C. minimax-m2.7 / claude-code (db446349) at step 9 correctly identifies Right and outputs [ANSWER]D[/ANSWER] in the final message but never invokes Write/echo for /app/answer.txt, so the verifier’s required file is absent. gpt-5.5 / codex (e776f4df) spends many steps seeking JPEG decoders, then writes [ANSWER]A[/ANSWER] (Left) without confident figure evidence. Timeout exemplar hy3-preview / terminus-2 (2c4538d2): steps 4–11 install pillow+pytesseract, apt-get tesseract-ocr, and run multi-section OCR on figure.jpg; step 10 still yields garbled text ("LFM Imaging C") and the run ends at step 11 without any [ANSWER] tag. deepseek-v4-pro / claude-code (3cbfd195) runs 48 steps with heavy cv2 usage and also times out.
reports.surface_failure_vs_root_cause: Surface failure is uniformly verifier reward 0: either missing /app/answer.txt, wrong letter vs shuffled mapping to ideal text "Right ", or agent timeout before submission. Root causes split by trajectory class: (A) perception-channel mismatch—terminal agents cannot see figure.jpg and substitute literature priors (27935e1a step 8); (B) scientific figure misreading even with vision—frontier models misinterpret panel c and choose Posterior or Left instead of Right (98320f5c step 6, c0c3fc0d step 16); (C) time/budget misallocation—OCR/apt/pip thrashing until 300s on a 5-minute MCQ (2c4538d2, 13 timeouts); (D) deliverable omission—correct semantic answer in chat but no graded file (db446349 step 9).
reports.intended_vs_unexpected_insight: Agents did fail on the intended capability—quantitative/multimodal reading of a neuroscience figure panel—when vision was available (opus and glm chose Posterior). However, the dominant mass of failures was not figure reasoning: most trials never reached a verifier-scored answer because of harness blindness or timeout-driven tooling loops. An unexpected but valuable secondary insight is that even a correct visual read (minimax: Right → D) can score zero if the agent treats chat output as sufficient and skips the explicit answer.txt contract enforced by test.sh.
reports.generalizability: Partially generalizable. Harness–modality alignment (do not run FigQA through text-only shells) and submit-the-artifact discipline apply across Harbor/LabBench-style tasks. Time-budget thrashing on heavyweight OCR/install paths for simple perception tasks also transfers to other multimodal-in-terminal evaluations. The specific confusion between anatomical axes (posterior vs right sections in habenula panel c) is narrower—real but more domain-specific than a universal agent weakness, and only directly testable when vision is actually wired in.
reports.confounds: Harness heterogeneity confounds model comparison: terminus-2 trials lack native image input while claude-code/gemini-cli trials embed figure.jpg as base64—so 0/18 mixes incompatible conditions. Per-trial choice shuffling (setup.py) changes letter labels, which is good anti-cheating but requires care when comparing stated rationales to letters. The instruction tells agents to finish in 5 minutes while task.toml allows 300s agent timeout, encouraging long OCR pipelines. Verifier only checks letter→text mapping, not reasoning traces, so we cannot distinguish lucky guesses from true reads except via trajectory prose. n=1 correct visual reasoning (minimax) failed procedurally, so pass rate understates rare perceptual success.
reports.implications_for_future_design: Benchmark design: gate FigQA tasks on multimodal harnesses (or provide a first-class vision tool) and report harness as a stratified factor; cap or penalize package-install steps on 5-minute MCQ items; add mid-run checks for /app/answer.txt existence before timeout. Agent training/tooling: teach early commit of formatted answers under tight budgets instead of full OCR reconstruction of publication figures; train panel-aware quantitative extraction (which subplot, which condition, change vs level) for dense multi-panel science figures; reinforce that [ANSWER] tags in chat are insufficient when the verifier reads a file. Evaluation protocols: separate metrics for perception available vs content accuracy vs submission completeness so a task like labbench-figqa-0104 cannot be summarized as a single opaque 0% without attributing failure mode.

reports.tldr: Verdict: medium. Across 17 trials (0 passes), agents that reached an answer overwhelmingly chose the optic-lobe neuron set label C2/C3 instead of the benchmark key dFB—the mapped cell-type identity—even when reasoning named dFB. Twelve trials timed out or crashed in OCR-heavy terminal workflows, so the signal is real but split between scientific figure QA semantics and harness vision friction.
reports.main_insight: This LabBench FigQA item tests whether an agent can read a dense neuroscience figure and answer a precise multiple-choice question about AUC. The trajectories show a consistent capability gap: models locate the highest-AUC optic-lobe cluster (usually C2/C3 in panel D’s boxplots/ROC readouts) but submit that cluster name as the answer instead of the benchmark’s intended target, the mapped identity dFB. Several trajectories even state in reasoning that dFB is the identity yet write the letter for C2/C3 (e.g., mimo-v2.5-pro claude-code, steps 9–10). A second, overlapping failure mode is terminal-first agents spending the 300s budget on tesseract installs, crops, and noisy OCR rather than grounded visual extraction.
reports.why_it_matters: Scientific figure benchmarks are only useful if failures isolate figure competence from workflow noise. Here, the repeated C2/C3 vs dFB confusion shows that strong models can parse plots yet fail to bind question wording (“identity of … neuron set”) to the correct entity level (predicted/annotated cell type vs cluster label)—a mistake that would break literature QA, diagnostic chart reading, and lab-notebook assistants even when raw vision works. Separately, the timeout cluster shows that evaluating vision tasks through text-only harnesses can measure OCR plumbing instead of the intended skill, which mis-ranks models and obscures training targets.
