reports.evidence_from_trajectories: Completed claude-code / gemini-cli runs all failed verifier reward 0.0 with wrong semantic choice: gemini-3.1-pro-preview (gemini-cli, trial a37eb3ba) spends step 5 tracing Figure D’s color legend, correctly finds the tallest blue (optic lobe) box labeled C2/C3 (65), and writes [ANSWER]E[/ANSWER] where E=C2/C3—not D=dFB. mimo-v2.5-pro (0452f77e, steps 6–8) first misclassifies the image as a Sankey plot, then at steps 9–10 reasons “C2/C3: dFBs (AUC=0.814)… The identity … is dFBs” but still writes [ANSWER]D[/ANSWER] where D=C2/C3 in that shuffle. glm-5.1 and minimax-m2.7 claude-code trials submit [ANSWER]C[/ANSWER] for C2/C3 after describing ROC/bar highest curves. gpt-5.5 codex (baf481d2, ~41 steps) sorts OCR’d labels, concludes “top blue optic-lobe candidate is C2/C3,” and writes [ANSWER]A[/ANSWER] (A=C2/C3 in its shuffle). Infrastructure dominates many other trials: 11/17 ended AgentTimeoutError (meta status=exception) while installing/using tesseract—e.g., gpt-5.5 terminus-2 (29bbbd5d, step 10) still planning OCR of rotated x-axis labels at timeout; claude-opus-4-7 terminus-2 (639f03a2, step 13) cropping for AUC OCR when time expired.
reports.surface_failure_vs_root_cause: Surface failure: binary reward 0.0 for every trial—missing or wrong /app/answer.txt letter versus /tests/choices.json ideal text dFB (verifier maps letters via /app/.letter_mapping.json). Deeper cause for the five submissions: mis-resolution of what “identity of the highest AUC optic lobe neuron set” denotes—agents answer which set peaks (C2/C3) rather than what identity that set carries (dFB), sometimes after correct numeric reading. Deeper cause for twelve exceptions: terminus/codex-style agents treat figure.jpg as a text-OCR problem, exhaust the 300s agent timeout on tooling, and never produce a scored answer—confounding vision capability with workflow choice.
reports.intended_vs_unexpected_insight: The task is designed to test scientific figure question answering (LabBench FigQA). Agents do fail on that core skill whenever they reach an answer, but the trajectories reveal two nuances beyond a simple ‘cannot read the figure’ story: (1) an entity-level binding error (cluster vs identity) even when plot values are cited correctly, and (2) an unexpected harness bottleneck where terminal agents without reliable vision spend the entire budget on OCR instead of the biology question. The intended insight is partially confirmed; the OCR/timeout pattern is an evaluation-design lesson as much as a model lesson.
reports.generalizability: The entity-level confusion—answering the category label when the question asks for an attribute/identity—should transfer to other scientific MCQ and chart-QA settings beyond this item, especially where questions use field terms like ‘identity,’ ‘annotation,’ or ‘predicted type.’ Improving that binding would help broadly. OCR-timeout failures generalize to any benchmark that gives agents a raster figure but scores them through a shell harness without native multimodal input; fixing that helps evaluation fairness more than domain reasoning. The specific dFB/C2/C3 content is narrow Drosophila neuroscience and does not generalize as knowledge.
reports.confounds: Question wording is somewhat ambiguous: ‘identity of the highest AUC optic lobe neuron set’ can be read as ‘which set has the highest AUC’ (C2/C3) versus ‘what cell-type identity does that set map to’ (dFB). The figure is not present in the static /insight task tree (only at runtime as figure.jpg), so reviewers rely on trajectory descriptions. Choice shuffling differs per run, so letter errors sometimes mix with semantic errors (mimo reasoning cites dFB but selects the C2/C3 letter). Twelve of seventeen trials never submitted a verifier-scored answer due to timeouts or model-access errors (hy3-preview NonZeroAgentExitCodeError at step 10), weakening cross-model comparability. All models scored 0%, so pass-rate alone cannot separate vision quality from harness effects.
reports.implications_for_future_design: Benchmark authors should tighten prompts when the key is an mapped identity (e.g., ‘What predicted cell type corresponds to the optic-lobe neuron set with the highest AUC in panel D?’) and include anti-confound distractors that separate cluster name from identity. Evaluations should provide native multimodal reading for vision items, or supply structured numeric extracts, rather than forcing OCR marathons in terminus harnesses with 300s caps. Trajectory logging should capture final chosen text, not only letters, to diagnose shuffle mismatches like mimo’s dFB reasoning with a C2/C3 letter. Reporting should split outcomes into ‘no submission (timeout/tooling)’ versus ‘wrong science’ to avoid attributing infrastructure failure to figure incompetence. For agent training, add supervision on scientific QA entity levels and on stopping OCR pipelines once vision tools return usable panel readings.

reports.tldr: Verdict: medium. This LabBench FigQA item cleanly targets quantitative reading of a Kaplan–Meier plot, but 17/17 failures mix two stories: (1) terminal agents burn the 300s budget on Pillow/OCR pipelines instead of answering, and (2) vision-capable agents that finish still misread survival at day 25 and/or refuse to map options to legend labels when alleles differ (tm465 vs by105). The lesson generalizes to scientific chart QA and multimodal workflow choice, but harness timeouts and label mismatch confound how sharply we can attribute failure.
reports.main_insight: The task is designed to test scientific figure question answering: read a multi-panel Kaplan–Meier survival figure and select which genotype had ~60% survival at 25 days (verifier ideal text: spr-4(tm465);daf-2;spr-3(ok2525)). Across 17 models/harnesses, every trial scores 0.0, but the trajectories split into two capability signals. Roughly 12/17 end with AgentTimeoutError while still installing or running OCR/pixel-analysis scripts (e.g., deepseek-v4-pro terminus-2 trial 00ecef84 spends steps 2–14 on pip install Pillow/tesseract and failed OCR on a 4459×1347 JPEG). The remaining trials that submit answer.txt do engage the figure yet converge on wrong letters by mis-estimating y-values at x=25, confusing curve colors/markers, or treating a legend allele mismatch as “insufficient information.” The deepest shared gap is quantitative chart-to-MCQ grounding under shuffled letters, not formatting or missing answer files.
reports.why_it_matters: Scientific FigQA is a core use case for lab agents (papers, survival curves, dose–response plots). This task shows that giving agents a JPEG plus a shell is not equivalent to evaluating vision: many frontier runs never reach a scored answer because they choose brittle computer-vision pipelines. Where vision is available (claude-code Read on figure.jpg), models still fail the biology question, which matters for training and benchmarks that assume multimodal competence. For benchmark designers, the 0/17 pass rate is informative only if failures are classified as workflow timeout vs perceptual/reasoning error; this dataset item helps calibrate both agent tool policies and FigQA difficulty.
reports.evidence_from_trajectories: Verifier bar (tests/test.sh): parse [ANSWER]X[/ANSWER] from /app/answer.txt and check the letter’s text in /app/.letter_mapping.json against tests/choices.json ideal spr-4(tm465);daf-2;spr-3(ok2525). Completed submissions: claude-opus-4-7 claude-code (e3c5c181) step 7 Read /app/figure.jpg with image payload, step 10 reasoning lists all panel-(a) curves at 80–100% at 25 days, step 11 Write answer.txt [ANSWER]D[/ANSWER] citing tm465 vs by105 mismatch in option F; mimo-v2.5-pro claude-code (0eece5de) step 10 message claims green spr-4(by105);daf-2 at ~60% and writes [ANSWER]F[/ANSWER]; glm-5.1 claude-code (47dbfe21) writes [ANSWER]A[/ANSWER] for spr-4(by105);daf-2; minimax-m2.7 claude-code (dddda892) step 9–12 vision read then [ANSWER]C[/ANSWER] for spr-4(by105);daf-2 while reasoning incorrectly that the x-axis only spans 0–25 days. Timeout pattern: gpt-5.5 terminus-2 (b498845d) step 12 still waiting on color-cluster script output when AgentTimeoutError fires; gemini-3.1-pro-preview gemini-cli (49c1a6f0) step 31 web-searching external datasets before timeout; deepseek-v4-pro terminus-2 (00ecef84) step 8 discovers .letter_mapping.json but continues OCR instead of answering. Infrastructure: hy3-preview claude-code (4a24b35d) step 10 exits with model access error before any answer. No trajectory contains the correct mapped letter for the ideal genotype.
reports.surface_failure_vs_root_cause: Surface failure: binary reward 0.0 for all 17 trials—either AgentTimeoutError (12 trials), one NonZeroAgentExitCodeError (model unavailable), or verifier rejection of a submitted wrong letter (4 claude-code trials with answer.txt present). Root cause is layered: (1) For terminus-2 / gemini-cli / qwen-coder harnesses, agents treat figure.jpg as a signal-processing problem (pip install, tesseract, numpy pixel scans) and exhaust the 300s agent timeout before writing answer.txt—workflow and time-budget failure on a task that needs one multimodal read. (2) For claude-code trials that finish, root cause is inaccurate quantitative reading of Kaplan–Meier curves at a specified day (survival percentages off by tens of points) plus difficulty aligning MCQ option strings to legend entries when the ideal answer uses spr-4(tm465) but panel (a) labels the triple mutant as spr-4(by105);daf-2;spr-3(ok2525)—leading several models to pick by105 double mutants or “Insufficient information” instead of the triple-mutant option.
reports.intended_vs_unexpected_insight: Intended insight: agents lack reliable scientific figure QA—extracting a numeric survival value at (t=25 days, y=60%) from a cluttered multi-panel figure with six genotypes. Agents do fail that capability in all scored submissions, but unexpectedly half the sample never reaches the verifier because of terminal/OCR thrashing, so the benchmark run also measures whether agents recognize a simple MCQ-over-image task versus a coding project. Another unexpected signal: the strongest model with native image Read (claude-opus-4-7) explicitly reasons about the tm465/by105 label conflict and chooses “Insufficient information,” showing meta-reasoning that blocks answering even when a curve might match semantically—suggesting the item tests legend–option reconciliation as much as raw curve reading.
reports.generalizability: Partially generalizable. Improving quantitative plot reading (axis calibration, reading values at gridlines, mapping legend markers to answer choices) would help across LabBench FigQA, chart-heavy exams, and biology/clinical agent tasks. Improving time/tool selection (answer from vision first; avoid OCR installs on tight budgets) transfers to any multimodal task in shell harnesses. Less generalizable elements include the specific C. elegans genotype strings, shuffled MCQ letters, and the tm465/by105 labeling inconsistency between options and figure—errors on those may not predict performance on cleanly labeled charts. Because 12/17 failures are timeouts, the 0% pass rate overstates vision weakness unless evaluations separate submission rate from answer accuracy.
reports.confounds: Several confounds weaken a “high” verdict: (1) Agent timeout_sec=300 while many trajectories spend minutes on apt/pip/OCR setup for a 5-minute MCQ; failures partly measure harness modality mismatch, not just FigQA ability. (2) Choice shuffling changes letters per run, so cross-trial comparison of wrong letters is meaningless; only mapped genotype text matters. (3) Possible label ambiguity: figure legend uses spr-4(by105) in the triple mutant while the keyed ideal answer uses spr-4(tm465);…—reviewers could disagree whether “insufficient information” is reasonable, blurring the ground truth. (4) Multi-panel figure (a–c) invites reading the wrong panel; some agents truncate the x-axis to 0–25 in reasoning (dddda892). (5) One trial failed for model availability, not task skill. (6) We cannot see post-timeout partial answers for most terminus runs, so their latent visual competence is unknown.
reports.implications_for_future_design: Benchmarks: report two metrics—answer submitted vs correct—and tag FigQA items with required modality (vision-native vs allowed tooling). Prefer single-panel crops or explicit “use panel (a)” instructions when testing numeric extraction; align option text with legend alleles or add a brief note that allele names may differ across panels. Keep anti-cheat shuffling but avoid exposing .letter_mapping.json early (deepseek step 8) without blocking it. Agents/training: default policy for ‘read figure.jpg’ tasks should be direct multimodal inspection, then write answer.txt within the first minute; treat OCR as fallback only. Tooling: terminal harnesses should expose the same image-read path claude-code uses, or pre-install lightweight image libs to prevent pip thrash. Evaluation protocols: stratify by harness (terminus vs IDE) when interpreting LabBench FigQA aggregates so timeout-heavy runs do not dominate capability estimates.

reports.tldr: Medium insightfulness. The task is a hard OmniMath combinatorics/optimization problem (ground truth 115440), and the trajectories show a real but partly confounded split: agents can discover the optimum computationally yet often fail to finalize `/workspace/answer.txt` under the 600s budget, while pure-reasoning paths frequently lock onto wrong closed forms such as 63000 or 176620. Roughly half the trials are uninformative harness/API timeouts with zero tokens.
reports.main_insight: This task–trajectory set tests olympiad-style discrete optimization (20-fold min-convolution under a monotone budget on f), but the decisive signal is not simply “cannot do hard math.” When agents make progress, they either (a) build correct computational models and empirically find the optimum 115440 with partition f(i)=24-i on i=0..23, or (b) produce long, plausible-but-wrong analytic shortcuts (constant-step f, miscounted c_k(m), or maximizing S_k/(k+1)). Failures are often workflow failures: continuing expensive search after the optimum is found, never writing the deliverable, or stalling on harness confirmation even after `echo 115440 > /workspace/answer.txt`.
reports.why_it_matters: Benchmark designers often treat math agent tasks as pure reasoning probes, but this item shows that scoring a single numeric file couples mathematical modeling, computation, and agent control. Improving answer commitment, early checkpointing, and time-budget awareness would lift scores on many timed “write answer.txt” tasks, not only this one. Conversely, interpreting the 0/16 pass rate as pure math weakness would overstate the case because infrastructure timeouts and verifier/harness effects dominate several runs.
reports.evidence_from_trajectories: Ground truth is 115440 (`ground_truths.json`); verifier uses an LLM-judge ensemble on `/workspace/answer.txt` (`llm_judge.py`, eval_mode `llm_verifier`). Of 16 trials, 15 end with `AgentTimeoutError` at 600s and reward 0; one completes without exception but still scores 0. Split: 8 trials have 0 input/output tokens (e.g. trials `0115f1bd`, `c07598b3`, `b524954a`)—stuck before first productive step. Trial `04b7c6e3` (mimo-v2.5-pro, terminus-2): step 2 runs `echo 115440 > /workspace/answer.txt` and calls `mark_task_complete`; terminal asks for confirmation; result shows a 577s API wait then timeout—correct answer likely written but run marked failed. Trial `c510cc91` (gpt-5.5, terminus-2): steps 10–12 print `struct best (115440, (1,2,...,24))` from `layer_search.py`, step 12 only polls (`keystrokes: ""`, duration 20s) for more random search, never writes `answer.txt`, times out. Trial `6de05e67` (mimo, claude-code): step 2 has extensive reasoning concluding 176620 with 0 output tokens and no write—verifier scores 0. Trial `745da5ee` (gpt-5.5, codex, 30 steps): early Python prints `(210.0, 63000, 300, 1)` as best ratio, later launches heavy PuLP MIP (`cutmip.py`) still running at timeout—never reaches 115440. Trial `9cfe04fe` (deepseek, terminus-2): step 2 analysis says “maximum sum might be 63000,” step 3 starts `explore.py`, times out. Trial `3a30e89f` (gemini, 13 steps): iterates brute-force/SA scripts (`solve.py`, `search.py`, `sa.py`) with empty final steps, no answer file.
reports.surface_failure_vs_root_cause: Surface failure: reward 0 on all trials, mostly `AgentTimeoutError` after 600s, no credited solve. Deeper causes are heterogeneous: (1) harness/API stalls (8/16 zero-token timeouts); (2) task-finalization failure after discovering 115440 (`c510cc91` keeps searching; `04b7c6e3` hangs on completion confirmation); (3) wrong optimization modeling leading to attractive wrong answers like 63000 (uniform step f) or 176620 (flawed S_k algebra in `6de05e67` reasoning); (4) over-expensive tooling paths that consume the budget before submission (`745da5ee` MIP, `3a30e89f` repeated script rewrites). The intended math capability is only directly tested in the ~7 trials that produced substantive work; even there, delivery and time management often—not algebraic inability—explain the score.
reports.intended_vs_unexpected_insight: Intended: hard combinatorial reasoning about pairs (f,g) with a 20-sum inequality and budget sum f(i)≤300. Agents did fail that capability on most reasoning-only paths (wrong extrema, fixation on 63000). Unexpected but valuable: two trials (`04b7c6e3`, `c510cc91`) reached the correct numerical optimum via closed-form or search, yet the benchmark still records failure—highlighting deliverable commitment, confirmation-loop fragility, and timeout sensitivity as first-class failure modes. The instruction’s “solve in 10 minutes” aligns with the 600s agent timeout, but agents routinely spend the budget on unbounded verification or slow LLM turns instead of submitting a candidate answer early.
reports.generalizability: Partially generalizable. Answer-file finalization under fixed wall-clock, avoiding perfectionist re-search after a strong candidate, and recognizing when computation has plateaued transfer to many timed agent benchmarks (coding, data, math). The specific pitfalls (20-fold convolution, step-function heuristics) are math-family specific. Infrastructure zero-token timeouts generalize to evaluation hygiene (detect non-runs) but do not teach model capability. Improving numeric exact-match grading (this answer is an integer) would reduce verifier noise for trials like `04b7c6e3` where the model likely submitted the right value.
reports.confounds: Heavy confounds weaken a “high” rating: 50% of trials never meaningfully started (0 tokens, timeout on first LLM call). We lack per-judge verifier logs to explain why `04b7c6e3` scored 0 despite `echo 115440`; possibilities include confirmation never finalized, sandbox state, or LLM-judge/API failure defaulting reward to 0.0 (`test.sh` fallback). The LLM ensemble verifier adds variance unrelated to problem solving. Model/harness mix (terminus-2 vs claude-code vs codex) conflates tool-use behavior with raw reasoning. Only one trial clearly executed a correct write command; cross-trial comparison of math ability is thin.
reports.implications_for_future_design: For benchmark tasks: (1) use exact string/numeric match when ideal_answer is a plain integer like 115440, reserving LLM judges for expressions; (2) add process metrics (time-to-first-answer-write, whether answer.txt exists at timeout) separate from correctness; (3) disable or shorten “are you sure?” completion gates for single-shot math submits; (4) cap or score expensive compute phases separately from reasoning. For agents: policies to write `/workspace/answer.txt` as soon as a candidate optimum is found, then optionally refine; treat instruction “10 minutes” as a hard stop with explicit remaining-time checks; prefer targeted DP/search on reduced state (partition of f) over full MIP or exhaustive f enumeration. For training: emphasize verifying convoluted min-over-partition constraints with small brute-force sanity checks before trusting closed forms; penalize continuing search after beating the incumbent by a wide margin.

reports.tldr: Medium insightfulness. The task was meant to test hard olympiad functional-equation reasoning, but 15/18 trials ended in AgentTimeoutError and 2 in verifier infrastructure failures, so outcomes are heavily confounded. Where agents did produce answers, they almost uniformly gave an incomplete characterization (f≡0 and f(n)=n²) and missed the ground-truth piecewise family f(even)=0, f(odd)=any perfect square. Several trajectories discovered that broader family computationally yet failed to commit it to answer.txt before timing out—revealing a synthesis/deliverable-prioritization gap alongside the math gap.
reports.main_insight: This omnimath functional-equation task exposes two coupled agent weaknesses: (1) incomplete structural characterization of solution sets in hard ∀-quantified math problems—agents latch onto obvious families (f≡0, f(n)=n²) and stop, even when Python search finds counterexamples to that closure; and (2) poor time-to-deliverable management in agent harnesses—many runs consume the full 300 s budget on extended reasoning or computation without ever writing /workspace/answer.txt. The reference solution requires two families: f(n)=0 on even integers with arbitrary perfect squares on odd integers, plus f(n)=n² globally. Agents who wrote answers omitted or mangled the first family; agents who found it computationally (notably gemini-3.1-pro-preview and qwen3.6-max-preview terminus runs) did not translate evidence into a final graded submission.
reports.why_it_matters: OmniMath-style benchmarks are increasingly used to measure frontier reasoning, but this task shows that a hard math item can fail to discriminate capability when paired with tight agent timeouts and expensive LLM-judge verifiers. The math lesson—that agents prematurely close the search space on 'characterize all functions' problems—is directly relevant to training and eval design for competition math. The workflow lesson—that computational exploration does not reliably collapse into a correct final answer under time pressure—is relevant across agent benchmarks where deliverables must be written to disk. Improving either premature closure or deliverable prioritization would transfer to many math, science, and planning tasks beyond this single problem.
reports.evidence_from_trajectories: Across 18 trials, 0 received a passing reward; only one (claude-opus-4-7 via claude-code, trial c4758350) completed verification with reward 0.0 after writing 'f(n)=0 … or f(n)=n²' at step 3—omitting the piecewise family in ground_truths.json. Fifteen trials hit AgentTimeoutError at ~300 s agent_execution duration; e.g., deepseek-v4-pro terminus (312258c7) has only step 1 (the prompt) and never responds. qwen3.6-max-preview terminus (da097e3e) is more informative: steps 2–4 run solve.py/solve2.py, confirming f(x)=0 and f(x)=x² pass, but step 4 output shows 'f(x)=(x mod 2)*x^2 PASSES' while the agent's analysis still concludes only two solutions—and no answer.txt is written before timeout. gemini-3.1-pro-preview terminus (b994dc2e) at steps 4–9 exhaustively searches small domains (1576 valid functions), tests f(even)=0 with random odd squares (test_family.py: 'All random … valid: True'), but never writes answer.txt and times out after repeated JSON parse failures at steps 2–3, 5, 7–8. claude-opus-4-7 terminus (7ff06de8) writes answer.txt at step 2 but hallucinates an 'IMO 2010 Problem 5' third family, revises three times, marks task_complete, and gets RewardFileNotFoundError—verifier ran ~16 s without producing reward files. MiniMax-M2.7 claude-code (7e3aeaac) spends ~4.5 min in a single reasoning block, then writes the wrong answer 'f(x)=0 … and f(x)=1' at step 4; f≡1 fails because f(1-b)+b=1+b is not always square (verified: b=1 gives 2). gemini-cli (ef59694c) at steps 2–3 confirms f3 (even→0, odd→x²) and f4 (even→0, odd→random square) pass, then step 4 pivots to web search instead of writing the answer.
reports.surface_failure_vs_root_cause: Surface failures: 0/18 pass; 15 AgentTimeoutError, 2 RewardFileNotFoundError, 1 graded failure (reward 0.0). Root cause is layered. Mathematically, agents fail to enumerate the full solution set—especially the parity-based family where f(2a)=0 makes the expression reduce to f(f(a)-b), allowing f(even)=0 and f(odd) any perfect square. Reasoning failures include false problem recall (opus terminus inventing IMO 2010 families), incorrect constant-function analysis (MiniMax concluding f≡1 works), and ignoring own computational counterexamples (qwen terminus seeing (x mod 2)*x² pass but not promoting it). Operationally, agents treat the 300 s wall clock as unlimited reasoning budget rather than prioritizing the required artifact; gemini terminus lost additional turns to terminus-2 JSON formatting errors. Evaluation infrastructure also failed twice when the 60 s LLM-judge ensemble (4 models × 2 repeats in llm_judge.py) did not emit /logs/verifier/reward.json despite agents having written answer.txt.
reports.intended_vs_unexpected_insight: The task was designed to test hard omnimath functional-equation solving (category 'math', difficulty 'hard'). Agents did fail on that capability—no complete correct answer—but the dominant signal across trajectories is not pure math inability alone. An unexpected, equally strong bottleneck is deliverable management under timeout: most agents never produce a gradable answer file. A secondary unexpected insight is the computation–conclusion gap: the agents closest to the truth used Python search to find the piecewise family, then either reverted to the smaller {0, n²} set or spent remaining time on web search/formatting retries. So the task reveals that tool-assisted exploration and final mathematical synthesis are separable failures, not a single 'can't do olympiad math' dimension.
reports.generalizability: The incomplete-solution-set closure problem generalizes to any 'determine all X satisfying P' benchmark in math, logic, or specification mining—agents often report a plausible subset and stop. The deliverable-prioritization failure generalizes broadly: coding agents that debug extensively but never commit, research agents that gather evidence but miss write-up deadlines, etc. The computation-to-conclusion gap also generalizes wherever agents use scripts as heuristics but lack proof obligations to reconcile counterexamples with stated theorems. These transfer beyond omnimath. The specific parity/perfect-square family is problem-specific and less generalizable. Heavy timeout and LLM-judge failure rates limit how cleanly this single task measures the math gap in isolation.
reports.confounds: Several confounds weaken causal attribution. (1) Agent timeout is 300 s while the instruction says '5 minutes'—agents may not treat them as the same constraint. (2) Verifier uses an 8-call LLM ensemble (JUDGE_MODELS × JUDGE_REPEATS=2) within a 60 s verifier timeout; two trials with valid answer.txt still got RewardFileNotFoundError, so infrastructure noise accounts for ~11% of trials before math is judged. (3) terminus-2 harness JSON parsing failures (gemini terminus steps 2–3, 5, 7–8) consumed turns without progress. (4) Only one trial received a numeric judge score, so pass/fail on the intended math capability is mostly inferred from partial answers, not verified grades. (5) The ground-truth piecewise family allows 'any perfect square' on odd inputs—a subtle infinite family that LLM judging may itself treat inconsistently. (6) Some timeout trials show zero agent steps beyond the prompt, suggesting model/harness stalls unrelated to the math content.
reports.implications_for_future_design: For benchmark tasks: separate 'reasoning correctness' from 'artifact delivery' metrics on math items; record whether answer.txt exists before timeout. For hard characterization problems, add intermediate checkpoints or require explicit 'candidate family list' before final write to surface premature closure. For agent training: reward reconciling computational counterexamples with stated conclusions (qwen's (x mod 2)*x² pass is a teachable moment). For harness design: enforce early draft writes ('write best-known answer by T/2, refine if time remains') especially when instructions specify short wall-clock budgets. For verifiers: LLM-judge ensembles need timeout budgets matched to call count; failed judge runs should degrade gracefully to partial credit rather than RewardFileNotFoundError. For omnimath specifically: this item discriminates incomplete structural reasoning, but at current timeout/eval settings it mostly measures whether an agent finishes at all—consider longer budgets for hard FE problems or split into 'find all families' (structured output) and 'write proof sketch' subtasks.

reports.tldr: Verdict: medium. This SWE-Lancer manager task exposes a systematic gap: agents rank competing bug-fix proposals by present-day codebase fit and technical elegance (modal lifecycle / keyboard timing), converging on proposals 0 or 1, while the verified human manager choice is proposal 4. Zero of 18 trials matched the label, giving clear evidence—but heavy confounds (post-fix repo snapshot, opaque historical acceptance criteria) keep it below a rare high rating.
reports.main_insight: The task is designed to test whether an agent can predict which Upwork proposal Expensify managers would accept—not whether it can implement a fix. Across models and harnesses, agents behave like senior engineers doing technical triage: they explore ContactMethodDetailsPage, ConfirmModal, BaseModal, and keyboard utilities, then pick the proposal that best matches what the current tree already supports or what looks architecturally clean. The trajectories show near-unanimous rejection of the ground-truth label (proposal 4: Keyboard.dismiss at confirm-delete plus disabling KeyboardAvoidingView on ContactMethodsPage) in favor of proposal 0 (onModalWillHide plumbing) or proposal 1 (dismiss keyboard before opening the delete modal). The stable failure mode is substituting technical merit under the checked-out codebase for organizational acceptance of a historical proposal set.
reports.why_it_matters: SWE-Lancer and similar bounty/manager benchmarks increasingly separate contributor work from reviewer/manager work. If agents cannot align with how maintainers actually choose among plausible fixes, automating proposal triage, payout decisions, or routing will systematically over-reward elegant abstractions and under-reward simpler patches that won because of demo evidence, scope discipline, or team norms. The trajectories also warn benchmark designers: giving agents a modern repo while asking them to judge 2023 proposals without temporal isolation teaches the wrong lesson and can masquerade as an agent capability gap when it is partly an evaluation design issue.
reports.evidence_from_trajectories: The verifier in tests/test.sh accepts only selected_proposal_id == 4; all 18 trials scored 0. Submitted choices clustered as proposal 0 in 10 trials (e.g., hy3-preview trial 3d394a9a step 13–14 writes id 0 after grep shows onModalWillHide already in BaseModal; qwen3.6-max trial 52dd22ef step ~13 explicitly rejects proposal 4 for side effects while picking 0) and proposal 1 in 7 trials (claude-opus-4-7 trial 959cdb59 step 10 lists proposal 4 has video proof but step 11 still writes 1 because current code already calls Keyboard.dismiss; glm-5.1 trial 8465e760 step ~15 cites KeyboardUtils.dismiss() as reason 1 is best). No trial selected 4. gpt-5.5 (trial dd5f0048, step ~781 message) explicitly asks whether the live code is already a mix of proposal 4, notes Keyboard in toggleDeleteModal, then still writes proposal 0 at step ~919. gemini-3.1-pro (trial d74c9994, step ~1192) briefly considers proposal 4 interesting but commits to 0. One trial (hy3-preview claude-code 71278491) ended after 4 steps with only reasoning—no manager_decisions.json. Agents repeatedly used codebase grep as decisive evidence (onModalWillHide in BaseModal, existing Keyboard.dismiss) even though the instruction frames a historical manager decision among frozen proposal texts.
reports.surface_failure_vs_root_cause: Surface failure: every agent wrote manager_decisions.json with selected_proposal_id 0 or 1 (or failed to write a file), so test.sh printed Expected: 4, Actual: 0/1 and assigned reward 0. Root cause: agents optimized for technically coherent fixes aligned with the current Expensify checkout, not for reproducing the historical manager label. Proposal 0 looked like the missing glue (ConfirmModal lacks onModalWillHide while BaseModal has it). Proposal 1 matched existing KeyboardUtils patterns. Proposal 4 was dismissed as redundant (keyboard dismiss already present), too broad (disable KeyboardAvoidingView on the list page), or lower quality (typo Keybord, less narrative depth)—and agents rarely weighted its attached demo video as decisive. claude-opus-4-7 step 10 even inverted the logic: seeing Keyboard.dismiss in today's file was taken as evidence for proposal 1, not for proposal 4.
reports.intended_vs_unexpected_insight: Intended insight: whether agents can exercise manager judgment—pick the proposal a human lead would fund among six competing write-ups for an iOS keyboard flash bug. Agents did fail that capability: 0/18 matched proposal 4. Unexpected but valuable secondary insight: codebase exploration actively hurt performance. The sandbox repo appears to reflect later evolution (partial fixes from proposals 0/1), so agents treated the task as which fix should we merge now rather than which proposal did managers pick in June 2023. Several trajectories show awareness of that tension (gpt-5.5 maybe a mix of proposal 4) without changing the final answer.
reports.generalizability: Partially generalizable. The lesson transfers to any workflow where agents must choose among multiple human-submitted plans (open-source proposal review, Upwork triage, internal design doc selection) rather than implement the best-looking patch. The bias toward architectural completeness over simpler, demo-backed fixes likely appears outside Expensify. It does not generalize as cleanly as pure coding gaps (e.g., patch construction, test execution) because the correct label here is an opaque historical organizational decision; improving agents may require explicit training on maintainer rubrics, temporal snapshots, or acceptance metadata—not just better React Native knowledge.
reports.confounds: Major confound: agents read a current /app/expensify tree while proposals reference 2023 line numbers and behaviors; present code already includes Keyboard.dismiss in toggleDeleteModal and onModalWillHide in BaseModal, which rationalizes rejecting proposal 4 and favoring 0/1. The verifier gives no rubric for why managers chose 4 (video proof, scope, reviewer preference, subsequent PR history)—only a single integer label—so reviewers cannot distinguish agents bad at organizational prediction from agents correctly ranking technical quality today. Instruction noise (duplicate step numbers, long Upwork boilerplate, misleading fix the issue framing) may push coding-agent heuristics. One trial never submitted. Proposal 4's typo and shorter write-up may penalize LLM scoring relative to proposal 0's detailed testing narrative.
reports.implications_for_future_design: For benchmarks: (1) pin the repo to the pre-merge commit for the issue when judging historical proposals, or forbid/strip anachronistic signals; (2) publish the manager rubric (e.g., must include demo, minimal blast radius, no shared-component API changes) so the label is inferable; (3) report partial credit or separate axes—technical correctness vs label match. For agents: train an explicit decision mode that treats proposal text and acceptance criteria as primary and codebase as contextual only when timestamps align; surface signals like attached Result videos. For harnesses: manager tasks should not reuse fix-the-bug prompts if the deliverable is only JSON selection; reduce exploration budget or reward faster submission when proposals are self-contained. For analysis: report consensus on wrong answers (here 17/17 among submitters missed label 4) as evidence of systematic bias, not random error.

reports.tldr: Verdict: medium. Across 18 trials, 0 agents pass (threshold 1.0), but 7/8 completed runs plateau at exactly 0.333 semantic score because they all implement the same wrong oracle: a 6-qubit CCX circuit for a simplified trit-valued f(x), while the verifier (and reference) require a 7-qubit coset-index oracle that XORs a 2-bit cycle label constant on each Simon coset. The pattern is a clear spec-to-semantics grounding failure, not random QASM bugs, but it is domain-narrow and confounded by 10/18 harness timeouts.
reports.main_insight: QCircuitBench’s generalized Simon ternary-oracle task exposes a systematic gap between reading a dense quantum-math prompt and implementing what the hidden verifier actually measures. The prompt describes f: {0,1,2}^n → {0,1,2}^n with c/b rules and also gives output width 2n + log₂(3^n/3) (6 qubits for n=2, s=02, b=20). The verifier simulates O_f|x⟩|y⟩ = |x⟩|y ⊕ g(x)⟩ where g(x) is the 2-bit index of which 3-element coset x belongs to under secret s=02 (cycles 00→02→01, 10→12→11, 20→22→21), not the full trit string from the prose. The reference QASM (7 qubits, multi-controlled X decomposition) encodes exactly those coset labels (00, 10, 01). Agents who finish overwhelmingly emit nearly identical 6-qubit oracle gates that XOR a function of only the first input trit—valid QASM, wrong semantics—yielding 3/9 simulation hits (0.333) every time.
reports.why_it_matters: For benchmark design, this task cleanly separates “writes syntactically valid OpenQASM” from “implements the oracle the Simon experiment needs.” For agent improvement, it shows that STEM prompts with both symbolic f(x) definitions and separate qubit-count formulas need explicit grounding checks; without simulation against the stated hidden structure (cosets), models confidently ship algebraically simplified but test-incompatible circuits. The identical 0.333 score across frontier models (GPT-5.5, Claude Opus 4.7, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Qwen 3.6 Max) makes this a reproducible evaluation signal rather than a one-off mistake.
reports.evidence_from_trajectories: Reward split: 7 trials at 0.333 (gemini-3.1-pro ×2, gpt-5.5 ×2, claude-opus-4-7 ×2, qwen3.6-max-preview ×1), 1 at 0.0 with solution (hy3-preview), 10 at 0.0 with AgentTimeoutError (no or late solution). Completing agents converge on the same template—for example trial 31e34694 (gpt-5.5, step 7) and ba6ab152 (gpt-5.5 terminus-2, step 2) write a 6-qubit gate with X/CCX on q[0],q[1] targeting q[4],q[5], ignoring q[2],q[3]; trial 5db1ffdf (claude-opus-4-7, step 3) does the same with 8 qubits but still only conditions on the first trit pair. Trial 49467574 (qwen, steps 2–4) spends thousands of tokens reconciling coset triples, correctly derives three outputs {20,00,10}, yet still emits the identical 6-qubit CCX circuit and marks complete without Aer simulation. Trial 230175b0 (gemini, step 4) writes an even simpler oracle (cx q1,q4; ccx on q0,q1,q5). Trial 3d680266 (minimax, 13 steps, 600s timeout) burns the budget in reasoning_content on modular arithmetic but writes to /dev/stdin/solution.py and times out. Timeout-only trials like 4a156b52 (deepseek-v4-pro[1m]) end at step 1 with no file. Local replay of the common agent circuit against the verifier gives score 0.333 with failures like input 00 expecting cycle label 00 but measuring 01; the reference QASM scores 1.0 with all coset members mapping to 00, 10, or 01 respectively.
reports.surface_failure_vs_root_cause: Surface: binary_reward 0, semantic_score 0.333 or 0, no pass at threshold 1.0. Root cause: agents implement a collapsed algebraic f(x) on the first input trit (often f ≈ (x₀+2, 0) in binary encoding) instead of the coset-index oracle the verifier checks. They miss that output register width log₂(3^{n-1})=2 bits labels which of three Simon cosets x lies in, constant on each coset. Secondary failures: no executable self-test with Qiskit Aer (available in the environment), and ~56% of trials hitting the 600s agent timeout before delivering solution.py.
reports.intended_vs_unexpected_insight: Intended capability: domain-specific quantum oracle synthesis for generalized Simon over Z₃—reversible circuit design, ternary encoding, OpenQASM constraints. Agents fail primarily on an earlier step: formal specification grounding (what y registers encode). Unexpected but valuable: the score cliffs at exactly 1/3 successes (one input per coset, not one full coset), revealing that wrong circuits partially correlate with coset structure for this fixed (s,b) instance; also that long verbal “verification” in trajectories (e.g., qwen step 4, opus step 5) does not prevent the same wrong circuit every model submits.
reports.generalizability: Moderately generalizable within scientific/algorithmic coding: binding formulas in prompts (qubit counts, output ranges) to implementation layout, and closing the loop with simulation against invariant structure (here, coset constancy). Less generalizable as a universal frontier gap—quantum oracle compilation via truth-table MCX is niche, and the specific 0.333 plateau depends on this verifier and (s,b). Improving spec grounding and “run the packaged checker before submit” would help many STEM benchmarks; learning the reference’s MCX decomposition would mostly help quantum-circuit tasks.
reports.confounds: Instruction ambiguity: prose defines f(x) as an n-trit string while qubit indexing implies a compressed coset label; agents are not shown test.sh. Pass threshold 1.0 with no partial credit above 0.333 rewards all-or-nothing grading. Agent timeout_sec 600 vs instruction “10 minutes” and hard task difficulty cause 10/18 exceptions unrelated to QASM quality. Harness differences (codex vs terminus-2 vs claude-code) do not change the 0.333 pattern among finishers. Cannot observe whether agents had QCircuitBench docs in the empty /app workspace.
reports.implications_for_future_design: Benchmarks: (1) state explicitly that the output register is the coset index in {0,…,3^{n-1}-1}, not the full f(x) vector, or align prose with verifier; (2) provide a small public example cycle check agents can run; (3) add submetrics for coset invariance (all three inputs per cycle) to avoid the misleading 0.333 partial signal; (4) separate syntax, coset-correctness, and gate-efficiency scoring. Agents: require simulation hooks before submit on scientific tasks; train/reward mapping from qubit-count formulas to register semantics. Evaluation: treat identical partial scores across models as a diagnostic of specification misunderstanding, not capability spread; cap reasoning-only steps or penalize timeouts without solution.py.

reports.tldr: Verdict: medium. Across 18 trials (0 passes, one partial score 0.2), agents consistently recognize a generalized Simon problem over Z_3 but implement the wrong quantum primitive (binary Hadamard + collision heuristics) instead of the required GH-based circuit and mod-3 linear-algebra recovery. The pattern is real and cross-model, but it is narrowly quantum-domain knowledge and is confounded by contradictory qubit-encoding specs and frequent 600s harness timeouts.
reports.main_insight: This task–trajectory set shows a specialized domain-knowledge gap: translating a stated generalized Simon problem over Z_3^n into the correct quantum subroutine (generalized Hadamard on 2-qubits-per-trit registers, oracle, inverse GH) plus the matching classical post-processing (collect constraints y·s ≡ 0 mod 3 via RREF over Z_3). Agents grasp the group structure and 3-to-1 collision semantics, but almost uniformly substitute binary H superposition and ad-hoc collision/voting classical recovery. None of 18 trajectories implements the reference GH gate or sympy mod-3 RREF pipeline from the hidden solution.
reports.why_it_matters: For QCircuitBench and quantum agent benchmarks, the failure mode is instructive: models can narrate the right problem class yet still ship an algorithmically wrong circuit when the answer depends on non-textbook encodings (ternary qudit embedding, custom QASM gates) and tight verifier coupling. For general agent design, it cautions against scoring “understood Simon” from prose alone—the verifier gates on executable circuit statistics (semantic_score > 0.25 on randomized oracles). For benchmark authors, the unanimous wrong-family submissions signal that task specs must pin encoding and oracle layout, or scores measure spec parsing rather than quantum reasoning.
reports.evidence_from_trajectories: Reference bar (test.sh): semantic_score is success rate over random secret strings; pass threshold is 1.0 when result_score > 0.25. Claude Opus (4ce70209, step 5 Write): H on q[0..4], Oracle on 10 qubits, measures all 10, post-processes with collision voting and dual bit-order heuristics—reward 0.0. Gemini terminus (be7cd0c2, step 4): explicitly chooses brute-force superposition + collision because domain is small; step 2 notes oracle.inc missing at runtime—reward 0.2 (only non-zero). GPT-5.5 codex (21181a85, step 9): same H+circuit but elaborate classical orbit-scoring over 27 inputs—reward 0.0. Hy3 (7787320b, steps 2–4): iterates BV/QFT-over-Z_3 narratives but still emits H and double-oracle tricks—times out at 600s. Eleven trials end with AgentTimeoutError (e.g. minimax 2591f1d0, deepseek a4a81416) before or after partial solution files. No trajectory defines a GH gate or recover_secret_string_3d-style mod-3 RREF; grep across all trajectory.json files shows no agent-authored GH circuit matching simon_ternary_n3.qasm.
reports.surface_failure_vs_root_cause: Surface: all binary_reward=0; semantic_score at or below 0.2. Root cause (most likely): wrong quantum algorithm family—binary Hadamard instead of ternary GH Simon—and mismatched classical decoder (5-bit integer / collision heuristics vs 2-bits-per-trit binary_to_ternary + mod-3 linear solve). Contributing causes: instruction says n_i=n_o=5 but also 2 qubits/trit with input indices 0..2n-1 (6 qubits), while the reference QASM applies GH to six input qubits and measures six bits; agents follow the n_i=5 wording and never align with the verifier’s encoding. oracle.inc is absent during agent runs (be7cd0c2 step 2: cat oracle.inc → No such file), so agents guess bit ordering without seeing the oracle’s true layout.
reports.intended_vs_unexpected_insight: Intended: test whether agents can design the generalized ternary Simon quantum algorithm end-to-end (QASM + Aer post-processing). Agents did fail on that capability—0/18 full pass—but many partially satisfied a different strategy (classical collision recovery after naive superposition), which the verifier only weakly rewards. Unexpected: (1) spec/encoding contradiction steers even strong models to a consistent wrong architecture; (2) 11/18 harness timeouts obscure whether more time would yield GH discovery; (3) one heuristic solution reaches 0.2 semantic_score, showing the benchmark partially conflates “almost Simon” collision logic with the true algorithmic bar.
reports.generalizability: Improving GH-based Simon construction would help only quantum-algorithm / QCircuitBench-style tasks, not broad coding agents. The more transferable lessons are narrower: (a) align natural-language specs with verifier encodings before testing reasoning; (b) expose or stub oracle.inc during agent execution when layout matters; (c) separate “problem comprehension” from “correct quantum primitive selection” in rubrics. The mod-3 linear-algebra post-processing pattern generalizes within hidden-subgroup / Simon task families but not to unrelated agent workloads.
reports.confounds: Instruction conflicts on qubit count (n_i=5 vs 2n=6 input lines and reference GH on q[0..5]). oracle.inc not present in /app during agent runs though verifier injects oracle definitions at test time. Agent timeout 600s vs prompt ‘10 minutes’—11 exceptions may reflect budget/thrashing (hy3 7787320b revises solution multiple times) rather than inability to finish a known algorithm. Codex gpt-5.5 sandbox lacked qiskit at step 7 (ModuleNotFoundError), so local simulation feedback was unavailable though verifier conda env has it. Partial credit threshold (>25% success) means 0.2 could be noisy; only one trial achieved it. Harness diversity (codex, claude-code, terminus-2) adds variance but failure mode is consistent across models.
reports.implications_for_future_design: Pin encoding in the prompt with a single canonical diagram (qubit indices, bit→trit map) matching the reference QASM; ship a read-only oracle stub or signature file in the agent environment. Consider decomposing into subtasks: (1) write GH QASM fragment, (2) write mod-3 RREF decoder—so failures localize. Report semantic_score components (qasm_syntax, code_syntax) separately in trajectories for judges. Raise agent timeout or require early checkpoint of solution.py if the task needs multi-iteration QASM synthesis. For insight harvesting, treat unanimous wrong-quantum-primitive submissions as domain-knowledge benchmarks, not general agent regressions—unless the goal is explicitly quantum algorithm synthesis.

reports.tldr: Verdict: medium. The task cleanly exposes a recurring failure mode in scientific toolchain tasks: agents can draft plausible QAOA + Qiskit solutions from instructions alone, but without in-sandbox execution they cannot reliably match a hidden canonical circuit/API and close the last mile on stochastic optimization quality. Zero of 17 trials passed the binary threshold (semantic_score = 1.0), yet two models reached ~0.86–0.89, showing the gap is calibration and verification rather than total ignorance of Max-Cut/QAOA.
reports.main_insight: QCircuitBench-qaoa-n8 is really two coupled tests: (1) encode an 8-node 3-regular Max-Cut instance as a valid OpenQASM 3.0 parameterized QAOA circuit plus a Qiskit-Aer post-processing loop using parameter_binds and scipy.optimize.minimize, and (2) achieve high cut quality against a hidden reference ansatz in /insight/task/tests/qaoa_n8.qasm (custom rzz_0 gate, two parameters beta_0/gamma_0, rx(2*beta_0), meas[i]=measure q[i]). Across 17 trajectories, agents consistently produce syntactically well-formed QAOA-like circuits (Hadamards, per-edge ZZ via cx-rz-cx or rzz, rx mixers) and optimization scaffolding, but they diverge on ansatz depth (p=1 vs p=2), gate conventions (rz(gamma) vs rz(2*gamma) vs rzz(-gamma)), measurement syntax, and simulator API details (parameter_binds shape, transpile target, get_counts indexing). The benchmark therefore measures domain-specific quantum programming fidelity under toolchain constraints more than raw graph reasoning.
reports.why_it_matters: Scientific coding benchmarks increasingly look like this: long constraint-heavy prompts, domain libraries only present at grade time, and success defined by numeric proximity to a hidden reference rather than by local syntax checks. For agent designers, the lesson is that 'knows QAOA' on paper is insufficient—agents need execution-grounded iteration against the exact stack (Qiskit 1.1.0, OpenQASM 3.0 dialect, AerSimulator parameter_binds). For benchmark designers, the 0/17 pass rate with two high partial scores signals a brittle all-or-nothing threshold on a stochastic metric (20 verifier runs) that may separate 'close' from 'pass' for reasons other than conceptual failure.
reports.evidence_from_trajectories: Outcome spread from meta.json: 0/17 binary_reward=1; continuous rewards cluster at 0.0 (13 trials) with near-misses hy3-preview terminus-2 trial 65fd425f at 0.893 (step 11 marks task_complete after 12 episodes of syntax self-checks but no Qiskit run) and gpt-5.5 terminus-2 trial 9b3a97b9 at 0.857 (step 2 brute-forces correct max cut=10 via python3 - <<'PY', step 3 writes a non-QAOA state-preparation circuit with maxiter=8 COBYLA, step 4 submits). Representative near-canonical attempts: claude-opus-4-7 trial 22153677 step 2 writes cx-rz-cx per edge plus rx(beta) (p=1, two params) but scores 0.0; gemini-3.1-pro trial 2063b9a4 step 2 hits ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'qiskit' on a probe script, then step 3 submits anyway. Failure modes: deepseek-v4-pro trial 4b2e5b35 step 2 builds p=2 with input float[4] params and OpenQASM comments (verifier may still parse); qwen3.6 trial ffeb2fdb times out at 600s while writing test_solution.py; six AgentTimeoutError trials (glm-5.1, minimax, mimo, qwen) and two VerifierTimeoutError trials on heavy agent circuits. Verifier bar from test.sh: semantic_score averages 20 runs of 1-(10-max(top_two cut))/10 with target cut 10 for bitstring 10011010; pass threshold clipped_score=1.0 only if result_score>=0.7 then requires 1.0 for binary pass per meta reward_metric.
reports.surface_failure_vs_root_cause: Surface failure: no agent reaches semantic_score=1.0, so binary_reward stays 0. Root cause is not inability to read the graph—gpt-5.5 step 2 correctly finds max cut 10—but inability to deliver a circuit+optimizer pipeline that reliably samples top_two bitstrings with cut 10 under the hidden reference distribution. Contributing sub-causes visible in trajectories: (a) agent sandbox lacks qiskit (gemini step 2), blocking closed-loop validation; (b) ansatz mismatch vs hidden qaoa_n8.qasm (agents use 2–4+ parameters, native rzz, or ad-hoc state prep instead of custom rzz_0(2*gamma_0) and rx(2*beta_0)); (c) optimization under-specification (gpt-5.5 maxiter=8, inconsistent sign handling for minimize vs -compute_expectation); (d) operational noise from 20× stochastic verifier runs combined with a hard 1.0 pass bar; (e) timeouts on long QASM files and verifier COBYLA loops.
reports.intended_vs_unexpected_insight: Intended insight: frontier agents struggle to implement constrained quantum workflows (OpenQASM 3.0 + Qiskit Aer parameter_binds + variational Max-Cut) end-to-end. That holds, but trajectories refine it: most agents pass the intended 'write plausible QAOA code' bar and fail the unstated 'match hidden reference ansatz closely enough for perfect sampling' bar. Unexpected insight: environment/tooling mismatch—agents are told qiskit==1.1.0 is required yet the agent container cannot import qiskit, pushing them toward submit-without-run behavior (gemini, hy3 syntax-only checks). Also, time/harness loss is large (6/17 agent timeouts, 2/17 verifier timeouts), so part of the 0% pass rate is budget/thrash rather than purely quantum knowledge.
reports.generalizability: Partially generalizable. The pattern—long-format scientific APIs, dialect constraints, optimize-then-score with hidden reference—will recur across QCircuitBench and similar science-code benchmarks, so improving execution-grounded iteration and constraint checklists would help that family. It is not as broadly transferable as cross-cutting gaps like time-budget awareness or wide-scale search: fixing QAOA angle conventions helps quantum tasks specifically. The near-miss scores suggest general coding agents are close on structure but weak on stack-exact integration and empirical tuning without runnable dependencies in the agent image.
reports.confounds: Several confounds weaken a 'high' rating: (1) binary pass requires semantic_score exactly 1.0 while internal clipped_score uses 0.7, creating a harsh ceiling on a noisy metric; (2) agent image missing qiskit contradicts task requirements and prevents fair self-test; (3) hidden reference qaoa_n8.qasm is not in the prompt, so low scores may reflect oracle distance not stated objectives; (4) 8/17 trials end in agent or verifier timeout, mixing capability with harness limits; (5) gate_count_ratio is computed but not gating reward, so some failures may be purely optimization/sampling; (6) verifier runs ground_truth with bitstring reversal [::-1] in one path but scores agent top_two without documenting endianness expectations.
reports.implications_for_future_design: Benchmark tasks should either ship the target conda env in the agent sandbox (qiskit_aer importable) or explicitly state that validation is grade-time-only. Prefer tiered scoring (syntax / runnable / cut>=9 / cut=10) over a single stochastic binary threshold. If testing QAOA implementation skill, provide the required ansatz family (p=1, gate decomposition template) or score cut value alone without hidden circuit matching. Cap verifier cost (fewer than 20 full optimizations) or cache seeds. For agents, add a mandatory 'smoke-run' step when scientific libraries are required, and teach parameter_binds list-of-dicts patterns for Qiskit 1.x. Report pass rates separately for timeout vs scored failures to avoid conflating capability with wall-clock.

reports.tldr: Medium insightfulness. Across 16 frontier-model trials, 0/16 passed the verifier (expected [8, 10.5] ± 0.2), yet most agents produced qualitatively plausible two-peak answers—especially the recurring [8.0, 10.2] cluster that misses the second peak by 0.3 kpc. The trajectories reveal a reproducible gap in scientific pipeline fidelity (substituting plain GMM/EM for error-deconvolved mixtures, paper-guided peak heuristics) compounded by poor compute-budget management (6/16 AgentTimeoutError on per-bin XDGMM over ~1M stars under 1 CPU / 2 GB / 1 hr).
reports.main_insight: This ReplicationBench task tests whether agents can reproduce a specific astrophysics numeric result from a masked paper plus pre-downloaded Gaia DR2 FITS data. The task–trajectory set shows that agents are strong at scaffolding the right workflow—read Section 3.2, select the All sample (l0/l180 FITS), compute R_gal and V_z, bin radially, fit two Gaussians, pick the dominant component, and find two peaks between 5–12 kpc—but weak at executing the prescribed methodology faithfully enough to hit tight numeric tolerances. A dominant failure mode is methodological substitution: agents label their code “extreme-deconvolution” while actually running sklearn GaussianMixture, hand-rolled EM without measurement-error deconvolution, or scipy.signal.find_peaks on binned means. A second mode is budget exhaustion: six trials hit the 3600 s agent timeout while fitting mixtures bin-by-bin on million-star catalogs. The result is not random guessing but a systematic near-miss bias, most visibly the repeated [8.0, 10.2] answer versus the verifier’s [8, 10.5].
reports.why_it_matters: ReplicationBench-style tasks are meant to measure whether agents can do real research reproduction, not just retrieve memorized constants. This task shows that current agents often pass the “looks like science” bar—multi-file pipelines, paper parsing, FITS handling—while still failing verification because small methodological deviations shift peak locations beyond tolerance. That distinction matters for benchmark designers (should tolerances reflect bin-grid quantization?), agent trainers (need stronger adherence to specified statistical methods), and tool-use protocols (need compute planning and intermediate validation on long numerical jobs). Improving reproduction fidelity and budget-aware execution would transfer to other scientific-computing, data-analysis, and paper-replication benchmarks beyond this one Gaia task.
reports.evidence_from_trajectories: Verifier bar: /tests/config.json expects {"value": [8, 10.5]} with per-element tolerance 0.2 kpc; all 16 trials scored reward 0.0. Convergent near-miss: gpt-5.5 (trial 150098b8, step 6) ran a full pure-Python pipeline on ~1.05M stars and wrote {"value":[8.0,10.2]} after LOCAL_MAXIMA at grid points 8.0 and 10.2; claude-opus-4-7 terminus (2bb81b7d, steps 22–23) and claude-code (6a406c29, steps 80–85) also finalized [8.0, 10.2]; qwen3.6-max (cf119823, steps 10–12) filtered three detected peaks down to [8.0, 10.2] using the paper’s “dip at 9 kpc” narrative. Method substitution: minimax claude-code (2cfb5d8a, step 116 reasoning) explicitly used sklearn GMM, not XDGMM, yielding [9.5, 10.5]; qwen (cf119823, step 9) wrote a custom fit_2gaussian_ed but still relied on find_peaks and paper-guided peak rejection. Compute failures: six trials (279a73cc, 38055070, 6c6c9826, b83d5f50, d2ad5299, d83caf71) ended with AgentTimeoutError after 3600 s—e.g., deepseek (279a73cc, step 45) was interrupted mid-sklearn GMM at R=8.0 with ^C after hours of per-bin fitting; opus terminus (2bb81b7d, step 13) was OOM-killed on SkyCoord for millions of rows before switching to memmap. Incomplete or divergent runs: mimo claude-code (4bc4d855) stopped at step 22 with todos still “in_progress” and no result.json; glm (d83caf71) pursued wrong peaks around 4.8–5.2 kpc; minimax terminus (b83d5f50, step 12) wrote [null, null] after finding zero local maxima.
reports.surface_failure_vs_root_cause: Surface failure: every agent’s /app/result.json failed pytest comparison against [8, 10.5] ± 0.2—either wrong peak radii, nulls, missing file, or timeout before a valid submission. Root cause is not inability to understand the question; agents consistently identify the All sample, the 0.2 kpc overlapping bins, and the two-peak expectation. The deeper causes are (1) statistical-method fidelity—replacing extreme-deconvolution Gaussian mixtures with faster approximations that shift peak locations, especially the second peak from 10.5 to 10.2; (2) peak-selection logic that uses paper prose (“dip near 9 kpc”) as a filter rather than strictly maximizing the dominant-component mean V_z curve; and (3) inadequate compute budgeting on a heavy per-bin fitting loop over ~1M stars within 1 CPU, 2 GB RAM, and 1 hour, producing timeouts and subsampled shortcuts (gemini 2a20dcaf, step 50, used subsampled data and wrote [7.8, 10.2]).
reports.intended_vs_unexpected_insight: The task was designed to test scientific reproduction of a published numeric result from masked paper instructions and local data. Agents did fail on that core capability, but the trajectories expose two layered bottlenecks rather than one. The intended insight—agents struggle with faithful extreme-deconvolution reproduction—is strongly supported by the [8.0, 10.2] cluster and GMM/EM substitutions. An additional, still valuable insight is compute/time-budget blindness: many agents launch full-resolution per-bin mixture fits without subsampling, caching, or staged validation and then time out (6/16). Premature completion is also visible—qwen (cf119823) declared success in 13 steps and gpt-5.5 in 8 steps after approximate pipelines—showing weak self-checking against the tight numeric bar even though outputs look structurally reasonable.
reports.generalizability: Partially generalizable. The lesson that agents substitute simpler numerical methods while claiming to follow paper-specified statistics applies broadly to replication, ML-for-science, and engineering tasks where procedure wording matters as much as code that runs. Likewise, poor planning on long CPU-bound loops under tight sandbox limits should transfer to other large-data benchmarks. However, much of the observed error is amplified by domain-specific choices (Gaia coordinate transforms, V_b≈V_z proxy, 0.2 kpc grid quantization) and by this task’s tight ±0.2 kpc tolerance relative to bin width. Fixing the weakness would help agents on similar replication tasks, but less so on unrelated coding or reasoning benchmarks.
reports.confounds: Several factors weaken certainty. The reference solve.sh hardcodes [8, 10.5] without demonstrating computation, so we cannot confirm from the sandbox alone which methodological deviation causes the 10.2 vs 10.5 split. Instructions cite “Section 3.2” while refined_spec.json omits section numbering, and the masked paper hides the true peaks—agents infer qualitative structure from prose about a 9 kpc dip. Resource limits (2 GB RAM, 1 CPU, 1 hr) likely cause timeouts independent of model reasoning; six exception trials are all AgentTimeoutError. Harness differences (terminus-2 vs claude-code vs gemini-cli) may affect tool reliability but do not explain the shared [8.0, 10.2] bias across models. Verifier logs in result.json do not expose per-field numeric diffs, though trajectories make the near-miss pattern clear.
reports.implications_for_future_design: Benchmark designers should separate reproduction into staged subscores—data selection, coordinate transform, mixture fitting method, peak extraction—so failures localize instead of collapsing to one binary numeric check. Tolerances should be justified relative to bin width (0.2 kpc grid may make 10.5 vs 10.2 ambiguous without interpolation rules). Tasks should either preinstall astroML/extreme-deconvolution or explicitly allow declared approximations with wider tolerance. Agent harnesses should encourage compute estimates before million-row fits, checkpoint intermediate curves, and validate against sanity plots before mark_task_complete. Training and evaluation should penalize method substitution (calling EM “extreme-deconvolution” without error convolution) and reward budget-aware strategies such as subsampling for development, memmap I/O, and progressive refinement. For ReplicationBench overall, report near-miss metrics (e.g., within 0.5 kpc) alongside strict pass rates to distinguish almost-reproduced science from total failure.

reports.tldr: Medium insightfulness. All 19 frontier trials failed despite many producing nearly correct NAME/REF ordering; the trajectories reveal a systematic gap in inferring unstated output-schema conventions (renumbering the ITEM column after reorder) plus overconfident partial self-verification, rather than a single clean inability to implement the core sort logic.
reports.main_insight: This SpreadsheetBench helper-column sort task exposes a compound failure mode in spreadsheet agents: most models correctly implement the hard parts—scanning multi-block A:C data, deduplicating on (B,C), and ordering groups by helper-list J as HASSAN→HAMAN→HAMMED—but then fail because they preserve original ITEM values (e.g., F2=5) when the hidden golden answer expects sequential re-indexing (F2=1, F3=2, …). A smaller subset (e.g., claude-opus-4-7) mis-parses the sort spec and groups all J-matched rows by global source order instead of iterating J’s list order, swapping HAMAN and HAMMED. Across trials, agents frequently declare success after reading back their own output without checking the full F:H tuple against any rubric.
reports.why_it_matters: Spreadsheet automation is dominated by ambiguous natural-language business rules where several interpretations are locally coherent. A 0/19 pass rate here is not evidence that frontier models cannot code openpyxl; it shows that benchmark success hinges on inferring implicit output conventions and validating every scored column. That matters for training (teach spec formalization and column-level oracles), for agent harness design (provide diff-style checkers before task_complete), and for benchmark construction (either state renumbering rules explicitly or accept both schemas).
reports.evidence_from_trajectories: Replaying agent logic against the verifier confirms two dominant error signatures. Opus (trial a7194462, step 3) writes F2:H11 with renumbered ITEM 1–10 but puts HAMMED before HAMAN (G4='HAMMED' vs gt='HAMAN'), using listed=[e for e in entries if e[0] in j_set] rather than looping helper names in J order. GPT-5.5 (567f0106, step 4) gets NAME order right—HASSAN, HASSAN, HAMAN, HAMMED—but writes preserved ITEM values F2=5, F3=1, failing the first cell. The same preserved-ITEM pattern appears in hy3-preview (28d2f3fb, step 6 verification: F2=5), qwen3.6-max-preview, minimax-m2.7 (54444655), mimo-v2.5-pro (48275c04, verify step expects F2=5), and deepseek-v4-pro[1m] (76ac1ccb, step 8: ws.cell(... column=6).value = a_val). Deepseek terminus (0adf8677) reaches the same correct NAME ordering at step 9 but still outputs F2=5 and times out at step 11 after extended exploration. Three trials never finish (deepseek-v4-pro, glm-5.1 timeouts; glm claude-code exit 1 at step 2). In multiple trials (e.g., b1458f8c step 5, ee32b291 step 7), agents print verification of F2=5 and mark task_complete despite that mismatch with the answer file’s F2=1.
reports.surface_failure_vs_root_cause: Surface failure: binary cell-by-cell mismatch in F2:H20 (most often Value diff at F2: gt=1, proc=5, or at G4 when HAMMED/HAMAN are swapped). Root cause: agents treat the task as ‘reorder rows and copy A:C into F:H’ rather than ‘emit a fresh sorted table with a new ITEM sequence,’ because the instruction never says whether column A should be preserved or renumbered after deduplication and reorder. Secondary root cause for Opus-like solutions: interpreting ‘names listed in column J appear first’ as one combined J-matched block in source order instead of ‘for each name in J’s top-to-bottom list, append its matching rows.’ Tertiary cause: agents stop after local sanity checks on NAME order and never validate ITEM against an oracle.
reports.intended_vs_unexpected_insight: The task intends to test multi-block spreadsheet ingestion, duplicate filtering, and helper-list custom sorting—most completing agents pass those sub-skills on NAME/REF. The unexpected but valuable insight is that the decisive gate is an unstated output-schema convention (ITEM re-indexing) combined with false completion: agents confidently finish with outputs that fail on the first scored cell. Timeout trials add a secondary lesson about dumping A1:J195 wholesale (deepseek step 2) rather than targeted inspection, but that is less central than the verifier–instruction gap on column F.
reports.generalizability: Partially generalizable. The pattern—implement the narrated transformation correctly on the ‘obvious’ columns but miss an implicit post-processing rule on a companion column—should transfer to other spreadsheet, ETL, and document-generation tasks where IDs, indices, or serial numbers must be recomputed after reorder. Helper-list ordering misreads are also broadly relevant to custom sort specs in SQL, pandas, and reporting tools. However, the specific ITEM-renumber convention is benchmark- and domain-specific unless tasks explicitly teach or test schema inference; improving it helps spreadsheet agents most, not all coding agents equally.
reports.confounds: The instruction does not state that ITEM must be renumbered 1..N after sorting; preserving source ITEM numbers is a plausible reading reinforced by phrases like ‘keep their original order from the source.’ The golden answer encodes a convention agents cannot derive unambiguously from text alone, inflating failure rates for reasons beyond core sorting ability. Verifier feedback is a single hard cell diff with no partial credit, so agents receive no signal that only column F is wrong. Some trials mix harness failures (timeouts, claude-code exit 1) with logic errors, and one trial (e307b25b) references a different task_id path in its result metadata though the trajectory content matches this spreadsheet. Despite 19 trials, no agent combines correct J-order grouping with ITEM renumbering, so we cannot observe a near-miss pass path.
reports.implications_for_future_design: Benchmark authors should either explicitly require ‘renumber ITEM sequentially in output order’ or accept both preserved and renumbered ITEM columns when NAME/REF order is correct. Agents should formalize instructions into an explicit output schema (column F semantics, group ordering algorithm) before coding, and run column-wise diff checks against small synthetic expected tables—not just read-back prints. Harnesses should block task_complete until a lightweight local oracle validates all cells in answer_position, or expose the first failing coordinate in verifier logs. For helper-list sorts, evaluation items should include cases where global source order of J-names differs from J-list order (as here: HAMMED appears before HAMAN in source) to discriminate ‘iterate J’ from ‘filter then append.’ Finally, cap exploratory dumps on large sheets to avoid timeout confounds on otherwise solvable tasks.

reports.tldr: Verdict: medium. All 18 trials scored 0.0 because agents miss hidden SciCode conventions (symbol names `e{j}{i}` without underscores, energy-difference sign opposite to the written ε_{ji}=ε_j−ε_i definition) and a non-obvious piecewise DOS formula in HDF5—not because they cannot code at all. Trajectories show confident self-tests against the wrong physics (standard Blöchl ρ(E)) and premature task completion, which is a generalizable evaluation-discipline failure, but instruction–verifier mismatch and unclear reference physics in regions 1 and 3 prevent a clean high rating.
reports.main_insight: This SciCode task pairs a condensed-matter DOS problem with a verifier that encodes a very specific symbolic contract plus hidden numeric targets. Across models and harnesses, agents produce plausible linear-tetrahedron code from training literature (Blöchl/Lehmann–Taut style piecewise ρ(E), often with `e_{j}{i}` names and ε_j−ε_i differences) but almost none match the HDF5 oracle. Step 17.1 is a pure formatting/convention step: the verifier expects 25 symbols named `e00`…`e44` with values ε_i−ε_j (e.g., for energy=10 and vertices [4,6,8,10], `e01=-6`), while most agents emit `e_01` and ε_j−ε_i. Step 17.2 requires a particular piecewise integral: Monte Carlo barycentric sampling in this sandbox gives ρ(1.5)≈0.125 and ρ(3.6)≈0.078, matching the agents’ textbook formulas, but hidden targets are ≈0.401 and ≈0.257 (~3.2× larger); the middle point E=2.7 is closer (MC≈0.719 vs target≈0.641). Agents therefore fail both domain translation and contract alignment, and many declare success after ad hoc tests that never touch the real bar.
reports.why_it_matters: Scientific-code benchmarks increasingly gate on exact symbolic interfaces and hidden reference data, not just narrative problem statements. This task shows that frontier agents can write runnable, physics-flavored code yet still score zero when (a) naming/sign conventions are underspecified relative to the verifier, and (b) no in-environment oracle exists. For benchmark designers, it argues for publishing interface invariants; for agent builders, it argues for deriving tests from the stated sub-steps (17.1 symbol map) before trusting literature formulas, and for treating ‘integration’ vs ‘DOS ρ(E)’ vs ‘occupation n(E)’ as distinct quantities—several trajectories implement cubic n(E) instead of ρ(E).
reports.evidence_from_trajectories: Universal outcome: meta.json lists 18/18 trials with binary_reward 0. Representative failures: (1) claude-opus-4-7 / terminus-2 (trial 0e684aa4, steps 2–4) writes `/app/solution.py` with `f"e_{j}{i}"` and standard 3·(E−e₁)²/(e₂₁e₃₁e₄₁) ρ formulas, runs a self-test on unrelated vertices, then calls `mark_task_complete` twice—verifier still 0.0. (2) gemini-3.1-pro-preview / terminus-2 (4a53bdc2, steps ~297–401) oscillates between 1/2 and 3 coefficients, greps the container for hidden tests (only finds its own `/app/solution.py`), and never fixes symbol names. (3) gpt-5.5 / codex (9e8f2ca9, steps 7–9) patches the middle-energy band but keeps `e_{j}{i}` naming. (4) glm-5.1 / terminus-2 (7eff50a4, steps 2–3) first writes `init_eji_array` with `e_{j}{i}`, then appends `integrate_DOS` using cubic (E−e₁)³ and cumulative-style middle band—explicit n(E) confusion. (5) MiniMax-M2.7 (ea7a2f1c, steps 4–5) self-tests expecting values up to 1.0 at E≥e₃, treating the result as a cumulative weight. (6) Three trials (6382cb1f, 84963d7a, f208734a) hit AgentTimeoutError at 1800s before reliable submission. Replaying extracted terminus solutions against `/insight/task/tests/test_data.h5` in this sandbox: typical ‘good faith’ code passes 0/3 tests on 17.1 and at most 2/5 on 17.2 (only out-of-band energies E=5 and E=0.9). A convention-correct `init_eji_array` (names `e{j}{i}`, values e[i]−e[j]) passes all three 17.1 tests here, proving step 1 is solvable but was missed by every submitted agent.
reports.surface_failure_vs_root_cause: Surface: reward 0.0 on both sub-steps for every model/harness. Root cause is layered: (A) Interface mismatch on 17.1—underscore symbol names and ε_j−ε_i vs verifier’s `eji` strings and ε_i−ε_j (instruction text says ε_{ji}=ε_j−ε_i, which contradicts the hidden values). (B) Physics/reference mismatch on 17.2—agents implement widely cited Blöchl piecewise ρ(E) (e.g., opus step 2 gives integrate_DOS(1.5,[1,2,3,4])=0.125) while HDF5 expects different numeric answers in the interior bands (~3.2× higher in the low and high bands; ~10% lower in the middle band vs the same textbook middle formula). (C) Workflow failure—agents rely on hand-rolled sanity checks, not the sub-step contract or hidden tests, then exit early (opus steps 3–4). Timeouts are a secondary surface failure for 3/18 trials, not the dominant pattern.
reports.intended_vs_unexpected_insight: Intended capability: domain-specific scientific/numerical coding—linear tetrahedron DOS with sympy scaffolding and piecewise barycentric logic. Agents do engage that intent (most trajectories derive tetrahedron formulas and sort vertices) but fail the tested capability because the verifier measures an exact symbolic/numeric fingerprint, not ‘reasonable DOS code.’ Unexpected but valuable bottlenecks: (1) hidden-spec alignment outweighs raw physics recall; (2) false verification confidence—agents treat literature-derived spot checks as ground truth; (3) quantity confusion (ρ vs n) in several trajectories; (4) possible benchmark inconsistency between energy regions (uniform scaling of standard ρ cannot fit all three interior HDF5 points). The task therefore teaches more about evaluation design and contract clarity than about a single missing primitive skill.
reports.generalizability: Partially generalizable. Lessons that transfer: validate against provided sub-step tests and explicit I/O schemas; treat symbol naming, index order, and sign conventions as first-class requirements in symbolic/scientific code; do not equate famous formulas with the benchmark’s hidden reference; separate ρ(E), n(E), and raw tetrahedron volume weights. These apply across SciCode, CodePDE-like suites, and numeric library bindings. Less generalizable: the exact DOS normalization (~3.2× in outer bands) appears specific to this hidden reference unless documented—improving it alone would not fix agents on other physics tasks. Fixing underscore vs `eji` naming would help any sympy-dict benchmark with strict string keys.
reports.confounds: Instruction–verifier conflict on ε_{ji} definition vs stored values reduces interpretability of ‘domain knowledge’ failures. No public reference solution (`solution/solve.sh` is a stub). Hidden tests live only in `test_data.h5`, so agents cannot calibrate—filesystem greps (gemini 4a53bdc2) cannot find them. Interior 17.2 targets disagree with standard Blöchl ρ and with Monte Carlo barycentric estimates in this sandbox (~0.125 vs 0.401 at E=1.5), suggesting either a non-documented normalization or verifier idiosyncrasy—reviewers could disagree on the ‘correct’ physics. Trajectory extraction is uneven (claude-code/codex often omit heredocs from simple regex), but the 0/18 official reward and direct HDF5 replay of terminus-style solutions are sufficient. Three timeout exceptions are harness budget noise, not the core signal.
