GPT-5.5 terminus/codex trajectories look like clean algorithmic wins (sample 9, randomized brute-force pass, O(N²) rook/DP), yet still scored 0—so the aggregate 0/18 pass rate overstates capability gaps and confounds evaluation.
reports.main_insight: This task–trajectory set primarily tests whether an agent can (1) derive the correct combinatorial characterization of “maximal” matchings in a threshold bipartite graph, (2) implement an O(N²) counting DP (rook-polynomial / event-sweep style, as in the reference solution), and (3) deliver a runnable artifact under a 600s agent budget. Across 18 trials, every recorded reward is 0, but the failure modes are heterogeneous: most trials never finish reasoning (AgentTimeoutError on the first or early LLM call), several that do write code use a wrong invariant (count all matchings or a flawed two-phase DP), and the three harness-completed trials include at least one that never persisted solution.py to disk. The strongest signal is not “models cannot code USACO” but a mixture of time-budget blowups, invariant mis-specification, weak self-testing, and likely grading/persistence noise for otherwise-correct submissions.
reports.why_it_matters: USACO-style tasks are common in agent benchmarks, yet this slice shows that raw pass rate can mislead: long reasoning timeouts dominate the denominator, and a correct trajectory can still register as failure. For benchmark designers, that implies separating (a) algorithmic correctness, (b) artifact delivery, and (c) wall-clock/step budgeting. For agent builders, the recurring wrong DP (MiniMax terminus step 2–3) shows that restating “maximal” in prose is insufficient without encoding the blocking constraint into the state machine—an error that will recur on matching, scheduling, and feasibility-counting tasks beyond barns and cows.
reports.evidence_from_trajectories: Harness outcomes: meta.json shows 18/18 binary_reward 0; result.json lists AgentTimeoutError for 15 trials (e.g., claude-opus-4-7 terminus trial 21bb6bdb times out during _query_llm with 0 output tokens; deepseek/claude-code/qwen trials show the same pattern). MiniMax terminus (186d92bb) writes a standard dp[i][j] “skip barn / match cow” program at step 2, runs the sample at step 3, and prints 1 instead of 9—demonstrating it counts general matchings, not maximal ones. Gemini terminus (ec2203bb) implements an event-sweep two-phase DP at step 2, runs the official sample, prints 4 at step 2 observation, then hits JSON parse errors at steps 3–4 and ultimately AgentTimeoutError—wrong sample yet near-completion. GPT-5.5 terminus (59b122ba) at step 2 writes a long O(N²) grouped DP, gets 9 on the sample, builds /tmp/verify.py at step 3, sees “all randomized brute-force tests passed,” and marks task_complete at steps 4–5; GPT-5.5 codex (c2ab6c01) similarly implements rook-polynomial DP (step 9), reports sample 9, brute-force checks, and ~2.92s on a max-N smoke test (step 23). Gemini-cli (167aee96) completes in 2 steps with ~34k output tokens but only embeds Python in the assistant message—no shell write—so the intended deliverable likely never existed for the verifier. Replaying extracted GPT-5.5 code from trajectories against all 20 files in tests/data passes every case in this sandbox, highlighting a mismatch between trajectory quality and recorded reward.
reports.surface_failure_vs_root_cause: Surface: 0/18 reward, often no passing pytest/USACO batch judge. Deeper causes cluster into four buckets: (1) agent timeout while thinking or waiting on the model (15 trials)—failure is budget/harness pacing, not proven inability to solve; (2) wrong mathematical object counted—e.g., MiniMax’s dp treats any partial matching, not matchings where no unmatched cow fits an empty barn; (3) insufficient or ignored validation—Gemini prints 4 on the official sample yet proceeds toward completion; GPT-5.5’s brute-force checker only randomizes tiny N≤6 with values in 1..5, which can miss bugs even though their final code appears correct here; (4) delivery/evaluation gaps—gemini-cli never writes /app/solution.py; GPT-5.5 trajectories contain fully passing programs yet scored 0, suggesting artifact capture or judge-environment divergence rather than algorithmic wrongness.
reports.intended_vs_unexpected_insight: Intended: hard competitive-programming / combinatorial DP for maximal matchings (reference solve.sh uses an O(N²) event DP over sorted cow/barn sizes). Agents mostly failed that bar in the logged scores, but the trajectories also reveal unintended bottlenecks: AgentTimeoutError during single LLM calls (often before meaningful terminal work), and benchmark false negatives when sophisticated solutions likely satisfied all 20 hidden tests. The most instruction-aligned misses are invariant errors (maximal vs arbitrary matchings) and not saving solution.py; the most evaluation-distorting miss is conflating reasoning latency with coding inability.
reports.generalizability: Partially generalizable. Mis-identifying problem invariants (here, “maximal”) transfers to other matching, flow, and feasibility-counting tasks. Poor time-budget stewardship—burning the full 600s agent timeout in one reasoning episode—applies broadly to tool-using agents on hard single-shot math/CP prompts. Weak custom testers (tiny N, narrow value ranges) generalize as a failure mode for any algorithmic task. Less generalizable are USACO-specific tricks (rook polynomials, Ferrers boards) and the apparent GPT-5.5 grading mismatch, which is benchmark-ops specific. Improving invariant formalization and validation discipline would help many tasks; mastering this exact DP helps mainly CP-heavy suites.
reports.confounds: Agent timeout_sec is 600 while the prompt says “solve in 10 minutes,” and many trials expire inside the LLM client (not Python TLE). Fifteen timeout exceptions make the 0% pass rate an upper bound on failure, not a clean capability measure. GPT-5.5 terminus and codex trajectories contain code that passes all 20 official .in/.out pairs when re-run here, yet harbor recorded reward 0—strong evidence of artifact persistence, environment teardown, or judge-path issues. Gemini-cli’s completion without a write tool call means the verifier’s test_solution_exists would fail regardless of code quality. Trajectories for timed-out runs often end after one step with solution.py mentioned only in planning text, so we cannot always observe the would-have-been submission. Finally, self-built brute-force checks can pass while hidden tests fail; here they coincided with true positives for GPT-5.5 but are not a substitute for the official suite.
reports.implications_for_future_design: Split metrics: reasoning latency, artifact written (solution.py exists), sample test, and full USACO batch. Cap per-turn reasoning or require an early scaffold write (template solution.py) before allowing long analysis. For maximal-matching-style tasks, add a minimal second sample or property test that distinguishes maximal from all matchings (would have caught MiniMax’s 1-vs-9 error immediately). Require harnesses to log judge stderr/result_type per test, not only binary reward, and snapshot /app/solution.py post-agent. Consider shorter agent timeouts with explicit mid-run checkpoints rather than one 600s wall clock vulnerable to a single slow completion. For insight harvesting, tag CP tasks with the target skill (invariant identification vs implementation vs complexity) so timeouts can be classified separately from wrong algorithms in aggregate dashboards.
